**Habeas corpus** (produce the body), **mandamus** (perform the public duty), **prohibition** (stop exceeding jurisdiction, before), **certiorari** (quash, after), **quo warranto** (by what authority do you hold this office). **Article 32** against the Supreme Court, **Article 226** — wider — against a High Court.

**Signature argument.** Courts wrote the administrative reform legislatures would not: **Vineet Narain (1997)** gave the **CVC** statutory footing and single-directive protection; **Prakash Singh (2006)** ordered **seven police reforms**; **T.S.R. Subramanian (2013)** ordered a **Civil Services Board**, **minimum tenure** and **written orders**.

Courts act **only when moved**, decide **the case not the system**, cannot supply **funds or personnel**, and are themselves **overloaded** — about **4.76 crore cases pending (NJDG, 2026)**. And every reform they order depends on an executive **willing to comply**; **Prakash Singh compliance has been nominal for nineteen years**.

items.t: The judiciary mandating rather than restraining
items.d: Review has moved from **negative** (striking down) to **positive** (directing what must be done) — continuing mandamus, guidelines with the force of law under **Article 141**, monitored implementation. **Vishaka (1997)** legislated in the legislature's silence.

The **Presidential Reference opinion (November 2025)** declined to impose **judicially fixed timelines on the Governor's assent** under **Articles 200 and 201**, unsettling the earlier **State of Tamil Nadu** approach. It is a deliberate step back toward **political and cooperative-federal remedies** — which raises whether the **Inter-State Council** can be revived.

India has **separation of functions**, not of personnel — the executive sits in the legislature. The balance is carried instead by **judicial review**, the **basic structure doctrine**, **independent constitutional offices** (CAG, EC, UPSC), and **federal division**. Say that, rather than reciting Montesquieu.

**Section 2(h)** public authority; **Section 4** **suo motu** disclosure — the section that would make most applications unnecessary; **Section 6** the application, no reasons required; **Section 7** thirty days, **48 hours** where life or liberty is involved; **Section 8** exemptions; **Section 19** appeals; **Section 20** penalty up to **₹25,000**.

Not from Parliament first. **MKSS** in **Rajasthan** ran **jan sunwais** from 1990 demanding muster rolls and bills; **Tamil Nadu (1997)** and eight other states legislated before the Centre; the **Freedom of Information Act, 2002** was never notified; the **RTI Act, 2005** followed the **NCPRI** campaign.

**Over 4 lakh appeals and complaints pending** across information commissions; **seven commissions non-functional** at points in 2024-25, **Jharkhand's defunct since May 2020**; penalties imposed in about **3% of disposed cases**; several State Commissions would take **four to five years** to reach a fresh appeal.

**RTI (Amendment) Act, 2019** moved the **tenure, salary and service conditions** of Information Commissioners from **statute to executive rules** — the independence that came from a fixed five-year term is now at the government's discretion. **Vacancies** do the rest without any amendment at all.

The **live 2026 issue.** **Section 44(3) of the DPDP Act, 2023** rewrites **RTI's Section 8(1)(j)** to exempt **all personal information** without the earlier **public-interest override**. Critics say it removes the basis for **beneficiary lists, muster rolls and officials' asset disclosures** — the very records RTI was built for.

items.t: Protecting the user, not just the right
items.d: The unfinished agenda: no working protection for **RTI activists**, with dozens killed since 2005. The **Whistle Blowers Protection Act, 2014** was passed and **never brought into force**; its 2015 amendment bill would have **narrowed** it to exclude disclosures touching Section 8(1) categories.

The highest-value reform is the cheapest: **enforce suo motu disclosure**. If **budgets, beneficiary lists, works, inspection reports and file notings** were published as a matter of course, most applications would not be filed, and the **backlog problem would shrink at its source**.

**Formalism** — the gap between the **prescriptive** and the **descriptive**. The Act is world-class on paper; **Section 4 compliance** is patchy, **penalties** near-notional, **commissions** unstaffed. India legislates the **norm** and under-supplies the **institution** — the single most reusable Paper II sentence.

**e-Procurement through GeM and CPP Portal**; **PFMS** tracing every rupee to the beneficiary; **faceless assessment** removing the officer-taxpayer interface; **open data on data.gov.in** and NITI's **National Data and Analytics Platform**. Transparency by **design** now outperforms transparency by **request**.

groups.g: Social audit and the citizen interface

items.d: Verification of a public work or scheme **by the community that received it**, using **official records read aloud in a public assembly**, with **findings recorded and acted upon**. It converts accountability from an **audit trail** into a **face-to-face account**.

**Section 17 of MGNREGA** makes the **Gram Sabha** the audit authority; the **MGNREGA Audit of Schemes Rules, 2011** require **independent Social Audit Units**; **Meghalaya's Community Participation and Public Services Social Audit Act, 2017** is the first **general** social audit law in India.

items.t: Why social audit works where audit does not
items.d: It reaches the **only fact that matters** — did the work happen and did the wage arrive — which no ledger can verify from a state capital. It is **timely**, **local**, and **hard to capture** where the assembly is genuinely open.

**SAUs are funded by the department they audit**; **elite capture** silences the assembly; **findings are recorded and not acted on**; and coverage outside MGNREGA is thin. Andhra Pradesh's SSAAT is the working model precisely because it has **separate funding and trained village social auditors**.

groups.g: Media, interest groups and civil society

items.d: **Agenda-setting** (what the public thinks about), **watchdog** (exposure), and **forum** (deliberation). Its comparative advantage over formal control is **speed and reach**; its weakness is that it is **episodic** and pursues the **spectacular** over the **structural**.

The pressures: **ownership concentration**, **advertising dependence including government advertising**, **paid news and the Press Council's own findings**, **defamation and sedition-adjacent charges**, and **regulatory leverage over broadcasters**.

items.t: From institutional lens to societal lens
items.d: Media once trained its attention on **institutions** — the file, the tender, the committee. It now largely reflects **society back to itself** — identity, outrage, personality. The shift matters administratively: **institutional failure goes unreported** unless it produces a **visible victim**.

It **lowered the cost of exposure** — a single video can move an administration in hours — and **removed verification**. The administrative consequences are real: **rumour-driven law-and-order incidents**, and the **IT Rules, 2021** fact-check provisions, whose **state-as-arbiter** design the **Bombay High Court** struck down in the **Kunal Kamra** case (2024).

They **elevate** issues onto the agenda and, more consequentially, **deny others the opportunity** — **Bachrach and Baratz's** non-decision-making. In India, **organised** interests (industry associations, employee unions, farmer bodies) are heard; **unorganised** ones (informal workers, tenants) are not.

**MKSS** produced the RTI; **SEWA** organised informal women workers; **Pratham's ASER** created the learning-outcomes debate; **AIDWA and allied groups** shaped the Domestic Violence Act; **Bachpan Bachao Andolan** on child labour. Name organisations, not 'NGOs'.

items.t: When civil society restricts rather than assists
items.d: Genuine tensions: **litigation delaying** infrastructure; **unrepresentative** office-bearers claiming to speak for communities; **donor agendas** displacing local priorities; and **accountability of the accountability-seeker** — most NGOs publish less than the departments they audit.

CSO effectiveness is a **function of state structure**: statutory entry points make CSOs productive — **Gram Sabha, social audit, pre-legislative consultation, PIL, the Forest Rights Act's gram sabha consent**. Where entry points are absent, CSOs are pushed to **protest and litigation**, which the state then reads as obstruction.

The **powers, procedures and liabilities of administrative authorities**, and the **remedies** available against them. **Wade** — it is "the law relating to the **control of governmental power**". Its subject is not what the state does but **on what terms it may do it**.

The **welfare and regulatory state**. Legislatures cannot foresee every case, so they delegate; administration acquires **rule-making and adjudicatory** power; and the citizen needs a body of law governing that power. administrative law evolved from the need for **a system of public administration under law**.

**A.V. Dicey (1885)** claimed England had **no administrative law** — his **rule of law** required (i) **supremacy of regular law** over arbitrary power, (ii) **equality before the ordinary law** for officials and citizens alike, and (iii) rights derived from **judicial decisions**, not a written charter.

He mistook the French **droit administratif** for **official privilege**; the **Conseil d'État** was in fact a robust check. And England already had **statutory tribunals and discretionary powers**. **Robson, Jennings and Wade** established that administrative law exists **wherever administrative power exists**.

India's Constitution **rejects Dicey's second proposition outright**: **Article 361** immunity for President and Governors, **Article 311** protection for civil servants, and **Article 300** state liability rules all treat officials differently. Yet **Article 14** delivers his substance — **arbitrariness is itself unconstitutional**.

items.t: Red light and green light theories
items.d: **Red light** (Dicey, Hewart) — administrative law exists to **control and restrain** the state; courts are the guardians. **Green light** (Robson, Griffith) — the state is a **force for good**; administrative law should **facilitate** effective administration and improve it from within.

**Harlow and Rawlings'** synthesis of red and green light: neither pure control nor pure facilitation. Courts intervene where **rights and procedure** are at stake and defer where **polycentric policy judgement** is involved. India is an amber-light system — **Wednesbury deference** on policy, **strict scrutiny** on liberty and procedure.

items.t: The rule of law and arbitrariness
items.d: **E.P. Royappa (1974)** — "equality is antithetic to **arbitrariness**"; arbitrary state action violates **Article 14** without more. **Maneka Gandhi (1978)** made procedure **fair, just and reasonable**. Arbitrariness in the application of law is not merely bad governance — it is **unconstitutional**.

items.t: What it is and why it exists
items.d: Rules, regulations, bye-laws and notifications made by the **executive under authority conferred by a statute**. Justified by **pressure on legislative time**, **technicality**, **flexibility to amend without an Act**, **local variation**, and the need to act in **emergency**.

**Essential legislative function cannot be delegated.** The legislature must itself lay down the **policy** and the **standard**; only the **filling in of detail** may be delegated. **In re Delhi Laws Act (1951)** settled this; **Hamdard Dawakhana (1960)** struck down delegation without a guiding standard.

**Skeleton legislation** that leaves everything to rules; **Henry VIII clauses** allowing the executive to modify the parent Act; **sub-delegation**; **retrospective** rules; **inadequate publication**; and rules made **years after** the Act, or not at all — a statute in force with no machinery.

items.t: 'A strategic tool in the hands of the executive'
items.d: The strategic use is real: the **substance** of a policy can be shifted into **rules** that never face a vote, changed by **notification**, and enforced before Parliament examines them. asked how to confine it — the answer is the three controls below.

**Laying** on the table — simple, negative (annulment within **30 days**) or affirmative resolution; the **Committee on Subordinate Legislation** in each House (**15 members**), which examines whether rules are **within the power conferred**; and scrutiny during passage of the **enabling clause** itself.

Rules may be struck as **substantively ultra vires** (beyond the parent Act, or the parent Act itself unconstitutional) or **procedurally ultra vires** (mandatory consultation or publication omitted). Courts also apply **unreasonableness** and, increasingly, **manifest arbitrariness** under Article 14.

**Prior publication and public consultation** — the **Pre-Legislative Consultation Policy, 2014** requires draft rules to be placed for **30 days**, and is honoured inconsistently. Add **mandatory laying**, a **time limit for framing rules**, and **regulatory impact assessment**, which the **FSLRC** recommended.

Without it, **technical standards** (drug schedules, emission norms, spectrum), **rates** (tariffs, duties), and **crisis response** would each require an Act. The remedy for its abuse is **scrutiny**, not abolition — no modern state can legislate every detail in primary law.

Discretion is controlled at **three points**: at **conferment** (a guiding standard in the statute), at **exercise** (relevant considerations, no mala fides, no fettering by rigid rules, no non-application of mind), and **after** (reasons recorded, appeal, judicial review). **Recording reasons** is the cheapest and most effective of the three.

**Speed**, **low cost**, **expertise**, **flexible procedure** free of the Evidence Act, and relief of the **court backlog**. the welfare state generates disputes of **volume and technicality** that ordinary courts are structurally unsuited to handle.

**Articles 323A and 323B**, inserted by the **42nd Amendment (1976)**. **323A** — Parliament may create tribunals for **public service matters** (hence the **Administrative Tribunals Act, 1985**, and the **CAT**). **323B** — legislatures may create them for **specified subjects** including taxation, land reform and elections.

**L. Chandra Kumar v. Union of India (1997)** — **judicial review under Articles 226 and 32 is basic structure** and cannot be excluded. Tribunals are **supplemental**, not substitutional; their orders are subject to **High Court division-bench review**. This is the single most quotable tribunal case.

**Appointments dominated by the executive** — which is often the **litigant**; **short tenures** breeding dependence; **administrative members** without judicial training; **vacancies** paralysing benches; and the **Chandra Kumar** appeal route reintroducing the delay tribunals were meant to remove.

**R.K. Jain**, **Chandra Kumar (1997)**, **Madras Bar Association (2014 and 2021)** — striking down provisions on **tenure, qualification and the selection committee's composition**. **Rojer Mathew (2019)** required a **National Tribunals Commission**; the **Tribunals Reforms Act, 2021** re-enacted provisions the Court had already struck down.

An independent **National Tribunals Commission** for appointment, funding and oversight — recommended by the Supreme Court and by the **2nd ARC**. Plus **uniform service conditions**, **fixed longer tenure**, a **single nodal ministry** rather than each tribunal under the department it adjudicates against.

items.t: Is administrative law now more constitutional than the Constitution?
items.d: In one sense yes: **Article 14 and 21 jurisprudence** — **Kraipak**, **Royappa**, **Maneka** — has made administrative fairness a **constitutional** requirement, so the ordinary citizen's daily encounter with the state is governed by **constitutional standards** rather than statute alone.

**Nemo judex in causa sua** — no one a judge in his own cause (bias: pecuniary, personal, official, policy). **Audi alteram partem** — hear the other side (notice, disclosure of material, opportunity to be heard, reasoned order). **A.K. Kraipak (1969)** extended both from **quasi-judicial to administrative** action.

groups.g: Ombudsman, Lokpal and the grievance remedy

items.d: A **parliamentary officer**, independent of the executive, empowered to **investigate maladministration** on complaint or *suo motu*, reporting to the legislature. Originating in **Sweden (1809)**; **Denmark (1955)** made it the modern export model.

The **Crossman catalogue** — "bias, neglect, inattention, delay, incompetence, ineptitude, perversity, turpitude, arbitrariness". It is broader than **illegality**: an act may be perfectly lawful and still be maladministration, which is exactly the gap courts cannot fill.

**ARC-I (1966)** proposed **Lokpal** (ministers and secretaries) and **Lokayukta** (other officials). Bills failed **eight times** between 1968 and 2011. The **Lokpal and Lokayuktas Act, 2013** followed mass mobilisation; the **chairperson was appointed in March 2019**, six years after enactment.

It has **no independent investigative machinery at scale**, depending on **CBI and CVC**; a **preliminary inquiry** stage that leaks; **prior sanction** requirements; and, critically, jurisdiction over **corruption** rather than **maladministration** — so the ordinary citizen's grievance is not its business at all.

**Maharashtra first (1971)**; **Karnataka's** Lokayukta was the strongest, with its own police wing and suo motu powers, and produced consequential reports. Most others have **no investigative wing**, **no suo motu power**, and **recommendatory** findings addressed to the very government complained against.

Its **12th Report** proposed **local grievance redress with a designated officer and a time limit**, escalation to an **independent** authority, and **compensation for failure of service** — the missing consequence. Grievance redress in India ends with a **reply**, not a **remedy**.

The **RBI's Integrated Ombudsman Scheme (2021)** — one scheme, one portal, free, binding awards with compensation; the **Insurance Ombudsman**; the **Banking Codes** standards. They work because they are **funded by the sector, decide within a time limit, and their awards bind**.

**Post-war decolonisation** and **US technical assistance**: American models transplanted into new states **did not work**, and nobody could say why. The **Comparative Administration Group (CAG, 1960-71)**, chaired by **Fred Riggs** and funded by the **Ford Foundation**, was built to find out.

**'The Science of Public Administration: Three Problems' (1947)** — a science of administration cannot exist until it confronts **values**, **human behaviour** and above all **cross-national transferability**: principles derived from one **social setting** cannot be assumed to hold in another.

**Ferrel Heady** — CPA exists for **theory building** (a general theory of administration), for **improved administrative technology** (what transfers and what does not), and out of **intellectual curiosity** about how other systems work. Most CPA delivered the second and failed at the first.

CPA moved from **normative to empirical** (from what administration ought to be to what it is), from **ideographic to nomothetic** (from single-case description to generalisation), and from **non-ecological to ecological** (from studying administration alone to studying it inside its environment).

Its **elitist and west-centric orientation** treated the Western system as the endpoint; it built **typologies rather than testable theory**; it was **funding-dependent** and collapsed when Ford withdrew in **1971**; and its concepts were **descriptive, not predictive** — they named the disease without prescribing.

items.t: 'It started with no paradigm and developed none'
items.d: CPA produced **no paradigm** but delivered a **durable analytical vocabulary** — formalism, overlapping, heterogeneity, ecology, prismatic — that every subsequent development literature uses without acknowledgment.

New objective, new orientation: the driver became **NPM diffusion** and **World Bank governance conditionality**; the method became **quantitative and index-based** — **WGI, Doing Business, Government Effectiveness**; and the object shifted from **bureaucracy** to **governance and institutional quality**.

The evolution: **institutional** description (structures) → **behavioural** comparison → **ecological** analysis → **political-economy** approaches asking who benefits and which coalition sustains the arrangement. The last has explanatory power the earlier ones lacked, but still no **general theory**.

items.t: NPM and ICT as comparative forces
items.d: Both create **convergence pressure**: NPM through **donor conditionality and policy transfer**, ICT through **shared platforms and international standards**. Both also expose **divergence** — the same e-governance tool produces different outcomes in different **ecologies**, which is Riggs's point restated.

Administration is **shaped by, and shapes, its environment** — economic, social, political, communication and symbolic. **John Gaus (1947)** listed the ecological factors: **people, place, physical technology, social technology, wishes and ideas, catastrophe, personality**.

items.t: Why it matters for developing countries
items.d: It explains **why a well-designed reform fails**: the design assumed a literacy level, a banking density, a caste-neutral village, a functioning land record — and the ecology did not supply it.

The two **ideal-type** poles. **Agraria** — **ascriptive** status, **particularistic** relations, **diffuse** roles, subsistence economy, few specialised structures. **Industria** — **achievement**-based, **universalistic**, **specific** roles, market economy, highly differentiated structures. Neither exists in pure form.

items.t: Why Riggs abandoned the two-pole model
items.d: Real transitional societies were not simply 'between' the two — they showed **both simultaneously**, and the mix was **stable rather than transitional**. That failure produced the **prismatic** model, which is the reason it exists.

items.t: Industria as a precursor to post-modern administration
items.d: Industria's features — **high differentiation, universalism, interdependence, a market-permeated society** — anticipate the **networked, contracted-out, interdependent** state that post-modern public administration describes. The interdependent economy is Industria's defining trait, not merely its technology.

The **specific factors** to name: **caste and kinship** cutting across formal roles; **linguistic federalism**; **agrarian dependence** in most districts; **electoral competition at four levels**; **judicial activism**; and a **legal-rational structure inherited before the society that would sustain it had formed**.

items.t: Social and historical factors shaping administration
items.d: Three forces shape it: the **colonial inheritance** (a revenue-and-order state, generalist-led); the **freedom struggle's** normative legacy (welfare obligation, DPSPs); and the **social structure** (hierarchy, plurality, patronage) into which both were placed. Design that ignores any one of the three fails.

It can slide into **determinism** and into **excuse** — if the ecology explains everything, no administrator is responsible for anything. The corrective is that administration **also shapes** its ecology: **RTI, panchayats, DBT and universal schooling** changed the very environment that constrained them.

**Fused** society = white light entering (agraria, undifferentiated). **Prismatic** = light inside the prism, **diffracting but not yet separated**. **Diffracted** = the emerging spectrum (industria, highly specialised). The **transitional** society sits **inside** the prism — and Riggs's claim is that this is a **stable condition**, not a way-station.

The **gap between the prescriptive and the descriptive** — between what the law says and what actually happens. Not simple non-compliance: the **form is maintained** while the substance is absent, and everybody knows it. **India's single most usable diagnostic term.**

**RTI Section 4** disclosure mandated and patchily done; **Citizen's Charters** without remedies; **State Finance Commissions** constituted years late; **District Planning Committees** that exist but do not plan; **penalties imposed in about 3% of disposed RTI cases**. The form is impeccable; the substance is absent.

The **simultaneous presence of different systems, practices and viewpoints** in one society. A district holds a **software park and bonded labour**, a **faceless tax assessment and a patwari's field book**. Administration must operate on all of them **with one set of rules**.

**Formal structures exist but are dominated by informal ones.** The formal panchayat decision passes through the **caste or khap** reality; the formal transfer procedure passes through the **recommendation letter**. The structure is **differentiated on paper and fused in operation**.

The prismatic society's **administrative sub-system** — a **sala** is neither the **chamber** of fused society nor the **bureau** of diffracted society. Its officials wield **power based on personal and family standing** as much as office, and **nepotism and poly-communalism** coexist with formal merit rules.

The prismatic **economy**: prices are **not fixed by the market** but by the **relationship between the parties**. The same service costs differently depending on who asks. Its administrative form is the **speed money** economy — a payment that buys **priority in a queue**, not an illegal outcome.

**Poly-normativism** — **several conflicting norms** operate at once, so nobody can say which rule truly governs. **Poly-communalism** — **multiple communities** whose members treat each other by different standards, producing a **dominant community** occupying the bureaucracy and 'pariah' communities excluded from it.

**Attainment norms** (achievement rhetoric with ascriptive practice); **motility** (movement without change of status); **price indeterminacy**; **clects** (associations using modern form for traditional ends — a caste association registered as a trust); and a **strong intellectual output with weak institutional capacity**.

One box, three zones: **Fused (agraria)** → **Prismatic** → **Diffracted (industria)**, with **formalism, heterogeneity and overlapping** labelled **inside** the prismatic zone, and one **Indian instance** written under each. Forty-five seconds; it earns the presentation mark because it **compresses** a paragraph.

**Excessively gloomy** — the model has no route out of the prism; **technically complex** — the neologisms obscure rather than explain; **ideal-typical and untestable**; **Western-normative** — diffraction is treated as the goal; and **static** — it does not explain **change**, only describes a condition.

**Ramesh K. Arora** — the model is **not operationalisable**: it cannot be measured, so it cannot be tested. **Ralph Braibanti** — it **under-weights the positive** capacity of transitional bureaucracies, which in India delivered **elections, famine prevention, green revolution and universal immunisation**.

items.t: Why Riggs remains a useful starting point
items.d: It supplies the **only vocabulary** that names the specific pathology of a state with **modern law and traditional society**; and its diagnosis is **empirically visible** in devolution indices, RTI compliance and scheme leakage. A weak theory with strong descriptive purchase.

**Formalism** now appears as **digital formalism** — a portal that exists and is not used, a dashboard green while delivery fails. **Overlapping** as **elite capture of digital access**. **Heterogeneity** as the **digital divide**. The concepts survived; the terrain changed.

The recurring challenges: **weak political control combined with political interference**; **generalist dominance** over technical work; **capacity and vacancy deficits**; **procedural risk aversion**; **corruption at the interface**; and **weak coordination** across a proliferation of agencies.

**Evans's embedded autonomy**; **Weberianness** — Evans and Rauch found **meritocratic recruitment and predictable careers** statistically associated with growth; a **pilot agency** with authority (Japan's MITI, Korea's EPB); and **performance discipline** on the firms it supports. India had this in **space and atomic energy**, not in industrial licensing.

Three contrasting configurations worth naming: **Britain** — parliamentary, generalist, ministerial responsibility, no separate administrative court. **France** — statist, **grands corps** trained at ENA/INSP, a distinct **droit administratif** under the **Conseil d'État**. **USA** — separated powers, **spoils-to-merit** history, **political appointees** to several thousand senior posts.

items.t: The French minister and party leadership
items.d: The French Constitution does **not** bar a minister from leading a party; the **convention** that they should not exists to protect the **impartiality of the administration** they head. **Conventions**, not text alone, carry administrative neutrality.

**Growth** is an increase in output; **development** is a change in **capabilities, distribution and institutions**. **Dudley Seers'** test — ask what has happened to **poverty, unemployment and inequality**; if all three have worsened, this has not been development even if income per head rose.

"**Development can be seen as a process of expanding the real freedoms that people enjoy.**" The measure is not **income** or even **utility** but **capability** — what a person is actually able to **do and be**. Income is a means; **agency** is the end.

**NITI Aayog's National Multidimensional Poverty Index** — health, education and standard of living, on the **Alkire-Foster** method. **Headcount fell from 29.17% (2013-14) to 11.28% (2022-23)**, about **24.8 crore** people out of multidimensional poverty. **NFSA, RTE and PM-JAY** are capability instruments, not income transfers.

**Mahbub ul Haq** with **Sen** — **UNDP Human Development Report, 1990**. "People are the real wealth of a nation." The HDI's power is **political, not analytical**: three simple indicators forced governments to be compared on something other than **GDP**.

**Brundtland (Our Common Future, 1987)** — meeting present needs "**without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own**". The **SDGs (2015-2030)** turn it into **17 goals and 169 targets**; India's national tracking is **NITI's SDG India Index**, which also drives **competitive federalism** among states.

**Robert Chambers** — "**putting the last first**". Outsiders' biases (**tarmac, dry-season, project, person, diplomatic**) systematically hide rural poverty from those who plan for it. The method is **Participatory Rural Appraisal**, and its administrative form in India is the **Gram Sabha's approval of the plan**.

The **concept** of development is inherently **participatory** — it is about people's own expansion of freedom. The **practice** has been **exclusionary** — expert-driven, displacement-generating, capital-intensive. That contradiction, not any implementation failure, is what makes it a **dilemma**.

items.t: SDGs depend on actors' willingness to cooperate
items.d: SDG delivery is a **horizontal coordination** problem: no single ministry owns a goal, most targets are on the **State list**, and **local bodies** must execute. India's coordination instruments — **NITI's SDG index, state SDG cells, the localisation of SDGs through panchayat theme-based plans** — are exhortation without authority.

Administration oriented to **planned change** rather than order maintenance: **goal-oriented, change-oriented, client-oriented, innovative, temporally committed** and **participative**. **Weidner** — administration directed toward **progressive political, economic and social objectives**.

**Development administration** (administration **of** development — delivering programmes) and the **administration of development** in its second sense, **administrative development** (building the **capacity** to deliver). The two are **mutually reinforcing** and India has consistently invested in the first while starving the second.

Development administration needs **flexibility, risk-taking and speed**; **general administration** needs **rule-adherence, uniformity and caution**. The **same officer** carries both roles — the Collector who must both **innovate** and **not deviate from the GFR**.

items.t: Weidner on output versus system change
items.d: Change in **output** (more roads, more enrolment) is not change in the **system** that produces it. And "**growth from one point of view may be decline from another**" — an irrigation project that raises yields and destroys a commons.

Four phases: **1950s-60s** state-led, plan-driven, community development; **1970s-80s** target-group programmes and poverty alleviation; **1990s** market-oriented, minimal state, structural adjustment; **2000s onwards** rights-based delivery, then **mission-based, digitally-mediated, outcome-tracked** administration.

items.t: Rights-based to mission-based — the signature argument
items.d: **RTI (2005), NREGA (2005), FRA (2006), RTE (2009), NFSA (2013)** created **justiciable entitlements** with an aggrieved citizen able to sue. **Missions** — Karmayogi, Aspirational Blocks, Jal Jeevan, VB-G RAM G — deliver by **target and dashboard** and create **no enforceable claim**. Speed rose; **standing fell**.

groups.g: The anti-development thesis and the state–market debate

items.d: Its claim is **epistemological**, not managerial: development is a **discourse** invented after 1945 that reconstituted two-thirds of the world as **'underdeveloped'** and made Western modernity the only imaginable destination. **Arturo Escobar, Encountering Development (1995)**.

**Escobar** — development as a discourse of power. **Wolfgang Sachs (The Development Dictionary)** — "the idea of development stands like a ruin in the intellectual landscape." **Ivan Illich** — institutionalised services **disable** the capacities they claim to serve. **Vandana Shiva** — 'maldevelopment' and the displacement of subsistence.

items.t: It contests epistemology, not merely practice
items.d: The precise formulation the question wants. Ordinary critique says development was **badly done**; the anti-development thesis says the **category itself** is the problem — it converts **difference into deficiency** and makes the expert, not the community, the authority on what a good life is.

items.t: The counter to the anti-development thesis
items.d: It offers **no programme**. A person without clean water, immunisation or literacy is not exercising an alternative epistemology. **Sen's** reply is decisive: the answer to imposed development is **agency and public reasoning about which capabilities matter**, not the abandonment of development.

Displacement without rehabilitation — the **Narmada** movement; **forest dwellers criminalised** until the **FRA, 2006**; **land acquisition** conflicts that produced the **RFCTLARR Act, 2013** with its **consent and social impact assessment** requirements. These are the thesis's strongest empirical ground.

The evidence points to **symbiosis**, not choice: every successful market economy rests on a **strong state** supplying contract enforcement, property rights, competition regulation, human capital and infrastructure. **Weak states produce weak markets**, not free ones.

**Chalmers Johnson** on Japan's **MITI** — a **plan-rational** state with a pilot agency. **Alice Amsden** on Korea — subsidies made **conditional on export performance**, so support was **disciplined**. **Ha-Joon Chang** — developed countries are "**kicking away the ladder**" they climbed.

items.t: Has the state's role been overemphasised?
items.d: The state's **direct production** role was overemphasised — that is the honest reading of the licensing era. Its **regulatory, capability-building and risk-absorbing** role was **under**emphasised, and is what **DPI, ISRO and the vaccine programme** show it does best.

The administrator's function shifted from **allocating scarcity** (licences, quotas, permits) to **regulating competition and managing contracts**. That change requires **different skills** — economics, contract law, risk pricing — which recruitment and training have not supplied. The **licence-era officer was retained for a market-era job**.

**Women in Development** (1970s, after **Ester Boserup**) — add women to existing programmes. **Women and Development** — the problem is the **terms** of their inclusion. **Gender and Development** — the object is not women but the **gendered relations of power**, so men and institutions are part of the target.

**Caroline Moser** — women carry **reproductive, productive and community-managing** roles simultaneously, so any programme that adds work without removing any **intensifies their burden**. Her distinction between **practical gender needs** (water, fuel, income) and **strategic gender interests** (control, voice, property) is the sharpest planning tool available.

**Naila Kabeer** — empowerment is the **expansion of the ability to make strategic life choices** by those previously denied it, and has three inseparable dimensions: **resources**, **agency** and **achievements**. A transfer that raises resources without agency is **not** empowerment.

**NABARD's SHG-Bank Linkage (1992)**, scaled through **NRLM/Aajeevika (2011)** and now **Lakhpati Didi**. **Kudumbashree** in Kerala is the most complete instance — neighbourhood groups federated to area and community development societies, with a **formal interface with the panchayat**.

items.t: Do SHGs play a marginal role?
items.d: **Not marginal** — they moved **practical needs** (credit at non-usurious rates, savings, thrift) and produced **collective bargaining** where women had none. **Marginal on strategic interests** — they rarely touch **land title, inheritance or household decision-making**, and can add work without power.

**Community resource persons** delivering NRLM; SHG members as **bank sakhis, pashu sakhis and krishi sakhis**; SHG federations running **mid-day meal kitchens and PDS outlets**; and their role in **COVID mask and relief distribution**. They became a **parallel delivery cadre** — which is also the critique: **unpaid or underpaid state work**.

items.t: Affirmative action has not eliminated discrimination
items.d: Reservation delivers **presence**, not **power** — hence **sarpanch pati**, proxy candidature, and elected women who are not permitted to chair. The instruments that shift power are different: **capacity building, tenure security, independent staff, and social audit** by women's collectives.

India's **female labour force participation** rose sharply in recent PLFS rounds while **unpaid domestic work** and **safety constraints** remained; growth alone does not touch **son preference, mobility restriction, unpaid care or asset ownership**. Growth **enables**; it does not **deliver** gender equality.

**Articles 14, 15(3), 16, 39(a) and (d), 42, 51A(e)**; **106th Amendment (2023)** reserving **one-third** of Lok Sabha and State Assembly seats, operative after the **census and delimitation**; **Gender Budget Statement 13**; the **POSH Act, 2013** after **Vishaka (1997)**; **Nirbhaya Fund**; **Mission Shakti**.

groups.g: Human resource development and the personnel function

items.t: Personnel administration to human resource development
items.d: **Personnel administration** treats staff as **posts to be filled and controlled**; **HRD** treats them as a **capability to be built**. The shift is from **establishment work** — sanction, seniority, service records — to **competency, career design and performance**.

items.t: Why HRD matters more in government
items.d: Government cannot **hire and fire** to change its capability, cannot **pay differentially** for scarce skills, and holds staff for **thirty-five years**. Every capability it will have in 2040 is **already recruited**. That is why **training and career design**, not recruitment, are the operative levers.

**Merit** (open competition), **equality of opportunity** (Article 16), **representativeness** (the service should resemble the society), **political neutrality of the recruiting body**, and **suitability** — the qualities tested must be those the job needs.

items.t: Merit without a fair civil service
items.d: The claim is defensible: where entry is **patronage-based**, the official's loyalty runs to the **patron**, not to the office. **Northcote-Trevelyan (1854)** and the **Pendleton Act (1883)** were both anti-corruption reforms first, and efficiency reforms second.

The **post** is classified by **duties and responsibilities**, and pay attaches to the **post**. Gives **equal pay for equal work**, precise **job descriptions** and **specialisation**. Used in the **United States**. Its cost is **rigidity** — mobility across posts is hard because each is separately defined.

The **person** carries a **rank** and pay follows the rank wherever posted. Gives **mobility, generalist career development and easy redeployment**. Used in **Britain, France and India**. Its cost is that **pay is disconnected from the job** — the same rank does very different work in Delhi and in a district.

India runs **rank classification** for the services with **position elements** grafted on: **cadre posts** listed against levels, the **Pay Matrix** of the 7th CPC, **Non-Functional Upgradation**, and **empanelment** for specific Union posts. The result carries the **rigidity of both** systems in places.

**Training is not a short affair; it is a step-by-step process** of developing **skills, habits, knowledge and aptitude** — It runs **induction → in-service → mid-career → specialised → leadership**, and its object is **behaviour**, not information.

Four purposes that pull against each other: **development** (feedback to improve), **administrative decisions** (promotion, posting), **documentation** (defending a decision in a tribunal), and **motivation**. A system optimised for the **third** — India's — cannot deliver the **first**.

**Performance Appraisal Report**, online through **SPARROW**; **numerical grading on a 1-10 scale**; **self-appraisal with targets**; **reporting, reviewing and accepting** authorities; adverse remarks **communicated with a right of representation** following **Dev Dutt v. Union of India (2008)**, which held even a 'good' entry must be communicated if it affects promotion.

Ratings **cluster at the top** because an adverse entry invites litigation and damages a career irreversibly; the reporting officer changes **before the year ends**; and the **cost of honesty is borne by the reporter**. The result is a document that **cannot rank** — which is why **empanelment relies on the 360-degree input instead**.

Administrative work is **not fully measurable** — integrity, judgement under pressure, willingness to record dissent, care for the weakest applicant. An appraisal obsessed with **countable targets** rewards the measurable and **silently penalises the valuable**. The remedy is **multi-source, moderated and narrative** assessment, not more numbers.

items.t: Appraisal is not only for promotion
items.d: Its other uses: **identifying training needs** (feeding FRAC), **matching officers to postings**, **succession planning**, **counselling the under-performer**, and **evidence for compulsory retirement** under **FR 56(j)**. A system used only for **vertical movement** wastes most of what it collects.

**Appraisal** is a **periodic, individual, backward-looking judgement**. **Performance management** is a **continuous, organisational, forward-looking system** — goal setting, monitoring, feedback, development and organisational alignment, of which appraisal is one component. **The RFD was performance management; the PAR is appraisal.**

items.t: The committees on appraisal and empanelment
items.d: **Surinder Nath Committee (2003)** — a **competency-based** PAR, disclosure of the full report, and empanelment on **domain competence**. **Hota (2004)** — **fixed tenure**, mid-career specialisation, and **compulsory retirement review at 15 and 25 years**. Both were partially adopted; the **disclosure** recommendation was the one that stuck.

**Central Pay Commissions** roughly every ten years. The **7th CPC (2016)** replaced pay bands and grade pay with a **Pay Matrix**, set a **minimum pay** using the **Aykroyd formula**, and rationalised allowances. The **8th CPC** — ToR notified **3 November 2025**, **Justice Ranjana Prakash Desai**, report within **18 months** — covers about **50 lakh employees and 69 lakh pensioners**.

Operational **1 April 2025**. Assured payout of **50% of average basic pay of the last twelve months** for **25 years'** service, **minimum ₹10,000 a month**, government contribution **18.5%**. It settles the **OPS-versus-NPS** fiscal argument by giving **assurance without an unfunded liability** — the design compromise worth naming.

items.t: Code of ethics versus code of conduct
items.d: A **code of conduct** is a **list of prohibitions** — enforceable, specific, and silent on everything it does not mention. A **code of ethics** states **values that guide judgement** in the cases no rule anticipated. India has an elaborate code of conduct and **no code of ethics**; the **2nd ARC's fourth report** proposed one.

The answer is **both, in sequence**. Conduct rules set an **enforceable floor** and catch the clear case; a code of ethics **shapes discretion** where rules run out — which is where most administrative harm occurs. A conduct code alone produces **compliance without judgement**: 'I broke no rule.'

groups.g: Neutrality, activism and the political interface

items.d: Government is a **monopoly employer** whose employees deliver essential services and **cannot strike lawfully**; that asymmetry makes **consultative machinery a duty, not a concession**. Where JCM works, disputes are resolved before they reach the street; where it is allowed to lapse, **agitation becomes the only channel**.

items.t: Why ethics and not just rules
items.d: Rules govern the **anticipated** case. Administrative discretion operates precisely where they run out — which resource-scarce claim to prefer, which enforcement to prioritise, what to record. **Ethics is what governs the space rules cannot reach**, and that space grows as administration becomes more discretionary.

Administrative ethics is the antidote because it locates responsibility in the **person**, not the **chain**. **Barnard's** executive creates moral codes; the **Nuremberg** principle denies superior orders as a defence; **Rule 3(3)(iii)** operationalises it — **put the order in writing and the chain becomes attributable**.

**Selflessness, integrity, objectivity, accountability, openness, honesty, leadership** — from the **Committee on Standards in Public Life (1995)**. The most quotable ethical checklist in the syllabus, and the model the **2nd ARC** used for its proposed **Code of Ethics** and **Public Services Bill**.

items.t: The four ethical pressures on an administrator
items.d: **Conflicting loyalties** (law, minister, public, subordinate); **conflict of interest** (personal, family, post-retirement); **information asymmetry** (what to disclose, when); and **the cost of dissent** (career risk for refusing). Naming which pressure a case involves converts a vague answer into an analytical one.

Working instances: **integrity pacts** in procurement (Transparency International's model, adopted by the CVC); **asset and interest disclosure**; **cooling-off periods**; **e-procurement removing the discretionary interface**; **behavioural nudges** in tax compliance; and **preventive vigilance** as against punitive vigilance.

**T.N. Seshan** — statutory authority used to its constitutional edge. **Ashok Khemka** — mutation cancellation and the cost paid in transfers. **Satyendra Dubey** and **Shanmugam Manjunath** — killed for reporting corruption, and the reason whistleblower protection is not academic. **S.R. Sankaran** — the officer who made bonded-labour release his career.

The channels are real: **UNCAC (ratified 2011)** and its conflict-of-interest obligations; **OECD** public integrity recommendations; **FATF** compliance shaping financial conduct; **Nolan** as the template for codes worldwide; and **ISO 37001** anti-bribery certification entering Indian PSUs.

groups.g: What policy is, and the models

items.d: Policy is "**whatever governments choose to do or not to do**." The value of the second half is the whole point — **non-decision is policy**. India's failure to enact a **Public Services Bill** or a national **grievance redress law** is a policy, made by omission and rarely examined as one.

**Demands and supports** enter as **inputs**; the political system is the **black box** where conversion occurs; **outputs** are policies; **feedback** alters the next round of inputs. **Withinputs** are demands generated **inside** the system by officials themselves — the concept most useful for India.

**Institutional** — policy is whatever the institution's structure and procedure permit; change the institution and you change the policy. **Group (Bentley, Truman)** — policy is the **equilibrium** reached in the struggle between interest groups, and shifts as their relative power shifts.

**Mills, Mosca, Pareto** — policy reflects the **preferences of a governing elite** and flows **downward**, not upward from mass demand. Its Indian bite: policy on **land, capital and taxation** has been consistently more responsive to **organised** than to **numerous** interests.

items.t: Rational choice and the maximum social gain
items.d: The rational model's test is **maximum social gain** — no policy should be adopted whose costs exceed its benefits, and among alternatives choose the greatest **net** benefit. It is rarely achieved because gains and costs fall on **different people**, and no politically neutral way exists to weigh them.

**Problem, policy and politics** streams flow independently. A **policy window** opens when a **focusing event** or a change of government couples them, and a **policy entrepreneur** who has kept a solution ready pushes it through. This is the sharpest model for explaining **timing**.

**GST (2016)** — a solution debated since 2000 that passed when a **political window** opened. **IBC (2016)** — the **twin balance sheet** problem coupled to a ready draft. **Aadhaar**, the **2020 farm laws and their repeal**, and the **Nirbhaya**-driven **Criminal Law Amendment, 2013** all follow the same shape.

**Baumgartner and Jones** — policy is **long stability punctuated by rapid change**, because attention is scarce and issues rise onto the agenda in bursts. It reconciles **incrementalism** (most years) with **transformation** (rare years), which neither model alone can explain.

**Rittel and Webber** — a wicked problem has **no definitive formulation**, **no stopping rule**, solutions that are **better or worse, not true or false**, **no immediate test**, every attempt is **consequential**, and each is **essentially unique**. Climate adaptation, urban air quality and antimicrobial resistance are wicked.

items.t: Is the Indian state prepared for wicked problems?
items.d: Partly. It handles **tame problems at scale** superbly — vaccination, elections, DBT. Wicked problems need **cross-ministry authority**, **long time horizons beyond electoral cycles**, **tolerance of failure**, and **adaptive, iterative delivery** — none of which the **annual budget, transferable officer and audit regime** supply.

**Cobb and Elder** distinguish the **systemic agenda** (issues the public discusses) from the **institutional agenda** (issues government is actually acting on). Movement between the two is the political act — and most issues never make the crossing.

**Bachrach and Baratz's second face of power** — the ability to **keep an issue off the agenda** entirely, so no decision is ever taken and no conflict is ever visible. asked about groups denying others the opportunity; this is the concept it wanted.

The chain: **ministry drafts → inter-ministerial consultation → Ministry of Law and Finance concurrence → Cabinet Note → Committee of Secretaries → Cabinet or its committee → legislation or executive order**. **NITI Aayog** enters as adviser, and the **PMO** increasingly as originator.

The **Pre-Legislative Consultation Policy, 2014** requires draft legislation and subordinate rules to be placed in the public domain for **30 days** with an explanatory note and a summary of feedback. It is a **policy, not a statute**, and compliance is inconsistent — one of the cheapest available governance upgrades.

Its instruments in India: **NSSO/PLFS/NFHS** survey data, **NITI's National Data and Analytics Platform**, **randomised evaluations** (J-PAL's work on Haryana immunisation), and **DMEO** evaluations. Its enemies are **timeliness**, **data gaps**, and the fact that **evidence arrives after the decision**.

Evidence answers **'what works'**; politics answers **'for whom, when and at whose cost'** — a different question. Where evidence recommends a policy with **concentrated losses and diffuse gains** (subsidy reform, user charges, land pooling), it loses reliably, and calling that irrational misdescribes it.

**Polanyi** — "we know more than we can tell." The field officer's judgement about which village will cooperate, the veteran's sense of when an order will be resisted: real knowledge, **not codifiable**, lost when tenure is short. It complements evidence; it cannot **substitute** for it, because it is **unverifiable and prone to bias**.

**Pluralist** — the state as a neutral arena for competing groups. **Elitist** — a cohesive elite decides. **Marxist** — the state as an instrument or a **relatively autonomous** manager of the interests of capital (**Poulantzas**). **Neo-liberal** — a state whose job is to secure markets. **The theory you hold determines which reform you think possible.**

**Implementation (1973)** — the **complexity of joint action**. With many **clearance points**, each requiring agreement, the probability of completion **collapses multiplicatively**: even 90% agreement at each of ten points leaves about a **35%** chance of success. Their subtitle says it: **great expectations dashed**.

A centrally sponsored scheme passes **Union ministry → State department → district → block → panchayat**, with **funds, guidelines, staff and approvals** each moving separately. **Jal Jeevan Mission's** convergence problem is Pressman and Wildavsky at scale — and **PFMS** exists to shorten exactly this chain.

**Top-down (Sabatier and Mazmanian)** — start from the statute's objectives and ask why they were not met; fix by clearer goals and tighter control. **Bottom-up (Lipsky, Hjern)** — start from the **street-level actor** and ask what she actually faces; fix by discretion, resources and realistic norms.

"The decisions of street-level bureaucrats... **effectively become the public policies they carry out**." Facing **demand that always exceeds resources**, they develop **coping routines** — rationing, creaming, routinising, stereotyping — and those routines **are** the policy the citizen experiences.

The **ASHA**, the **Anganwadi worker**, the **patwari**, the **PDS dealer**, the **constable**, the **primary school teacher**, the **electricity lineman**. Policy is written for them and experienced **as them**. Any implementation answer that does not name them stays abstract.

Policy change occurs within a **subsystem** of competing **advocacy coalitions** bound by shared **core beliefs**, over a horizon of **a decade or more**, driven by **external shocks** and **policy-oriented learning**. It explains why some debates — the OPS-NPS argument, forest rights — never resolve, only realign.

items.t: The classic implementation gaps in India
items.d: **Funds** arriving late in the financial year; **functionaries** absent or answerable elsewhere; **guidelines** too rigid for local variation; **capacity** at the last mile; **information** not reaching the beneficiary; and **no consequence** for non-delivery.

Be specific and evidence-led: **DBT** removed intermediation — **₹3.48 lakh crore** cumulative savings and subsidy share down to about **9%**; **PFMS** made release traceable; **Aadhaar-based authentication** cut duplication; **PRAGATI** created apex-level unblocking; **geo-tagged asset monitoring** made physical verification cheap.

The honest counter. **Authentication failure excludes** the very poorest — the elderly, manual labourers with worn fingerprints, those without connectivity. **Efficiency in disbursement is not the same as accuracy in entitlement**, and exclusion errors are less visible than inclusion errors because the excluded do not appear in the data.

**Monitoring** is **continuous** and asks whether the plan is being followed — inputs, outputs, timelines. **Evaluation** is **periodic** and asks whether it **worked** — outcomes, impact, attribution, and whether the theory behind the design was right. Monitoring cannot substitute for evaluation, and India does far more of it.

**Formative** (during, to improve design), **summative** (after, to judge worth), **process** (was it implemented as intended), **impact** (what changed because of it), **cost-benefit and cost-effectiveness**, and **participatory** evaluation by the beneficiaries themselves.

The hardest question in evaluation: would the outcome have occurred **anyway**? The answer requires a **counterfactual** — randomised assignment, difference-in-differences, regression discontinuity. Without one, a rising indicator proves **correlation with a scheme**, not its effect, however large the dashboard number.

**Development Monitoring and Evaluation Office (DMEO)** in NITI Aayog, successor to the **Programme Evaluation Organisation (1952)**; the **Output–Outcome Monitoring Framework** with the Finance Ministry; **CAG performance audits**; and **social audit**. Coverage remains thin relative to the number of schemes.

The argument: a policy system without evaluation **cannot learn**, so it repeats designs that failed and cannot defend those that worked. **Argyris's** single-loop learning at best. The corrective is a **statutory evaluation requirement with published results** and a **sunset clause** on schemes that fail it.

Analysis is crippled when it **omits alternatives** — comparing a scheme only against doing nothing — and when it **truncates outcomes**, counting the intended effect and ignoring displacement, substitution and distributional consequences.

Analysis commissioned **after** a decision, with terms of reference that foreclose the answer, becomes a **legitimation device** — the appearance of rigour attached to a settled conclusion. The safeguard is **independence of the evaluator and publication of the terms of reference**.

It **forces the alternatives to be compared in one unit** and makes assumptions explicit. Its limits: valuing **non-marketed goods** (a life, a forest, a heritage site), choosing the **discount rate** — which decides how much the future counts — and its silence on **who** bears costs and who takes benefits.

**Work study** seeks efficiency in **method** — how a specific task is done. **Organisation and methods** seeks efficiency in **structure and procedure** — how work flows between posts and units. The first optimises a step; the second asks whether the step should exist.

items.t: The two halves of work study
items.d: **Method study** — recording and critically examining the existing method to develop an easier, more economical one (process charts, flow diagrams, the **questioning technique**: purpose, place, sequence, person, means). **Work measurement** — establishing the **standard time** for a qualified worker, through time study, activity sampling or synthesis.

**Staffing norms** grounded in measurement rather than precedent; **elimination of redundant steps**; **standardised procedure** that makes training and audit possible; and a **baseline** against which any later improvement can be proved. It is the only technique that produces a **defensible number** for how many staff a task needs.

The **O&M Division** in the **Cabinet Secretariat (1954)**, created on **Appleby's** recommendation, moved to the **Department of Administrative Reforms (1964)**, now **DARPG**. The **Staff Inspection Unit (1964)** in the Ministry of Finance fixes **staffing norms** for Union offices by work measurement.

items.t: Where the technique reaches its limit
items.d: Work study can tell you the **standard time** for issuing a certificate. It cannot tell you whether the certificate should be **required**, whether the applicant should have to appear, or who should bear the cost of the visit. **Efficiency questions cannot answer purpose questions** — Taylor's original blind spot.

**PERT (US Navy Polaris, 1958)** — **probabilistic**, event-oriented, for projects whose activity times are **uncertain**, using **optimistic, most likely and pessimistic** estimates in a weighted formula. **CPM (DuPont, 1957)** — **deterministic**, activity-oriented, for **repetitive** projects with known times, and it costs the time-cost trade-off.

The **longest path** through the network, and therefore the **shortest possible project duration**. Activities on it have **zero float** — delay any one and the whole project slips. Everything off it has **slack**, which is where resources can be borrowed from without cost.

**Crashing** = shortening a **critical** activity by adding resources. CPM's value is that it shows **which** activity to crash for the least cost per day saved — the only rational basis for spending money to accelerate a project rather than spending it everywhere.

items.t: What network techniques give an administrator
items.d: A **defensible schedule**, a clear view of **which delay actually matters**, a basis for **resource levelling**, and **accountability by activity** rather than by project. **PM Gati Shakti's** integrated planning and **PRAGATI's** project reviews both rest on this logic.

items.t: Why networks do not remove delay
items.d: A network **schedules activity**; it cannot resolve the **uncertainty** that causes delay — land acquisition, forest clearance, litigation, contractor default, fund release. It **makes the delay visible and attributable**, which is valuable, and is often mistaken for preventing it.

items.t: The efficacy of management aid tools
items.d: State the governing principle: a tool's value depends on **fit between the tool and the problem**. Use **CPM** for a defined project with known steps; **PERT** where durations are uncertain; **cost-benefit** for choosing between alternatives; **MIS** for continuous control. Applying the wrong one produces **precision without relevance**.

items.t: The other aid tools worth naming
items.d: **Gantt chart** (bar schedule, no dependencies); **Management by Objectives (Drucker)**; **operations research** and linear programming; **queueing theory** for counter design; **decision trees**; **simulation**; **balanced scorecard** for multi-dimensional performance. Name two that fit; do not list.

An **integrated system** that converts data from internal and external sources into **information**, delivered at the **right level, in the right form, at the right time**, to support **planning, control and decision-making**. Note the emphasis: not data storage but **decision support**.

**Transaction processing** at the bottom (routine, detailed, operational); **MIS** in the middle (summarised, exception-based, tactical); **decision support and executive information systems** at the top (aggregated, ad hoc, strategic). Sending **operational detail to the top** is the commonest design failure.

The system is built for **upward reporting** rather than for the **level that acts**; data is **entered but not used**, so quality decays; there is **no process redesign** alongside; and **fear of exposure** produces defensive reporting. **Garbage in, gospel out.**

items.t: MIS's evolution beyond its traditional role
items.d: It has moved from **periodic reports** to **real-time dashboards**, from **internal** data to **integrated external** feeds, from **descriptive** to **predictive** analytics, and from **specialist** access to **public** access — **data.gov.in**, the **NDAP**, scheme dashboards.

items.t: Indian MIS that carry real weight
items.d: **PFMS** — tracking every release to the beneficiary; **NREGASoft** with muster rolls online; **CCTNS** linking police stations; **e-Hospital and ABDM**; **UDISE+** for schools; **PRAGATI** with geo-tagged project data; **National Judicial Data Grid** making pendency publicly visible.

It adds value by **shortening the decision cycle**, **exposing exceptions** rather than reporting everything, **standardising definitions** so units can be compared, and **making performance visible** — which is also why it meets resistance from the units it renders visible.

A live warning. When the **dashboard becomes the object**, staff optimise the **entry** rather than the **service** — Goodhart's law again. The safeguard is **third-party verification**, **outcome rather than output indicators**, and **beneficiary-side data** (call-back surveys, social audit) that the reporting unit does not control.

**G2C** (citizen services — passports, DBT, land records), **G2B** (business — GeM, single-window clearance, GST), **G2G** (inter-government — e-Office, PFMS, treasury), **G2E** (employees — iGOT, e-HRMS). Sorting a question into one of these four is the fastest way to structure the answer.

**Broadcasting** (information dissemination); **critical flow** (targeted release of critical information to those who can act); **comparative analysis** (benchmarking against best practice); **e-advocacy or mobilisation and lobbying** (networked civil action); **interactive service** delivery.

It **lowers the cost of collective action** — online consultation on **MyGov**, campaign mobilisation, crowdsourced evidence, RTI data used publicly. Its limits: the **digitally connected are not representative**, so it can **amplify already-heard voices**, and **manufactured consensus** is cheap.

**Presence** (a website) → **interaction** (downloadable forms) → **transaction** (payment and delivery end-to-end) → **transformation** (integrated, seamless, life-event-organised) → **engagement** (co-production and open data). India's variance across departments spans **all five stages simultaneously** — Riggs's heterogeneity, digitally.

**NICNET (1987)** → **National e-Governance Plan (2006)** with mission-mode projects and the **CSC** last mile → **Digital India (2015)** with its nine pillars → **India Stack and Digital Public Infrastructure**. The shift is from **departmental computerisation** to **shared population-scale rails**.

**Partly.** It removed **discretion at the interface** — faceless assessment, online allotment — and **flattened information access**. It did **not** flatten hierarchy: approvals still climb the same levels, now in **e-Office**. It **relocated** bureaucratic power to whoever **designs the workflow and owns the data**.

What changed the contours: **mobile-first** rather than desktop; **cloud** (MeghRaj) removing per-department infrastructure; **API-based interoperability** rather than monolithic systems; **real-time payments**; and **AI/ML** moving from analysis to **decision support**.

The necessary counterweight. **Connectivity and device access** are unequal; **digital literacy** more so; **authentication failure** excludes the elderly and manual workers; **language** narrows reach — which **Bhashini** addresses; and **assisted access through CSCs** reintroduces an **intermediary** with the discretion the system was meant to remove.

**Monetary policy** is the **central bank's** control of **money supply and the price of credit** — repo rate, CRR, SLR, open market operations. **Fiscal policy** is the **government's** use of **taxation, expenditure and borrowing**. Both regulate demand; only fiscal policy can change **who** bears the cost.

**Flexible inflation targeting** since the **RBI Act amendment, 2016** — CPI inflation at **4% with a ±2% band**, set by the government in consultation with the RBI every five years, and delivered by a **six-member Monetary Policy Committee** (three RBI, three external), decisions by majority with the **Governor's casting vote**.

items.t: The three functions of fiscal policy
items.d: **Musgrave's** classification: **allocation** (supplying public goods the market will not), **distribution** (altering the pattern of income and wealth), and **stabilisation** (countering the cycle). — Musgrave is the frame that answer needs.

**Inequity** — reliance on **indirect taxes**, which are regressive. **Intricacy** — exemptions, cesses and multiple rates raising compliance cost. **Obscurantism** — **off-budget borrowing, contingent liabilities and tax expenditures** that keep real fiscal position out of the headline number.

**Direct** — the **Income-tax Act, 2025** replacing the 1961 Act; faceless assessment; corporate rate cuts (2019); **BEPS Pillar Two** global minimum tax. **Indirect** — **GST (2017)** subsuming seventeen taxes and thirteen cesses. Direct tax reform matters more for **equity**, because indirect taxes cannot discriminate by ability to pay.

India's **combined tax-to-GDP ratio** remains well below the OECD average, and the **direct tax share**, while rising, leaves a **narrow base**. **Buoyancy** improved with **GST e-invoicing, TDS/TCS widening and analytics**; the structural constraints are the **agricultural income exemption**, a large **informal sector**, and **exemptions and cesses**.

Liberalisation **expanded** the tax opportunity even as it cut rates: a **larger formal economy**, **digitised transactions leaving an audit trail**, **new tax bases** (services, capital gains, digital transactions), and **international cooperation on evasion**. Lower rates on a wider, more visible base can raise more revenue.

**FRBM Act, 2003** — annual targets, a **Medium Term Fiscal Policy Statement**, and an escape clause. The **N.K. Singh Review Committee (2017)** proposed a **debt anchor of 60% of GDP** (Centre 40, States 20) and an **independent Fiscal Council** — the Council was **never created**, which is the standing gap in India's fiscal architecture.

**Internal** versus **external**; **funded** (long-term, with a sinking fund) versus **unfunded** (short-term); **productive** (self-liquidating, financing an asset that yields a return) versus **unproductive** (financing consumption, war or deficit). The **productive-unproductive** distinction is the one an examiner wants.

**No, for internal debt** in the classical view — we owe it to ourselves, so it is a **transfer**, not a net burden. **Yes, in three real senses**: **interest payments pre-empt** future budgets, **distributional transfer** runs from taxpayers to bondholders, and **crowding out** reduces the capital stock future citizens inherit.

The **golden rule** — borrow for **capital**, not for **revenue** expenditure. Borrowing that finances an asset yielding a return above the interest rate **raises** future capacity; borrowing for salaries and subsidies transfers consumption from the future to the present. India's **capex share** is the relevant test.

**Article 292** — the Union may borrow on the security of the Consolidated Fund within limits Parliament may fix (Parliament has **never** fixed them). **Article 293** — States may borrow within India, but need the **Union's consent** while indebted to it, which is the Centre's principal lever over State finance.

Debt is sustainable while the **growth rate exceeds the effective interest rate** (**g > r**), because the ratio then falls even with a primary deficit. India's arithmetic has generally been favourable; the risks are a **growth slowdown**, **contingent liabilities from guarantees**, and **off-budget borrowing by parastatals**.

The traditional form: appropriation by **object of expenditure** — salaries, travel, supplies. Its virtues are **control and accountability**; you can see exactly what was sanctioned and audit against it. Its defect is that it tells you **what was bought and nothing about what was achieved**.

Classifies expenditure by **function, programme and activity**, linking **inputs to outputs** with physical targets and unit costs. Introduced in India from **1968-69** on **ARC-I's** recommendation, following the **Hoover Commission (1949)** in the United States. It asks what the money **does**, not what it **buys**.

It became a **parallel document** rather than the appropriation itself; **outputs** were measurable but **outcomes** were not; unit costs were rarely computed honestly; and it **never governed the allocation decision** — the line-item budget remained the one that was voted and audited.

**Planning-Programming-Budgeting System** — US Defence under **McNamara (1961)**, extended government-wide 1965. It links **objectives → programmes → alternatives → costs over a multi-year horizon**, using systems analysis. Abandoned by **1971**: it demanded analytical capacity and clear objectives that government did not have.

**Peter Pyhrr at Texas Instruments; Jimmy Carter in Georgia and then federally.** Every activity must be **rejustified from zero** each cycle through **decision units**, **decision packages** at alternative service levels, and **ranking**. India adopted it formally in **1986-87**.

items.t: ZBB became the most incremental of approaches
items.d: Because the **workload is impossible** — no organisation can rejustify everything annually — decision units are defined at a **level of aggregation that hides choices**, and rankings **reproduce last year's order**. ZBB produced a **rejustification of the base**, which is incrementalism with more paperwork.

Not annually and not everywhere. It works as a **periodic, selective** exercise — apply it to a **few programmes each year on a rotating cycle**, at a **sunset review**, or when a **fiscal shock** forces genuine reprioritisation. Used that way it does what its designers intended.

From **2005-06**, now the **Output–Outcome Monitoring Framework** run by **NITI Aayog** with the Finance Ministry. Every major scheme carries **output indicators** (what was produced) and **outcome indicators** (what changed) against its outlay. It is performance budgeting's **surviving descendant**.

**2019-family and a reliable 10-marker.** It is **not a separate budget for women** — it is an **accountability device**: **Statement 13** of the Expenditure Budget reports **Part A** (100% women-specific allocations) and **Part B** (schemes with at least 30% for women). Introduced **2005-06**, with **Gender Budget Cells** in ministries.

**Revenue and capital**; **surplus, balanced and deficit**; **cash versus accrual**; **plan and non-plan** (abolished 2017-18); and the deficit measures — **revenue deficit**, **fiscal deficit** (total expenditure minus non-borrowed receipts), **primary deficit** (fiscal deficit minus interest), and **effective revenue deficit**.

"**Budgeting is incremental, not comprehensive.**" The base is accepted and attention focuses on the **increment**, because comprehensive review is **cognitively impossible** and **politically explosive**. **Aaron Wildavsky, The Politics of the Budgetary Process (1964)** — the most quotable line in the whole unit.

"**On what basis shall it be decided to allocate X dollars to activity A instead of activity B?**" — the **lack of a budgetary theory (1940)**. Seventy years of PPBS, ZBB and outcome budgeting have been attempts to answer it, and none has, because the question is finally **political, not technical**.

groups.g: The budget as a political instrument

items.d: Is the budget-maximising bureaucrat still real? **Not in the aggregate** — PFMS, TSA and outcome frameworks watch the money. **Yes in a modified form** — agencies maximise **staff strength, jurisdiction and scheme count** rather than budget, because those are the currencies that survived the fiscal controls.

A **treatise on statecraft**, not a work of political philosophy — a manual of **administration, revenue, war, law and espionage** written for a working ruler. **Arthashastra** literally means the science of **artha**: material well-being, the livelihood of the people and the means of acquiring and protecting it.

The state as **seven limbs (prakritis)** in order of importance: **Swami** (ruler), **Amatya** (ministers and officials), **Janapada** (territory and people), **Durga** (fortified capital), **Kosha** (treasury), **Danda** (army and coercive force), **Mitra** (allies). The **organic** metaphor — weakness in any limb weakens the whole.

"In the **happiness of his subjects** lies the king's happiness; in their **welfare** his welfare. He shall not consider as good only that which pleases him but treat as beneficial to him **whatever pleases his subjects**." The **yogakshema** duty — acquisition and protection of the people's welfare.

**Amatyas** selected by **upadha** — tests of integrity against religious, monetary, romantic and fear-based temptation. **Adhyakshas** as departmental superintendents (about **30 departments**); **Samaharta** for revenue; **Sannidhata** as treasurer; **Gopa and Sthanika** in local administration; the **Mahamatras** at the top.

items.t: Ethics in public service, Kautilya's version
items.d: He is **realistic rather than moralistic**: "just as it is impossible not to taste honey placed on the tongue, so it is impossible for a government servant **not to eat up at least a bit of the king's revenue**." Hence **forty ways of embezzlement** enumerated, **rotation of officials**, **espionage** and **graded punishment**.

**Upadha** ≈ **integrity testing and vigilance**; **rotation of adhyakshas** ≈ **transfer policy against entrenchment**; **espionage on officials** ≈ **preventive vigilance and CVO reporting**; the **Samaharta's** revenue survey ≈ the **land record and revenue administration** the Collector still runs; **danda** ≈ **the state's legitimate monopoly of force**.

Both. It contains **theory** — saptanga, mandala, the four upayas (**sama, dana, danda, bheda**), the sources of law (**dharma, vyavahara, charitra, rajasasana**). It is delivered as **operational instruction** with rates, staffing, penalties and procedures.

Its ethic is **instrumental** — the ruler's welfare duty is justified by the **stability it buys**, not by the subject's right. It is **authoritarian**, resting on surveillance and graded punishment, and it is **hierarchical** on varna.

**Akbar's** system of ranked service: **zat** (personal rank, status and pay) and **sawar** (cavalry obligation). Mansabdars were **paid in cash or through jagir** (assignment of revenue, not land), were **transferable**, and their **assignments were non-hereditary and resumed on death** — a **service nobility**, not a feudal aristocracy.
