**Todar Mal's Zabti or Bandobast** — **measurement (paimaish)**, classification of land by continuity of cultivation (**polaj, parauti, chachar, banjar**), a **ten-year average of produce and prices (dahsala)**, and a fixed **cash** demand of about **one-third**. Revenue administration became **survey-based and record-based** — the direct ancestor of the Indian revenue system.

**Diwan** (revenue and finance, the highest official), **Mir Bakshi** (military pay and mansabdar records, and effectively the intelligence head), **Mir Saman** (imperial household and karkhanas), **Sadr-us-Sudur** (religious endowments and charity), **Qazi-ul-Quzat** (judiciary). Provinces mirrored this in the **subah**.

**Subah** under a **Subahdar**, with a **Diwan** as a **parallel revenue authority reporting separately to the centre** — a deliberate **check on the governor**. **Sarkar** under a **Faujdar** (law and order) and **Amalguzar** (revenue); **Pargana** with **Shiqdar, Amil, Qanungo and Patwari**; the **village** left largely to itself.

**Centralised in design** — mansabdars appointed and transferred by the emperor, non-hereditary assignments, parallel reporting by the provincial Diwan, a uniform revenue method. **Decentralised in practice** — **zamindars** collected on the ground, the **village community** was untouched, and distance made **local autonomy** inevitable.

items.t: The Mughal legacy in the district
items.d: The **sarkar** became the **district**; the **faujdar's** law-and-order function and the **amalguzar's** revenue function were **fused in one officer** by the British — which is precisely how the **Collector-cum-District Magistrate** acquired both hats. The **patwari and qanungo** survive under their Mughal names.

items.t: How the trader became a magistrate
items.d: **Diwani of Bengal, Bihar and Orissa (1765)** gave the Company **revenue** authority while the Nawab retained **nizamat** — the **dual government** that collapsed by 1772 when **Warren Hastings** brought both under the Company. **The revenue collector acquired magisterial power because revenue collection required coercion.**

items.t: The Permanent Settlement and its alternatives
items.d: **Permanent Settlement (Cornwallis, 1793)** in Bengal — the **zamindar** made proprietor, revenue **fixed in perpetuity**. **Ryotwari (Munro, Read)** in Madras and Bombay — settlement **directly with the cultivator**, periodically revised. **Mahalwari (Holt Mackenzie, R.M. Bird)** in the North-West — settlement with the **village community**. Each produced a different **agrarian structure** that outlived it.

**Separation of revenue and judicial** functions; **abolition of the Collector's judicial powers** (later restored in part); **Europeanisation** of the higher services on the premise that Indians were corrupt; **increased salaries** to end private trade; and the **Code of 1793** — the origin of the **rule-bound, written, hierarchical** Indian civil service.

**Haileybury** training from 1806; the **Charter Act, 1853** introduced **open competition**; examinations held in **London only** until **1922**, when simultaneous examination began in **Allahabad**. **Satyendranath Tagore** was the first Indian, in **1864**. **Lloyd George (1922)** called it "**the steel frame** of the whole structure".

"The **ICS** is neither **Indian**, nor **civil**, nor a **service**." Set it against **Patel's** insistence in the Constituent Assembly that the successor service was the **sine qua non** of sound administration. The two positions together are the whole debate about continuity in 1947.

**Regulating Act 1773** (Governor-General of Bengal, Supreme Court at Calcutta); **Pitt's India Act 1784** (Board of Control — dual government); **Charter Act 1833** (Governor-General of India, all-India legislation, Law Member); **1858** (Crown rule, Secretary of State); **Morley-Minto 1909**; **Montagu-Chelmsford 1919** (**dyarchy**); **Government of India Act 1935**.

Provincial subjects split into **transferred** (education, health, local government, agriculture — administered by **ministers responsible to the legislature**) and **reserved** (police, land revenue, justice, irrigation — administered by the **Governor with executive councillors**). It failed because **finance stayed reserved**: ministers held responsibility **without money**.

It supplied the **structural template** of the Indian Constitution: **federal division through three lists**, **provincial autonomy** replacing dyarchy, a **Federal Court**, an **RBI**, **Governor's discretionary powers**, and **emergency provisions**. About **two-thirds** of the Constitution's provisions descend from it — including **Article 356**'s ancestor, **Section 93**.

The surviving features: the **district as the unit of administration** with a **generalist Collector**; **land revenue records** as the state's basic dataset; a **regulatory rather than developmental** orientation in police and revenue law; **secrecy** (**Official Secrets Act, 1923**); and **rank classification with a generalist elite service**.

items.t: The balanced verdict on the legacy
items.d: It bequeathed **institutional continuity, a professional civil service, a codified legal system, an audited treasury and an independent judiciary's foundations** — assets most post-colonial states lacked. It also bequeathed a machinery designed for **extraction and order**, which had to be **redirected to development** without being rebuilt.

items.t: The Preamble as an administrative mandate
items.d: **Justice — social, economic and political; Liberty; Equality; Fraternity.** For an administrator these are not sentiments but **decision rules**: where two lawful courses are open, the one advancing social and economic justice is the one the Constitution prefers. **Kesavananda (1973)** made this part of the **basic structure**.

items.t: The DPSPs as the administrative charter
items.d: **Article 37** — not enforceable by any court, yet **fundamental in the governance of the country** and a **duty of the State to apply in making laws**. **Articles 38, 39, 39A, 41, 43, 46, 47, 48A, 50** are the specific mandates that every welfare scheme, legal aid programme and environmental regulation traces back to.

**Champakam Dorairajan (1951)** — rights prevail. **Kesavananda (1973)** — harmonious construction. **Minerva Mills (1980)** — the **balance between them is itself basic structure**; neither may be sacrificed to the other. This is the doctrinal ground on which every reservation and land reform question is settled.

The administrator's own question. **State** includes the government, Parliament, legislatures, **local authorities** and **other authorities**. **Ajay Hasia (1981)** laid down tests for a body being an instrumentality — financial control, deep state control, monopoly status, public function. **Zee Telefilms (2005)** limited it. **It decides whether a body faces writ jurisdiction at all.**

**Ambedkar**, quoting Grote, warned that constitutional morality is "**not a natural sentiment; it has to be cultivated**". His companion warning is the one to quote: "**however good a Constitution may be, it is sure to turn out bad because those who are called to work it happen to be a bad lot.**"

items.t: Who upholds constitutional values in practice
items.d: The text supplies a **framework**; the working depends on **institutions** (EC, CAG, UPSC, courts), **civil society** (RTI users, PILs, social audit), and **citizens** (voting, participation, dissent). This is **Riggs's formalism**: the strength of the framework and the weakness of practice are the same country.

The **elected head is the real executive** — **Article 74** makes the President bound by ministerial advice (after the **42nd and 44th Amendments**, with one reconsideration), and **Shamsher Singh (1974)** settled that Governors likewise act on advice. Administratively this means **ministerial responsibility**, and therefore **an anonymous, permanent civil service** behind it.

Know which is which. **Constitutional** — EC, CAG, UPSC and SPSCs, Finance Commission, AG, NCSC, NCST, NCBC (**102nd Amendment, 2018**), Special Officer for Linguistic Minorities. **Statutory** — NHRC, CIC, CVC, Lokpal, NCW, NGT, TRAI. The distinction decides how the body may be **abolished or altered**.

**Ambedkar**: the Constitution is "**federal in structure and unitary in spirit**"; **K.C. Wheare** called it "**quasi-federal**"; **Granville Austin**, "**cooperative federalism**". The textual evidence for the centralising tilt: **single citizenship, integrated judiciary, All India Services, Article 3, emergency provisions, residuary powers with the Union**.

**Seventh Schedule** — **Union List (97 entries)**, **State List (66)**, **Concurrent List (47)**. **Article 246** gives Union primacy; **Article 254** resolves repugnancy in favour of Union law unless the State law received **Presidential assent**. **Article 248** places residuary power with Parliament — the reverse of the American arrangement.

items.t: How the Union reaches State subjects
items.d: **Article 249** (Rajya Sabha resolution in national interest); **Article 250** (during Emergency); **Article 252** (two or more States request); **Article 253** (treaty implementation); **Article 256-257** (directions to States); and, most consequentially, **centrally sponsored schemes** — spending power reaching subjects legislative power cannot.

items.t: The pros and cons of Union spending on State subjects
items.d: **For** — **national minimum standards** in health and education, **fiscal capacity** States lack, **externalities** across borders, and **counter-cyclical** capacity. **Against** — **matching contributions crowd out State priorities**, **one-size guidelines** ignore variation, and it makes States **implementing agencies** for programmes they did not design.

**Article 256** — States shall ensure compliance with Union laws. **Article 257** — Union may give directions, including on **means of communication of national importance** and **protection of railways**. **Article 258** — Union may entrust functions to a State. **Article 355** — Union duty to protect States against external aggression and **internal disturbance**.

items.t: Centre–State relations are undergoing drastic change
items.d: The drivers: **GST** removing independent taxation; **cesses shrinking the divisible pool**; **direct benefit transfer bypassing States** to reach the citizen; **centrally sponsored schemes** dominating social-sector spending; and **agency withdrawal of consent** under the DSPE Act as a new site of friction.

**Inter-State Council (Article 263)**, constituted **1990** on **Sarkaria's** recommendation and meeting rarely; **Zonal Councils** under the States Reorganisation Act, 1956; the **GST Council (279A)**; **NITI's Governing Council**; and **National Development Council**, now largely dormant. Note which of these **actually meets and decides** — only the GST Council does.

**Divergent political interests** — different parties at the two levels turn every coordination question into a contest. **Financial constraints** — States carry **about 60% of general government expenditure** on a smaller share of receipts. Add **asymmetric information**, and forums that are **consultative without being decisional**.

The 2015-onward alternative: instead of bargaining in a council, States compete on **published indices** — **SDG India Index, Fiscal Health Index, Ease of Doing Business/BRAP, Composite Water Management**. It is **public choice applied to a federation** — reputational competition substituting for central direction. Its limit is that **rank without resources changes only the willing**.

India's federation is **not uniform**. **Article 371** and its variants for Maharashtra, Gujarat, Nagaland, Assam, Manipur, Andhra, Sikkim, Mizoram, Arunachal, Goa and Karnataka; the **Fifth and Sixth Schedules** for tribal areas; **special category** treatment in transfers; **UTs with and without legislatures**. Asymmetry is the device that held a plural federation together.

groups.g: The Governor and the federal flashpoints

items.d: Appointed by the **President** under **Article 155**, holding office **during the President's pleasure (156)** — no fixed tenure. Acts on the aid and advice of the Council of Ministers (**163**), **except** where the Constitution requires **discretion**. **Shamsher Singh (1974)** confined that discretion narrowly.

items.t: Where the Governor has real discretion
items.d: **Appointing a Chief Minister** in a hung house; **dismissing a ministry that has lost confidence**; **recommending President's Rule (356)**; **reserving a bill for the President (200)**; **reporting on the State's administration**; and, in specified States, functions under **Article 371** and the **Sixth Schedule**.

**Article 200** — the Governor may **assent**, **withhold assent**, **return** a non-money bill for reconsideration (and **must assent** if it is passed again), or **reserve** it for the President. **The Article prescribes no time limit**, and indefinite inaction — the 'pocket veto' — is the flashpoint of the last three years.

The **live 2026 issue.** After the **State of Tamil Nadu** litigation on delayed assent, the **Supreme Court's advisory opinion of November 2025** declined to impose **judicially fixed timelines** on the Governor or the President under **Articles 200 and 201**. The Court is **returning the question to political and cooperative-federal channels**.

The recurring sites: **delayed assent**; **timing of floor tests**; **appointments as Chancellor of State universities**; **prosecution sanction**; **speeches and public commentary**; and **reports to the Centre**. The structural cause is that the office is **appointed by, removable by, and dependent for its next post on the Union**.

items.t: The reform recommendations on the Governor
items.d: **Sarkaria (1988)** — appoint an **eminent person from outside the State**, not recently in active politics, in **consultation with the Chief Minister**; a **five-year tenure** not disturbed except for compelling reasons. **Punchhi (2010)** — a **fixed tenure**, **impeachment-style removal by the State legislature**, deletion of the 'pleasure' doctrine, and **no Chancellorship of universities**.

**S.R. Bommai (1994)** is the controlling authority: the **floor of the House** is the sole test of majority; the proclamation is **justiciable**; the **Assembly may only be dissolved after both Houses of Parliament approve**; and the power is **not available for a mere failure of law and order or corruption**. Its use fell sharply thereafter.

**Sarkaria (1983-88)** — **247 recommendations**, the **Inter-State Council** (created 1990), sparing use of Article 356, consultation before **Article 200** reservation, and **All India Services strengthened, not weakened**. **Punchhi (2007-10)** — a **localised emergency** confined to a district or part of a State, and **fixed tenure** for the Governor.

The **129th Constitution Amendment Bill** and the accompanying Union Territories law, examined by a **Joint Parliamentary Committee**. The **Ram Nath Kovind Committee (2024)** recommended a two-step move — Lok Sabha and Assemblies together, local bodies within **100 days** — with an **appointed date** and mid-term houses serving only the **unexpired term**.

items.t: The administrative argument on simultaneous elections
items.d: **For** — the **model code** freezes new schemes repeatedly through the cycle; **security forces and teachers** are diverted several times a year; **expenditure** duplicates. **Against** — it needs **curtailment or extension of assembly terms**, weakens the **accountability of a government to a mid-term verdict**, and requires **ratification by half the States**.

**Article 324** — superintendence, direction and control of elections, held to be a **plenary reservoir of power** where the law is silent (**Mohinder Singh Gill, 1978**). The **Model Code of Conduct** binds by consent and convention, not statute — the largest exercise of **non-statutory administrative authority** in India.

The **Special Intensive Revision** exercises of 2025-26 raised the classic administrative-law questions in a live setting: **burden of proof** on the elector, **adequacy of notice**, **time for objections**, and the **remedy for wrongful deletion**. It is the best current illustration of why **procedural fairness in a mass administrative process** is a constitutional question.

**Anoop Baranwal (2023)** directed appointment by a committee of **PM, Leader of Opposition and the Chief Justice of India** until Parliament legislated. The **CEC and Other ECs (Appointment) Act, 2023** replaced the CJI with a **Union Cabinet Minister** — restoring an executive majority on the panel, and now itself under challenge.

**Second Judges (1993)** and **Third Judges (1998)** created the collegium; the **99th Amendment and NJAC Act** were struck down in **2015** as violating **judicial independence**, itself basic structure. The unresolved issue is the **Memorandum of Procedure**, and the **transparency and delay** in the collegium's own working.

items.t: Judicial efficiency as an administrative problem
items.d: About **4.76 crore cases pending (NJDG, 2026)**. The administrative levers: **judge strength and vacancies**, **court infrastructure**, **e-Courts Phase III (₹7,210 crore)**, **National Judicial Data Grid** making pendency public, **mediation under the Mediation Act, 2023**, and **government as the largest litigant** — the **National Litigation Policy** target that has never been met.

items.t: Data protection and the constitutional turn
items.d: **Puttaswamy (2017)** held **privacy** a fundamental right under Article 21, with a **three-fold test** — legality, legitimate aim, proportionality. The **DPDP Act, 2023** with **Rules 2025** is its statutory expression, and its **Section 44(3)** amendment to **RTI Section 8(1)(j)** is where privacy and transparency now collide.

The constitutional position is that they are **not in tension**: **Article 38(2)** requires the State to minimise inequalities in income, status, facilities and opportunities. Administratively the tension is real — **land acquisition, forest diversion and urban renewal** all trade aggregate gain against concentrated loss, which is why **RFCTLARR 2013 and FRA 2006** attach **consent and compensation** conditions.

**Department** — full ministerial control, budgeted through the legislature, no separate legal personality. **Corporation** — created by a **special statute**, autonomy defined by that statute. **Company** — incorporated under the **Companies Act, 2013**, flexible, easy to create and to wind up.

**Maximum control, minimum flexibility.** Financed by the **Consolidated Fund**, staffed by **civil servants**, audited by the **CAG**, answerable through the minister. Examples: **Railways**, **Posts**, **All India Radio**, the **ordnance factories** before their 2021 corporatisation.

Created by a **special Act** which fixes its powers, finances and accountability — so autonomy is **as wide as the statute makes it**. Examples: **LIC (1956), FCI (1964), Airports Authority, Damodar Valley Corporation (1948)**, India's first. Its weakness: **amending the Act to change anything**.

**Section 2(45), Companies Act 2013** — not less than **51%** paid-up capital held by government. Easy to form by executive decision, flexible on staffing and pay. The critique is constitutional: it **escapes legislative scrutiny** at birth — a public enterprise created **without a debate**.

**Local knowledge**, **speed of response**, **adaptation to variation**, and the **legitimacy of a visible official**. no central design survives contact with **11 agro-climatic zones and 2.55 lakh gram panchayats** without field discretion.

items.t: Why India built a public sector
items.d: **Industrial Policy Resolution, 1956** and the **Mahalanobis** second plan: **capital scarcity**, the need for **heavy industry** no private investor would fund, **balanced regional development**, **employment** and the avoidance of **concentration of economic power**. Nehru's "**temples of modern India**."

**Schedule A** — 17 industries exclusively for the state (arms, atomic energy, railways, heavy industry). **Schedule B** — 12 industries progressively state-owned. **Schedule C** — the rest, left to the private sector. This is the architecture the **1991 policy** dismantled.

**New Industrial Policy, 1991** — reserved industries cut from **17 to 8**, then to **2** (atomic energy, railways) by 2001; **licensing abolished** except for a short list; **MRTP** pre-approval scrapped; loss-making units referred to the **BIFR**; **disinvestment** begun.

**New Public Sector Enterprise Policy, 2021** — **four strategic sectors** (atomic energy/space/defence; transport and telecom; power, petroleum, coal and minerals; banking, insurance and financial services) with a **bare-minimum** presence; **privatisation or closure** everywhere else.

A **graded autonomy** scheme rather than a status symbol. **Maharatna** may invest up to **₹5,000 crore** or **15% of net worth** in a single project without government approval; **Navratna** up to **₹1,000 crore**; **Miniratna I** up to **₹500 crore**. Autonomy here means **financial delegation**, nothing more.

**Arjun Sengupta Committee, 1987-88** — a negotiated **performance contract** between the enterprise and its ministry, scored annually on **financial and non-financial** parameters. India's earliest and most durable **NPM** device, now run by the **Department of Public Enterprises**.

A PSU carries **social obligations** a private firm does not — universal service, strategic supply, regional development, employment. Judge it on **capacity utilisation, technology absorption, safety, energy intensity, CSR under Section 135** and **social cost-benefit**, not profit alone.

Both things are true. It built **capabilities no private firm would have** — **ISRO, BHEL, ONGC, IOCL, the DRDO chain, LIC's household savings mobilisation**. It also produced **chronic loss-makers**, **overstaffing** and a **licence-era rent structure**.

**Peter Evans (Embedded Autonomy, 1995)** — a developmental state needs a bureaucracy **autonomous** enough to resist capture and **embedded** enough in industry to know what it needs. India's **space and atomic energy** programmes had both; the **licensing system** had embeddedness without autonomy — and became **capture**.

Largely, yes. Autonomy is granted by **executive delegation, not statute**; the **administrative ministry** controls the **board's composition**, the **capex approval**, and the **CMD's appointment through the PESB**. What exists is **delegated financial power**, not independence.

The classic statement: **the more autonomy an enterprise is given, the weaker the citizen's chain of accountability becomes**; the tighter the accountability, the less it can behave commercially. There is **no design that removes the tension** — only choices about where to sit on it.

**Parliament** — the **Committee on Public Undertakings (COPU)**, 22 members, no ministers. **CAG** — commercial audit under **Section 143(5)-(6), Companies Act 2013**, including **supplementary audit** and the **non-review certificate**. **Executive** — DPE guidelines, presidential directives, the **PESB** for appointments.

Worth quoting because it cuts against the grain: **Appleby opposed bringing public enterprises under CAG audit**, arguing that an audit designed for **regularity** would smother **commercial risk-taking**. The counter-argument is that **public money without public audit** is indefensible.

**Minority stake sale** (revenue, no control change); **strategic sale** with transfer of management (**Air India to Tata, 2022**; **VSNL, BALCO, Hindustan Zinc** earlier); **ETF route** (**CPSE ETF, Bharat 22**); and **asset monetisation** under the **NMP**, which transfers **operation** without **ownership**.

items.t: The case for and against disinvestment
items.d: **For** — fiscal space, better capital allocation, exposure to competition, and the state exiting sectors where it has **no comparative advantage**. **Against** — sale of **profit-making** assets to meet a **revenue** target, loss of the **strategic and social obligation** layer, and **employment** effects.

Evidence is mixed and should be written that way: competition **did** force efficiency in **telecom and aviation**; **listed CPSEs** improved governance under **SEBI's LODR**. But **valuation timing**, **strategic sale to a thin market**, and the **absence of a post-privatisation regulator** repeatedly weakened outcomes.

**SEBI's LODR** requires listed CPSEs to have **independent directors**, but a large share of positions stay **vacant** and independent directors are **appointed by the same ministry** that owns the shares. **Independence appointed by the controlling shareholder is a contradiction in terms.**

**Disinvestment Commission (G.V. Ramakrishna, 1996)** — a **National Investment Fund** ring-fencing proceeds so they finance **capital**, not **revenue** deficit; professional boards insulated from the ministry; and **DIPAM** as a single, transparent, calendared process rather than a year-end scramble.

items.t: Departmental to corporate — a live instance
items.d: The **ordnance factories** were converted into **seven Defence PSUs (2021)** — the largest recent transfer of form. Watch it as the natural exam case: did **corporatisation** deliver **autonomy**, or reproduce the same ministry control through a **shareholding department**?

groups.g: The Prime Minister and the Cabinet

items.d: **Article 74** — a Council of Ministers with the **Prime Minister at the head** to aid and advise the President, who **shall act** in accordance with that advice (**42nd Amendment**), with **one reconsideration** permitted (**44th**). **Article 75** — ministers appointed by the President on the PM's advice, **collectively responsible** to the House of the People.

items.t: The three tiers of the Council
items.d: **Cabinet Ministers** (the inner body that decides), **Ministers of State** (with or without independent charge), and **Deputy Ministers**. The **Cabinet is not mentioned in the original Constitution** — it entered through **Article 352's** reference inserted by the **44th Amendment**. **91st Amendment (2003)** capped the Council at **15% of the House**.

items.t: Did the 91st Amendment right-size the Council?
items.d: **Yes at the margin** — it ended jumbo ministries in several States and, with the **anti-defection** provision disqualifying a defector from ministerial office, removed the incentive to buy loyalty with berths. **No in substance** — the 15% cap is generous for large houses, and **parliamentary secretaries** were used to evade it until courts intervened.

items.t: Why the Indian PM is stronger than the British
items.d: **A written Constitution names him** (Article 74). He is **sole channel of communication** with the President (Article 78). India has **no elected upper chamber with real veto**, **no separate head-of-state convention constraining him**, a **larger patronage in appointments** through the ACC, and — decisively — **command of a federation's central transfers**.

He is constrained by **coalition arithmetic** where it exists, **judicial review** far stronger than in Britain, **federal resistance** from opposition-ruled States, and the fact that most administrative subjects are on the **State List**. The British PM faces a **unitary state**; the Indian PM must **negotiate one**.

The real decision-making sites: **Cabinet Committee on Security**, **on Economic Affairs**, **on Political Affairs**, **on Appointments (ACC)**, **on Parliamentary Affairs**, **on Investment and Growth**, **on Employment and Skill Development**. The **ACC** — PM and Home Minister — decides every senior appointment, and is where the political-permanent interface is actually managed.

**Article 77(3)** authorises the President to make rules for the more convenient transaction of business. The **Government of India (Transaction of Business) Rules, 1961** prescribe **which cases must go to the Cabinet**, which may be disposed of by a minister, and how **inter-ministerial consultation** occurs. **Read with the Allocation of Business Rules, this is Gulick's POSDCORB in Indian statutory form.**

groups.g: The Cabinet Secretariat and the PMO

items.d: The **Cabinet Secretary** is the **senior-most civil servant**, head of the **civil services**, ex-officio chairman of the **Committee of Secretaries**, and secretary to the Cabinet. Its function is **coordination**, not policy origination: it circulates Cabinet Notes, records decisions, monitors implementation and resolves inter-ministerial disagreement.

**Civil** (Cabinet coordination, the Rules of Business); **Military** (Military Affairs, and the Chief of Defence Staff's interface); **Intelligence** (the **Directorate General of Security** and **R&AW**, which report through the Cabinet Secretariat). It also houses the **Performance Management Division** that ran the **RFD** from 2009 to 2014.

items.t: The Cabinet Secretary as staff, not line
items.d: **Gulick's** distinction, exactly applied. The Cabinet Secretary has **no command over any ministry** — he cannot direct a Secretary to do anything. His authority is **advisory, persuasive and derived from proximity to the PM**. This is why **Committee of Secretaries** meetings matter more than any circular he could issue.

**Not a constitutional or statutory body** — an office of the PM's personal staff, headed by a **Principal Secretary**, with additional and joint secretaries, and no allocated subjects of its own. Its power is entirely **derived**: it is influential because the PM is, and to the degree the PM chooses.

From **Nehru's small secretariat** to a body that **clears files across ministries, drives flagship programmes, runs PRAGATI reviews, and holds the interface with States**. Its rise tracks the **presidentialisation** of parliamentary systems everywhere, and in India also the **decline of the Planning Commission** as a rival apex.

items.t: 'The people's PMO, not the Prime Minister's PMO'
items.d: The critique is about **accountability**: an office with great influence and **no departmental answerability** — no Demand for Grants of substance, no Standing Committee, no minister answerable for its decisions in the House. The defence is that **executive coordination** at scale requires an apex staff, and its output is the PM's own responsibility.

**Pro-Active Governance and Timely Implementation (2015)** — a **PM-chaired, multi-modal, video-conference** platform where the PM reviews stalled projects and grievances **directly with Union Secretaries and State Chief Secretaries**, on geo-tagged and dashboard data. It works because **the apex leader personally uses the data** — the strongest available instance of **Mayo's** attention effect at institutional scale.

It compresses **five layers of hierarchy into one meeting**, which is its power and its problem: it delivers **speed for the projects the apex looks at** and leaves everything else on the ordinary chain, and it **substitutes personal attention for institutional process** — a solution that does not survive a change of occupant.

The **Secretariat** frames policy, prepares legislation, allocates resources and evaluates; **executive agencies, attached and subordinate offices** implement. It is **Gulick's** policy-implementation split, adopted from the British model, and it is the reason a Secretary is not personally accountable for delivery in the field.

**Secretary → Additional Secretary → Joint Secretary → Director → Deputy Secretary → Under Secretary → Section Officer → Assistant Section Officer.** The **Joint Secretary** is the pivotal level — the first at which a file can effectively be settled and the first with a defined **charge** of subjects.

**Attached offices** provide **executive direction** and technical advice to the ministry on the implementation of its policies — the Directorate General of Health Services, the Central Water Commission. **Subordinate offices** are the **field agencies** that actually execute — customs houses, income tax circles, post offices.

Recommended by **ARC-I (1968)** and again by the **2nd ARC's 13th Report**: replace the **section with a hierarchy of clerks** by a **desk manned by an officer** who handles a subject end-to-end, cutting the file's journey from six or seven levels to **three**. Adopted **partially and reversibly** — the standing example of a structural reform that never landed.

They supply **local knowledge**, **adaptation to variation**, **speed of response** and the **visible official** whose presence gives an order legitimacy. Without them a central design meets a country of **11 agro-climatic zones and 2.55 lakh gram panchayats** with a single template.

**CBDT and CBIC** under the Central Boards of Revenue Act, 1963; the **Railway Board**. A board is used where the function is **technical, quasi-judicial and continuous**, and where **collective deliberation** is preferable to a single officer's decision — the classic case for **plural headship**.

items.t: Recruitment and appointment machinery at the top
items.d: **Appointments Committee of the Cabinet** for senior posts; **empanelment** at Joint Secretary and above, using **360-degree** inputs alongside the PAR; **Central Staffing Scheme** governing deputation to the Union; **Public Enterprises Selection Board** for CPSE boards; and **UPSC** for direct recruitment and lateral entry selection.

**Thompson's** reciprocal interdependence requires **mutual adjustment**, but the Indian Union's default device is a **committee**. Instruments that work: **Committee of Secretaries**, **Group of Ministers**, **PRAGATI**, **PM Gati Shakti's** shared spatial data layer, and **e-Office** making inter-ministerial reference traceable.

**M. Visvesvaraya's Planned Economy for India (1934)**; the **National Planning Committee (1938)** under **Nehru**; the **Bombay Plan (1944)** by eight industrialists; **M.N. Roy's People's Plan**; **Gandhian Plan (S.N. Agarwal)**. India had a **planning consensus before it had a state** — worth one line in any planning answer.

Created by a **Cabinet Resolution, 15 March 1950** — **never a constitutional or statutory body**. Chaired by the **Prime Minister**, with a Deputy Chairman of Cabinet rank. It formulated the Plans, allocated **Plan assistance** to States, and evaluated implementation through the **PEO**.

Also created by **resolution (1952)** — **PM, all Chief Ministers, Union ministers and Planning Commission members**. It **approved** the Plan, reviewed its working and recommended measures for national resources. Its purpose was **federal legitimation** of a Plan drafted centrally; in practice it **ratified rather than shaped**.

The basis of **Plan assistance** to States from **1969**, revised as **Gadgil–Mukherjee (1991)**: **population 60%, per capita income 25%, fiscal performance 7.5%, special problems 7.5%**. It mattered because the Planning Commission — a **non-statutory body** — was distributing **transfers** alongside the constitutional **Finance Commission**.

items.t: Why the Planning Commission was criticised
items.d: **No constitutional standing** yet real allocative power; **one-size-fits-all** schemes imposed on very different States; a **Plan–non-Plan** distinction that starved **maintenance** to fund new assets; **duplication** with the Finance Commission; and irrelevance to a **liberalised economy** where the state no longer directed investment.

The **French model** adopted from the **Eighth Plan (1992)**. The state ceased **directing** and began **signalling** — projections, priorities and incentives to guide private investment rather than allocate it. The Plan became a **statement of intent** with the **budget** as its only enforcement.

items.t: The end of the Plan–non-Plan distinction
items.d: **Rangarajan Committee (2011)** recommended abolition; implemented from **2017-18**. The distinction had produced a perverse incentive — build a school (Plan) and underfund its teachers and repairs (non-Plan). Expenditure is now classified as **revenue and capital**, which is the economically meaningful split.

Preparing one holistic national plan is hard because most subjects are on the **State List**, States have **divergent capacities and priorities**, data arrives at **different frequencies**, and **electoral cycles differ** across the federation. A single plan requires a **uniformity the Constitution deliberately denies**.

groups.g: NITI Aayog and the post-Plan era

items.d: **Cabinet Resolution, 1 January 2015.** **PM as Chairperson**; a **Vice-Chairperson**; **full-time and ex-officio members**; **special invitees**; a **CEO** of Secretary rank; the **Governing Council** of all Chief Ministers and Lieutenant Governors; and **Regional Councils** for specific issues.

From **allocation to advice** — no funds to distribute, so no leverage. From **top-down to 'cooperative and competitive federalism'**. From **five-year plans to strategy documents** — the **Three-Year Action Agenda**, **Seven-Year Strategy**, **Fifteen-Year Vision**, now **Viksit Bharat @2047**.

**Indices** — SDG India Index, Composite Water Management, School Education Quality, Health, Export Preparedness, **Fiscal Health Index** (first edition **January 2025**, Odisha first among 18 major States; **2026 edition released 11 March 2026**). Plus **Aspirational Districts and Blocks**, **DMEO** evaluation, and the **National Data and Analytics Platform**.

items.t: The National Data and Analytics Platform
items.d: A single interoperable portal for government datasets with standardised metadata and open access — its claim is the **democratisation of data**, letting States, researchers and citizens use the same evidence base as the Union. Its limits are **data quality at source, update frequency and coverage of State data**.

It has **no funds** and therefore no leverage; its recommendations are **not binding**; the **Finance Ministry** controls transfers and the **PMO** sets priorities; the **Governing Council** meets infrequently; and an **index without a consequence** changes behaviour only where a State chooses to care about rank.

items.t: The case that NITI works as designed
items.d: It was **never meant** to allocate — that was the criticism of its predecessor. As a **think tank plus federal convener**, it produced the **MPI**, the **SDG index**, **Aspirational Districts** (a genuinely new delivery model), and a **language of competitive federalism** that States now use themselves.

The real fiscal instrument that replaced Plan transfers. **Chaturvedi Committee (2011)** and the **Sub-Group of Chief Ministers (Shivraj Singh Chouhan, 2015)** rationalised them into **core of the core, core and optional**, with **60:40** sharing (**90:10** for North-Eastern and Himalayan States). States argue they **crowd out State priorities** through mandatory matching.

items.t: Political interference in the development process
items.d: Its specific administrative forms: **scheme naming and launch timing** around elections, **beneficiary selection pressure**, **project location** decided by constituency rather than need, and **transfer of the officer who resists**. The structural remedies are **objective targeting criteria, published allocation formulas and social audit**.

**Article 243ZD** — every State shall constitute a **District Planning Committee** to consolidate the plans prepared by panchayats and municipalities into a **draft district development plan**, with **four-fifths of members elected** from among panchayat and municipal members. **Article 243ZE** requires a **Metropolitan Planning Committee** for areas above ten lakh.

They are **constituted late or not at all** in several States; they lack **technical planning staff**; the **funds they would plan for are tied** to scheme guidelines set elsewhere; **parastatals and mission societies** bypass them entirely; and the **draft plan** they produce has no statutory consequence.

**Kerala's People's Plan Campaign (1996)** devolved **35-40% of the State Plan outlay** to local bodies with **untied funds**, mass **Gram Sabha** participation, **volunteer resource persons** and technical **expert committees** to vet projects. It is the reference case because it transferred **money and technical capacity together**.

It **is** context-sensitive — local bodies know which hamlet lacks water. But **local politics reproduces local inequality**: the dominant caste's ward is prioritised, and the marginalised may be **better protected by a rule made far away** than by a decision made nearby. Decentralisation needs **earmarking and social audit** to be equitable.

**Signature argument.** The **73rd and 74th Amendments** made local bodies **planning authorities**; the **fiscal and administrative system** kept planning **central**. Money arrives as **tied scheme funds** with pre-set components, so the panchayat's plan can only **ratify** what has already been decided.

**Untied funds** as a meaningful share of local receipts — which is exactly what **16th Finance Commission local body grants** could become if largely untied; **technical planning support** at block level; **activity mapping** that assigns each of the 29 subjects to a specific tier; and **making the DPC's plan a statutory input** to the State budget.

groups.g: The political executive in the State

items.d: "There shall be a Council of Ministers with the **Chief Minister at the head** to **aid and advise** the Governor in the exercise of his functions, **except in so far as he is by or under this Constitution required to exercise any of his functions in his discretion**." The whole federal argument sits in that exception.

**Article 163(2)** makes the Governor's own view on **whether a matter falls within his discretion** final, and **not questionable on the ground that he ought or ought not to have acted in his discretion**. **Shamsher Singh (1974)** narrowed discretion to what the Constitution **expressly or by necessary implication** requires — but the clause remains a **self-certifying** power.

**Article 164** — appointed by the Governor; ministers hold office during the Governor's pleasure; the Council is **collectively responsible to the Legislative Assembly**. In practice the CM's power exceeds the PM's within the State, because **transfers and postings of the entire State cadre** are effectively at his disposal.

The **administrative head** of the State — principal adviser to the CM, head of the State civil services, chairman of coordination committees, and the **crisis manager** in disaster and law-and-order emergencies. Like the Cabinet Secretary he is **staff, not line**: influence flows from **proximity to the Chief Minister**, not from command.

Departments headed by **Principal Secretary or Secretary**, mirroring the Union's structure. Its functions are **policy, legislation, budget, personnel and coordination**. Its characteristic weakness is that it is **staffed largely by generalists** on short tenures supervising **technical directorates** with career specialists.

They vary with the **nature of leadership** (a dominant leader can hold a coalition that a consensual one cannot), the **character of the parties** (ideological versus regional-personal), and **conditions** — pre-poll alliances behave differently from post-poll arrangements. Administratively the effect is **departmental fiefdoms** and slower Cabinet decisions.

**Secretariat** — policy formulation, legislation, budget, rules, personnel and control. **Directorate** — technical advice, execution, field supervision, and the **professional memory** of the department. Health, education, agriculture, PWD and police each have this **two-headed** structure.

There is **no statutory allocation** between the two; the Secretariat drifts into **case work and transfers**, and the Directorate is drawn into **policy notes**. Both then do **each other's work badly** — the generalist decides technical questions and the technical head spends the day on files.

**Delay** — the same file is examined twice; **demoralisation** of the technical cadre, whose advice can be overturned without reasons; **diffused accountability** when a programme fails; and **loss of technical memory**, because the officer who decided is transferred and the one who knew was not asked.

Three, and they conflict. **Merge** the two at the top so one officer both advises and executes (the **integrated** or **Bihar** pattern). **Separate** them sharply, giving the Directorate statutory delegation. Or **shrink** the Secretariat to policy alone, as the **2nd ARC's 15th Report on State and District Administration** proposed.

items.t: The generalist–specialist question at State level
items.d: It bites harder here than at the Union, because State departments are **overwhelmingly technical** — irrigation, power, health, forests. The workable answer is **specialist headship of the Directorate with statutory delegation**, generalist headship of the Secretariat, and **domain-trained generalists** through Mission Karmayogi's competency framework.

**Articles 315-323** apply to States as to the Union — appointment by the **Governor**, removal only by the **President** on a Supreme Court reference, expenses **charged** on the State's Consolidated Fund. Yet several SPSCs have faced **recruitment scandals, prolonged vacancies and delayed results** — insulation of tenure without insulation of process.

**State Electricity Regulatory Commissions** under the Electricity Act, 2003; **State Information Commissions**; **State Human Rights Commissions**; **Lokayuktas**; **State Consumer Commissions**; **State Election Commissions** under Article 243K. Their common failure mode is **vacancy** — a body that exists on paper and cannot sit.

**Article 243I and 243Y** — the constitutional bridge between the State and its local bodies, and the weakest link in Indian fiscal federalism. Late constitution, delayed reports, **no action-taken memorandum laid before the legislature**, and recommendations **routinely not accepted** — the third tier's fiscal fate is decided here and mostly by default.

The structural critique to write. **Water boards, housing boards, development authorities, Smart City SPVs, mission societies and DRDAs** carry out functions listed for local bodies in the **Eleventh and Twelfth Schedules**, and report to the State, not the elected local body. **Rhodes's hollowing out**, applied downward inside a federation.

The technical fix that would matter most. For each of the **29 and 18 subjects**, specify which **activity** within it belongs to which **tier** — planning, execution, maintenance, supervision, financing — and attach the **funds and functionaries** to that assignment. **Kerala and Karnataka** did it; most States published a list of subjects and stopped.

Quote the proportion when arguing about capacity: States carry **roughly 60% of general government expenditure**, employ the overwhelming majority of public servants, and own the subjects that touch the citizen daily — **police, land, health, education, water, agriculture**. **Reform that does not reach the State does not reach the citizen.**

It has been the **unit of Indian administration** since the Mughal **sarkar**, survived the Company, the Crown and independence, and remains the level at which **land, law and order, elections, disaster and welfare delivery** converge on one accountable officer. **No reform has ever proposed abolishing it** — which is itself the argument for its fitness.

items.t: The three hats, and the fourth
items.d: **Collector** — land revenue, land records, acquisition, treasury. **District Magistrate** — law and order, preventive powers, licensing, jail supervision, executive magistracy. **Deputy Commissioner** — development coordination, scheme implementation, chair of committees. The **fourth hat** is now **Chairperson of the District Disaster Management Authority** under **Section 25 of the DM Act, 2005**.

Under the **BNSS (in force 1 July 2024)** — orders in urgent cases of nuisance or apprehended danger (the successor to **Section 144 CrPC**), **security proceedings**, **dispersal of unlawful assembly**, **requisition of armed force**, and **executive magistracy** distinct from the judicial magistracy separated by **Article 50** and the 1973 Code.

Still the office's legal foundation: **maintenance of land records** (khatauni, jamabandi, mutation), **settlement operations**, **land acquisition** under the **RFCTLARR Act, 2013**, **recovery of public dues as arrears of land revenue**, **relief and remission** in calamity, and **custody of the district treasury**.

Where the modern Collector actually spends his time: chairing the **District Development Coordination and Monitoring Committee (DISHA)** with MPs, the **DDMA**, the **district grievance forum**, and the **district-level bankers' committee**; and acting as **District Election Officer**, **District Census Officer** and **returning officer**.

**Sub-Divisional Magistrate / Sub-Divisional Officer** at the subdivision; **Tehsildar / Mamlatdar** at the tehsil with revenue and executive magisterial powers; **Kanungo** and **Patwari / Talathi / Village Accountant** at the base — the **Mughal-named** officers who still hold the land record on which most of the district's work rests.

groups.g: The changing role and the reform debate

items.t: Why the role must be redefined
items.d: Four pressures: **panchayats and municipalities** now hold constitutional functions the Collector once discharged; **parastatals and missions** deliver outside his chain; **regulatory bodies and courts** have taken parts of his discretion; and **DBT and digital delivery** removed the intermediation that made him the citizen's point of access.

**Divest** — strip development functions to the elected **Zila Parishad**, leaving the Collector with **regulation, revenue, law and order and disaster** (the **G.V.K. Rao** direction, with a separate **District Development Commissioner**). **Retain and reorient** — keep him as the **single coordinating authority**, because no other office can convene every department in a crisis.

Its **15th Report, State and District Administration**, favoured **strengthening the elected district government** while retaining the Collector for **regulatory, law-and-order, land and disaster** functions, and recommended a **minimum tenure**, a clear **activity map** between him and the Zila Parishad, and a **District Council chaired by an elected head**.

The case: modern district work is **multi-departmental and time-critical** — a heatwave, an epidemic, an aspirational-district target — and hierarchy cannot move at that speed. **Follett's law of the situation** and the **Incident Response System** are the theory; the practical form is a **district team with pre-assigned incident roles**.

items.t: The limit of the teamwork argument
items.d: Necessary balance. Hierarchy exists in the district for reasons that have not disappeared: **statutory powers vest in a named officer**, **coercive decisions need a single accountable signature**, and in a **law-and-order emergency** consensus is a luxury. The answer is **hierarchy for authority, teams for delivery** — not one replacing the other.

The average district tenure in many States is well under two years. Its consequences are exact: **no incentive to begin anything that outlasts the posting**, **loss of local knowledge**, and **the transfer as the enforcement mechanism** for every improper pressure. **T.S.R. Subramanian (2013)** ordered a two-year minimum; compliance is partial.

The administrative case for smaller districts is **span of control and access** — travel time to headquarters, population per officer. The critique is that the actual drivers are **politico-populist** — a new district as an electoral promise — and the costs are real: **new establishment, split cadres, divided records and thinner senior staffing across more units**.

The district phase of IAS induction is where **field judgement** is formed — revenue cases decided, magistracy exercised, a subdivision independently run. The critique is that it has become **shorter, more ceremonial and less supervised**, so officers reach senior posts without having been **personally answerable for a decision** in the field.

groups.g: The district as a delivery platform

items.d: **2018, 112 districts**, on five themes — health and nutrition, education, agriculture and water, financial inclusion and skill development, basic infrastructure. Its method is **delta ranking**: scoring **improvement, not level**, so the weakest can top the table. **Converge, collaborate, compete**, with a **central prabhari officer** attached to each district.

It supplied the four things district programmes usually lack: **a small number of measurable indicators**, **real-time data with public ranking**, **a senior officer with a personal stake**, and **peer competition** rather than central direction. **Mark Moore's** strategic triangle — public value, authorising environment and operational capacity — aligned for once.

**2023, 500 blocks** — the same method taken one tier down, on the finding that **district averages conceal block-level deprivation**. Watch it as the natural exam case: does delta ranking survive at a level with **no dedicated officer, no separate budget and far weaker data**?

**DDMA** under **Section 25, DM Act 2005** — chaired by the **District Magistrate**, with the elected district head as co-chair. It prepares the **District Disaster Management Plan**, and in an emergency the **Incident Response System** assigns pre-designated roles so command does not have to be improvised. The **2025 amendment** strengthened planning and urban arrangements.

**Common Service Centres** as the assisted last mile; **e-District** for certificates; **SVAMITVA** property cards (**2.5 crore+** issued); **land record digitisation** under DILRMP; **geo-tagged** asset monitoring for MGNREGA; **CPGRAMS** feeding district grievance review. The district became a **data node**, not merely a field office.

The honest closing critique. The Collector **chairs** many committees and **commands** only the revenue establishment. Line department officers answer to their **directorate**; mission societies to the **State**; parastatals to their **board**. He carries **responsibility without authority**, which is why the office's effectiveness varies so sharply with the individual.

groups.g: Human resource development and the personnel function

items.t: The personnel machinery of the Union
items.d: **Department of Personnel and Training (DoPT)** under the **PMO** — cadre controlling authority for the **IAS**, policy on recruitment, training, conduct and vigilance. **UPSC** for recruitment and disciplinary advice; **Staff Selection Commission** for Group B and C; **MHA** for the **IPS**, **MoEFCC** for the **IFoS**.

**All India Services as on 1 January 2025** — **IAS sanctioned 6,877, in position 5,577, vacant 1,300**; **IPS sanctioned 5,099, vacant 505**; **IFoS sanctioned 3,193, vacant 1,029**. Close to a fifth of the sanctioned IAS simply does not exist.

items.t: The Baswan finding on cadre strength
items.d: **B.S. Baswan Committee (2016)** found the shortfall structural: **intake was cut in the 1990s** and the gap compounds for **thirty years**, since a missing 1996 batch is a missing 2026 Joint Secretary. **Promotee quotas** cannot close a deficit at the senior levels where it bites.

items.t: The constitutional position of the services
items.d: **Article 308-314, Part XIV.** **Article 309** — Parliament or the legislature may regulate recruitment and conditions; until then, **rules by the President or Governor**. **Article 310** — the **doctrine of pleasure**. **Article 311** — the **procedural protection**. **Article 312** — Rajya Sabha may create a **new All India Service** by **two-thirds** resolution.

items.t: Why India kept an All India Service
items.d: **Sardar Patel's** case in the Constituent Assembly — a service with a **national outlook** serving under States is the **link that holds a federation of continental scale together**. "An efficient, disciplined and contented service... is a **sine qua non** of sound administration under a democratic regime **even more than under an authoritarian** rule."

**Articles 315-323.** Members appointed by the **President**, removable only for **misbehaviour on a Supreme Court reference**, **expenses charged on the Consolidated Fund**, **no further employment under government** after office (Chairman barred entirely).

Insulation exists at the **appointment and tenure** end. It does not extend to **which posts are referred**, to **cadre strength**, to the **timing of requisitions**, or to State Public Service Commissions, several of which have faced **recruitment scandals and delayed appointments**.

**Kothari Committee (1976)** created the present **Preliminary–Main–Interview** structure with optionals. **Satish Chandra (1989)** added the **essay** and cut interview weightage. **Alagh (2001)** proposed a common aptitude test, producing **CSAT (2011)**. **Baswan (2016)** reviewed age, attempts and the optional's role.

**Kingsley's** concept: a bureaucracy that **mirrors the society** it serves. **Passive** representation (composition) is expected to produce **active** representation (responsive decisions). India's instruments are **reservation under Articles 16(4) and 335**, and the **AIS insider-outsider cadre allocation** balancing State representation.

India uses **quotas** (a hard floor); the **US** uses **goals and timetables** after **Bakke** and **Grutter** limited quotas; **South Africa** uses **employment equity plans**; **Malaysia's** bumiputra policy is the closest analogue. The Indian design is unusual in being **constitutionally mandated rather than administratively adopted**.

The live controversy. Introduced for **Joint Secretary, Director and Deputy Secretary** posts through UPSC-conducted selection from **2018**; the **2024 advertisement for 45 posts was withdrawn** after objections that **contract appointments carried no reservation**. The unresolved questions are **reservation, conflict of interest and cooling-off**.

items.t: The case for and against lateral entry
items.d: **For** — domain depth in **finance, energy, digital and climate** that a generalist career cannot supply; contestability at the top. **Against** — it **bypasses reservation**, weakens the **career incentive** of the regular cadre, and risks **revolving-door capture** if the entrant returns to the sector he regulated.

**Generalist** — trained mind, coordination, breadth, political sense, resistance to capture. **Specialist** — domain competence, credibility with the sector. The Indian answer since **ARC-I** has been to keep generalist leadership and add **domain specialisation after mid-career**, which **Hota (2004)** and **Mission Karmayogi** both pursue.

The dichotomy is false at the top. Senior posts require **judgement under political conditions** (generalist) and **command of the sector's evidence** (specialist). The design answer is **specialised career streams within a generalist service** plus **lateral depth** — not a choice between two cadres.

**LBSNAA Mussoorie** (IAS and the common Foundation Course); **SVPNPA Hyderabad** (IPS); **NADT Nagpur** (IRS); **IGNFA Dehradun** (IFoS); **ISTM** for Secretariat staff; **NIRDPR** for rural development; **State ATIs**; and the **National Training Policy, 2012** requiring an annual training plan and a training manager in every department.

**National Programme for Civil Services Capacity Building, September 2020.** Its shift is from **rule-based to role-based** training: **FRAC** (Framework of Roles, Activities and Competencies) defines the competencies a post needs; **iGOT-Karmayogi** delivers online; **behaviour, functional and domain** competencies are tracked per official.

Established **2021** — it approves **Annual Capacity Building Plans**, harmonises training institutions, audits their quality, and builds shared learning resources. It is **recommendatory to ministries**, which is the structural limit on what it can enforce.

**1.7 crore+ registered users (August 2026)**; about **10.5 lakh officials** trained under **Rashtriya Karmayogi Jan Seva** (Phase II ended **10 February 2026**) with **16,000+ master trainers**; MoUs with **30 States and UTs**; **1.75 lakh ULB officials** onboarded; **Amrit Gyaan Kosh** with **70+ case studies**.

**Completion is not competence** — a course finished on a portal is an **output**, not an outcome. There is **no link to posting or promotion**, so the incentive is weak; **behavioural change** is untested; and the **course-hour metric** is a textbook instance of **Goodhart's law**.

**Training** is **individual, skill-focused, episodic and course-shaped**. **Capacity building** is **institutional** — it includes **systems, data, processes, structures and organisational culture** as well as people. A fully trained officer in a broken institution still cannot deliver.

The district phase is where an officer acquires **field judgement** — revenue, magistracy, disaster, and the habit of being personally answerable. The critique is that it has become **shorter, more ceremonial, less supervised**, and that officers reach senior posts having **never independently run a subdivision**.

Linking **FRAC competencies** to **postings and empanelment** would supply the **instrumentality** that **Vroom's** expectancy theory says is missing. The risks are real — **gaming, subjective assessment, and a competency framework that becomes a paper exercise** — so it must be **externally validated**.

**AIS (Conduct) Rules, 1968** and **CCS (Conduct) Rules, 1964**. **Rule 3** — every member shall maintain **absolute integrity**, **devotion to duty**, and do nothing **unbecoming**; and shall maintain **political neutrality**. **Rule 3(3)(iii)** requires **oral directions to be confirmed in writing**.

**Political activity and candidature**; **criticism of government policy** in public; **joining associations prejudicial to sovereignty**; **acceptance of gifts** beyond limits; **speculation in securities**; **private trade**; and **annual immovable property returns**. Note the pattern: they restrain **expression and association** far more than they compel **performance**.

**311(1)** — no dismissal or removal by an authority **subordinate to the appointing authority**. **311(2)** — no dismissal, removal or **reduction in rank** except after an **inquiry** in which the charges are communicated and a **reasonable opportunity of being heard** is given.

**(a)** conviction on a **criminal charge**; **(b)** where the authority is satisfied that holding an inquiry is **not reasonably practicable**, for **reasons to be recorded in writing**; **(c)** where the **President or Governor** is satisfied that in the **interest of the security of the State** an inquiry is not expedient. Each requires a **recorded, reviewable** satisfaction.

**CCS (CCA) Rules, 1965** — **minor penalties** (censure, withholding of increment or promotion, recovery) and **major penalties** (reduction in rank, compulsory retirement, removal, dismissal). Major penalties require a **charge sheet, inquiry officer, presenting officer, defence assistant, inquiry report and second-stage UPSC consultation**.

The proceedings take **years**, run in parallel with **criminal trials**, and are **appealable to a tribunal and then a High Court**. **Suspension** becomes the real penalty and is often prolonged. The net effect is that **procedural protection designed against arbitrariness has become protection against consequence**.

Take a careful position. It protects the officer who **refuses an unlawful order** — remove it and neutrality has no floor. The defect is not the **protection** but its **operation**: the answer is **time-bound inquiry, fewer stages, and independent inquiry officers**, plus honest use of **FR 56(j)** review, not repeal.

groups.g: Neutrality, activism and the political interface

items.d: Not indifference to **outcomes** but **impartiality between parties**: the civil servant serves the **government of the day** with equal energy, gives **frank advice in private**, and **executes the lawful decision in public**. The **Whitehall** convention, imported with the ICS and preserved by **Rule 3**.

The evidence for the charge: **transfer as a political instrument**, **empanelment sensitive to preference**, **post-retirement appointments** creating anticipatory alignment, and officers publicly identified with a regime's programmes. put it as civil servants exhibiting their political masters' values.

The 1970s debate, still live. **Committed** — an administration must share the **constitutional and developmental commitment** of the elected government to implement it energetically. **Neutral** — commitment to a **government** is indistinguishable in practice from commitment to a **party**. Resolve it as **committed to the Constitution, neutral between parties**.

The officer who **publicly** pursues an agenda — through the press, social media or litigation. Defensible where it enforces **law against illegality** (**Ashok Khemka's** mutation cancellation, **T.N. Seshan's** enforcement of the model code); corrosive where it substitutes **personal preference for the elected government's mandate**.

**T.S.R. Subramanian v. Union of India (2013)** — a **Civil Services Board** to recommend transfers and postings, a **minimum tenure** of two years, and **oral instructions to be recorded in writing**. States were directed to comply; **compliance has been partial and reversible**, since the Board's advice can be overridden with reasons.

The **single most consequential** personnel issue in India. Frequent, mid-tenure, punitive transfers destroy **institutional memory**, remove the **incentive to start anything**, and are the **enforcement mechanism** for every other pressure. **Fix tenure and half the neutrality problem resolves itself.**

Three drivers: **coalition and then single-party dominance** changing the space for advice; the **PMO and CMO** centralising decisions and reducing the Secretary's role; and **media and social media** pushing officers into visibility that the neutrality convention assumed they would not have.

items.t: The line between direction and interference
items.d: The formulation to write. The political executive is **entitled to decide policy, set priorities and demand results**. It is not entitled to direct **who gets a licence, who is transferred, or how a case is investigated**. Every reform proposal — Civil Services Board, State Security Commission, PESB — is an attempt to **draw that line institutionally**.

They may **vote**; they may **not** join or assist a political party, canvass, contest, or express public political views. The justification is that the **appearance of impartiality** is part of the service's capital. The counter is that a **blanket bar on all political expression** is disproportionate to that end.

**Joint Consultative Machinery (1966)** — **National, Departmental and Office Councils**, with **compulsory arbitration** on pay, allowances and hours; recognised associations under the **CCS (RSA) Rules, 1993**. **Strikes are not a right** — **All India Bank Employees Association (1962)** held there is no fundamental right to strike.

**Total expenditure ₹53.5 lakh crore; capital expenditure ₹12.2 lakh crore; fiscal deficit 4.3% of GDP; debt 55.6% of GDP; net tax receipts ₹28.7 lakh crore; Finance Commission grants to States ₹1.4 lakh crore.** Always **date the figure** — an undated number reads as recall, a dated one as scholarship.
**Centre's fiscal deficit target 3.5% of GDP by 2030-31**; **States 3% of GSDP**. It fixes the **glide path** the next five years of budgeting must follow, and it binds States as well as the Union.

**Article 112** — the **Annual Financial Statement**. **Article 113** — Demands for Grants, moved only on the **President's recommendation**. **Article 114** — the **Appropriation Bill**; no money may be withdrawn from the **Consolidated Fund** except under an appropriation made by law. **Article 266** Consolidated and Public Accounts; **Article 267** Contingency Fund.

**Presentation** (1 February since 2017); **general discussion**; **Standing Committee scrutiny** of Demands during a recess; **voting on Demands** with **cut motions** — policy cut (₹1), economy cut (specified reduction), token cut (₹100); the **guillotine**; the **Appropriation Bill**; the **Finance Bill** within **75 days**.

**Disapproval of policy cut** — 'that the amount be reduced to ₹1', a challenge to the policy itself. **Economy cut** — a specified reduction, arguing waste. **Token cut** — 'reduced by ₹100', to ventilate a **specific grievance**. All three are devices for **discussion**, since none has passed in decades.

items.t: Vote on account and the other grants
items.d: **Vote on account (Article 116)** — an advance for part of the year pending completion of the process. **Supplementary, additional and excess grants (Article 115)** — excess grants require **PAC** examination first. **Token grant** for a new service. **Vote of credit** and **exceptional grant** for unforeseen or non-routine demands.

**Charged on the Consolidated Fund** — not submitted to the vote: **interest and debt charges**, the **salaries of the President, Speaker, judges, CAG, UPSC Chairman**, and **court decrees**. It exists to protect **independence** and **contractual obligation** from an annual majority — but it also places a large share of expenditure **beyond the vote**.

**Department of Economic Affairs** — budget formulation, macro policy, capital markets, external finance. **Department of Expenditure** — sanctions, the **GFR 2017**, PFMS, pay. **Department of Revenue** — CBDT and CBIC. **DIPAM** — disinvestment. **DFS** — banking and insurance. It is both **guardian of the purse** and **macro-policy authority**.

**Advancement to 1 February (2017)** so appropriation is complete before the financial year begins and departments can spend from April; **merger of the Railway Budget** into the general Budget; **abolition of the Plan–non-Plan** distinction; and a **Treasury Single Account** with **PFMS** just-in-time release.

groups.g: The budget as a political instrument

items.t: Why the budget is political, not technical
items.d: It **allocates scarce resources between competing claims**, and each allocation names a **winner and a loser**. It is a **statement of priorities in numbers**, an instrument of **federal bargaining**, a **signal to markets**, and, at its most visible, an **electoral instrument**.

Its distributive levers: the **direct-indirect tax mix** decides who pays; **subsidies and transfers** decide who receives; **capital expenditure** decides which regions and sectors grow; **cesses and surcharges** are **not shareable with States**, so their use shifts the federal balance without any change to the Finance Commission's award.

The problem is not **welfare expenditure**, which is a constitutional obligation, but **unfunded, untargeted and unreviewed** commitments — **free power, farm loan waivers, old pension restoration** — that create a **permanent revenue liability** for a **one-time political return**.

Institutional, not exhortatory: **FRBM targets** with a transparent escape clause; an **independent Fiscal Council** costing announcements (**N.K. Singh, 2017** — still not created); **medium-term expenditure frameworks**; **RBI's** State finance report as a public benchmark; and **Article 293's** borrowing consent.

**Consolidated Fund (Article 266(1))** — all revenues, loans raised and loan recoveries; nothing leaves it without an **appropriation by law**. **Public Account (266(2))** — money where government acts as a **banker** (provident funds, small savings); no appropriation needed. **Contingency Fund (267)** — at the **President's disposal** for urgent unforeseen expenditure, later regularised.

items.t: The separation of accounts from audit
items.d: Completed at the Union in **1976**. Previously the **CAG both kept the accounts and audited them** — auditing his own work. Now the **Controller General of Accounts** in the Finance Ministry compiles accounts; the CAG **audits** them. In the **Railways, Posts and Defence**, departmentalised accounting applies.

**Cash** records receipts and payments **when money moves** — simple, matches appropriation, and is what India uses. **Accrual** records **when the obligation arises** — it reveals **liabilities, depreciation and the real cost of assets**. The **12th Finance Commission** recommended a **move to accrual**; the **GASAB** has been developing standards since.

items.t: Why the shift to accrual is slow
items.d: It requires an **asset register** that mostly does not exist, **valuation** of assets acquired decades ago, **retraining** of the entire accounting cadre, and — the real obstacle — it would **disclose liabilities** (pensions, guarantees, arrears) that cash accounting keeps invisible.

items.t: PFMS and the Treasury Single Account
items.d: **Public Financial Management System** tracks a release from sanction to **the beneficiary's account**, ending **float** parked in implementing-agency accounts. The **Treasury Single Account** for autonomous bodies means money is drawn only when needed. Together they addressed the oldest Indian problem: **released is not the same as spent**.

It delivered **real-time expenditure data**, ended **ways-and-means surprises** for States, made **bill-passing time measurable**, and cut the **March rush** somewhat. It did not change **what** was budgeted or **why** — an efficiency gain in **execution**, not in **allocation**.

**General Financial Rules, 2017** as the procedural code; **Delegation of Financial Powers Rules**; **internal audit** by the Chief Controller of Accounts; **Financial Adviser** in each ministry, reporting to both the Secretary and the Finance Ministry; and the **Integrated Financial Advice** scheme. Internal control **precedes** external audit and is the weaker of the two in India.

**Articles 148-151.** Appointed by the **President**; removable only **like a Supreme Court judge**; **salary and expenses charged** on the Consolidated Fund; **ineligible for further office** under the Union or any State after demitting. **Ambedkar** called the CAG "probably the **most important officer** in the Constitution of India".

**Regularity or compliance** — was the expenditure within the sanction and the rules? **Propriety** — was it wise, faithful and economical, even if lawful? **Performance** — did the programme achieve **economy, efficiency and effectiveness**? The third is where the CAG's real influence now lies.

Expenditure should not **prima facie be more than the occasion demands**; no authority should sanction expenditure **directly or indirectly to its own advantage**; public money should not be used for the **benefit of a particular person or section** unless justified; and **allowances should not be a source of profit**.

The chain: **CAG audits → reports to the President or Governor (Article 151) → laid before the legislature → examined by PAC or COPU → Action Taken Notes from the ministry → further PAC report.** Executive answerability to Parliament in finance runs through this chain and nowhere else.

Reports are **tabled late**, sometimes years after the transaction; the **PAC's** capacity limits it to a fraction of paragraphs; **Action Taken Notes** are delayed or perfunctory; the CAG's findings are **recommendatory** with no power to **surcharge or disallow**; and **audit follows the money after it is gone**.

items.t: The office under the public eye
items.d: Performance audits on **spectrum, coal blocks and the Commonwealth Games** put the CAG at the centre of public debate — and drew the counter-charge that **presumptive-loss** estimation strays from audit into **policy evaluation**. The same reports raised both its salience and its exposure.

The modern position: audit's purpose is **assurance and improvement** — confirming that accounts present a true picture, that controls work, and that lessons feed back into design. **Constructive audit** engages the auditee during the exercise; a purely adversarial audit produces **defensive record-keeping**, not better administration.

items.t: The reform agenda for the CAG
items.d: A **multi-member CAG** (2nd ARC and the Shunglu-era debate) so a single officer does not carry the institution; a **statutory audit board**; **audit of PPP concessionaires and of bodies substantially financed** by government; **timely tabling**; and **capacity in data analytics** to audit systems rather than sample vouchers.

The weakest link. **Article 243J and 243Z** leave local audit to State law; the CAG provides **Technical Guidance and Supervision** to the Director of Local Fund Audit. **Local body accounts are frequently years in arrears**, which is why **Finance Commission grants** are increasingly conditioned on **online publication of audited accounts**.

groups.g: Fiscal federalism and the 16th Finance Commission

items.d: **Article 280** — constituted every **five years**, it recommends the **distribution of net tax proceeds between Union and States** (vertical), the **allocation among States** (horizontal), the **principles of grants-in-aid under Article 275**, and measures to **augment State funds to supplement the resources of panchayats and municipalities**.

**Dr Arvind Panagariya**, report tabled **1 February 2026** for the award period **2026-31**. **Devolution held at 41%.** Horizontal weights: **income distance 42.5%, population (2011) 17.5%, demographic performance 10%, area 10%, forest and ecology 10%, contribution to GDP 10%.**

items.t: What is new in the 16th FC award
items.d: The examinable change: a **new 10% weight for contribution to GDP** — rewarding the larger producing States — and the **dropping of tax effort** as a criterion. It is a partial answer to southern States' long complaint that the formula **penalised those that performed on demography and growth**.

**₹7.91 lakh crore** for local bodies — **rural ₹4.35 lakh crore, urban ₹3.56 lakh crore** — plus a **disaster corpus of ₹2,04,401 crore**. This is the single largest lever available for fixing the third tier's fiscal hollowness, and its effect turns entirely on **how much of it is untied**.

The sharpest States' grievance. **Cesses and surcharges are not part of the divisible pool** under **Article 270**, so their rising share means the States' **effective** receipt is **below the notified 41%**. The award can be honoured in full while the shareable base itself shrinks.

**Article 243I and 243Y** require a **State Finance Commission every five years** to recommend the distribution between the State and its local bodies. In practice they are **constituted late**, **reports are not tabled with an action-taken memorandum**, and recommendations are **frequently not accepted** — the break in the fiscal chain.

items.t: Is the Finance Commission strengthening local bodies?
