items.d: **Yes** — successive Commissions have made local grants a **direct, formula-based, growing** transfer, conditioned on **audited accounts and own-revenue effort**. **No** — most of it is **tied** to water and sanitation, it **bypasses the State's own devolution failure**, and it cannot substitute for **functionaries and taxation powers**.

**Article 279A** — the **GST Council**, with the Union holding **one-third** and all States together **two-thirds** of the weighted vote, and a **three-fourths** majority required. States surrendered the **power to tax goods and services independently** — the largest single transfer of fiscal sovereignty since 1950 — in exchange for a **seat in a joint decision-making body**.

items.t: How to judge the GST Council
items.d: It is the **best working instance of cooperative federalism** — almost all decisions taken by **consensus** despite the voting formula, which is **Follett's integration** in constitutional form. It is also the instrument through which States **lost fiscal autonomy**, and its consensus depends on the Union not using its **blocking third**.

GPR asks the question work study does not: **should this process exist at all?** It **redesigns from the outcome backwards** rather than optimising existing steps. The **2nd ARC's 11th Report (Promoting e-Governance)** insisted GPR must **precede** computerisation — otherwise you **automate an unnecessary procedure**.

**Faceless assessment and appeal** in income tax abolished the **jurisdiction-based officer-taxpayer interface** rather than digitising it. **Passport Seva** redesigned the whole application chain around a **single visit**. **Self-attestation** replacing attestation by a gazetted officer removed a step entirely — the purest GPR of all, and free.

**SCDPM (DARPG)**, run annually — **record weeding, space released, files closed, pending references disposed, scrap disposal revenue**. It is **O&M in contemporary form**: unglamorous, measurable, and the kind of housekeeping that determines whether a department can find anything.

items.t: Cyber security as an administrative problem
items.d: The vulnerability is **behavioural, not technical** — phishing, shared credentials, unpatched systems, personal devices on official work. Instruments: **CERT-In** directions, **CISO** in every ministry, **cyber crisis management plans**, the **National Critical Information Infrastructure Protection Centre**, and mandatory **iGOT** cyber-hygiene modules.

**Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023**, **Rules 2025** — consent, purpose limitation, a **Data Protection Board**, and **significant data fiduciary** obligations. Every department is now a **data fiduciary**: it needs a grievance officer, breach notification, and a lawful basis for processing. **Puttaswamy (2017)** is the constitutional root.

groups.g: Digital public infrastructure and the 2026 frontier

items.d: **Interoperable, open, population-scale digital rails** on which both government and private services are built — **identity, payments and data exchange** as public goods rather than departmental assets. Its administrative significance is **reuse**: one rail, many services, no rebuilding.

**Identity** — Aadhaar, e-KYC, e-Sign, **140 crore+ enrolments**. **Payments** — UPI, **20 billion+ monthly transactions** at 2025-26 peaks and **80%+** of retail digital payment volume. **Data empowerment** — DigiLocker (**45 crore+ users**), Account Aggregator, consent artefacts. **Commerce** — ONDC. **Language** — Bhashini.

It **advanced development goals** (DBT reaching the beneficiary directly), **raised public sector efficiency** (authentication and payment as a shared service), and **unlocked private innovation** (fintech built on UPI). It is **Dunleavy's reintegration and needs-based holism** delivered at population scale.

**For** — deduplication, portability of entitlement, DBT at scale, financial inclusion through JAM. **Against** — **authentication failure and exclusion**, function creep beyond the original purpose, and privacy. **Puttaswamy (2018)** upheld it for **subsidies and taxation** under a law, and struck down **Section 57**'s private-party mandate.

A public procurement marketplace producing **price discovery, transparency and MSME participation**. Its implementation problems: **specification gaming** to favour a supplier, **quality assurance** at the point of receipt, **payment delays** to sellers, **seller verification and counterfeits**, and **State adoption** that remains uneven.

Live uses: **grievance routing on CPGRAMS**, **judicial translation (SUVAS) and transcription**, **crop-yield and flood forecasting**, **GST fraud analytics**, **faceless assessment allocation**, and **Bhashini** for multilingual delivery.

items.t: The administrative case against unexamined AI
items.d: The 2026 argument to have ready. **Opacity** — a citizen cannot be told why a claim was rejected, defeating the **reasoned order** requirement. **Bias** — trained on historical data, it reproduces historical exclusion. **Accountability** — **who is the officer** when the model decides? The answer must be that **AI advises and a named official decides**.

**IndiaAI Mission**; **NITI's Responsible AI for All** principles (safety, equality, inclusivity, privacy, transparency, accountability); **DPDP Act** obligations on the training data; **sectoral regulators** (RBI on model risk, SEBI on algo-trading). India's stated position is **pro-innovation regulation** rather than a single horizontal AI Act.

groups.g: Administrative reform — theory and the Indian record

items.d: Administrative reform is "**the artificial inducement of administrative transformation against resistance**." Every word is doing work: **artificial** (deliberate, not evolutionary), **transformation** (not adjustment), and **against resistance** — resistance is **constitutive**, not an obstacle that competent design avoids.

**Interest-based** — the reform removes someone's discretion, rent or status. **Cognitive** — officials cannot see how the new way would work. **Cultural** — the change conflicts with the organisation's self-image. **Structural** — statutes, service rules and federal division make the change legally slow.

**Political sponsorship at the highest level** — no reform survives without it; **a compelling crisis or trigger**; **compensation for the losers** (redeployment, protected pay); **early visible wins**; **legal backing** so the change survives a transfer; and **a champion who remains in post** long enough to see it through.

**Secretariat Reorganisation (N. Gopalaswami Ayyangar, 1949)**; **Gorwala (1951)** on integrity; **Appleby (1953, 1956)**; **Santhanam (1962-64)** producing the CVC; **ARC-I (1966-70, Morarji Desai then K. Hanumanthaiah)** with **20 reports**; **2nd ARC (2005-09, Veerappa Moily)** with **15 reports** — the master reference.

Know at least five by name and number: **1st RTI**, **4th Ethics in Governance**, **5th Public Order**, **10th Refurbishing of Personnel Administration**, **11th Promoting e-Governance**, **12th Citizen Centric Administration**, **13th Organisational Structure of Government of India**, **15th State and District Administration**.

items.t: The signature argument on Indian reform
items.d: **India reformed processes, not structures.** Every demonstrable gain since 2005 — **RTI, DBT, UPI, GeM, PFMS, faceless assessment** — came from **re-engineering transactions**. Every **structural** recommendation — the **three-level secretariat**, **executive agencies**, a **Public Services Bill**, a **Fiscal Council**, a **multi-member CAG** — remains unimplemented.

items.t: Why structural reform fails and process reform succeeds
items.d: Process reform is **technocratic**: it can be done by executive order, shows measurable results within a term, and **creates no identifiable loser at the top**. Structural reform **redistributes authority** — it needs legislation, federal consent, and asks the political executive to give up **the discretion it most values**.

True, but say something more precise. **Political will is not a personal virtue** — it is produced when the **political cost of not reforming exceeds the cost of reforming**. Reform succeeds where a **crisis, a court order, a fiscal constraint or an electoral incentive** creates that arithmetic: **GST, IBC, RTI, Aadhaar**.

The standing obstacles: **federal division** — most administrative subjects are with the States; **service rules and Article 311** making personnel change slow; **fiscal cost** of any restructuring; **no owner** once the commission dissolves; and **no implementation tracking** — India has no standing body reporting on which recommendations were accepted and acted on.

items.t: What a serious reform agenda would contain
items.d: Close with these five: a **Public Services Bill** codifying values and tenure; a **three-level secretariat** with the **desk officer system**; **independent evaluation with sunset clauses** on schemes; a **National Tribunals Commission**; and **fiscal empowerment of the third tier**. Each has an authoritative recommendation behind it and none needs a new idea.

items.t: Bureaucracy as an impediment to development
items.d: The charge: **rule-orientation over result**, **generalist leadership** of technical work, **risk aversion** created by vigilance exposure, **transfer instability**, and the **file** as a device for **diffusing responsibility**. All true; none of it argues for **less** bureaucracy — it argues for a **differently incentivised** one.

items.t: Bureaucracy as the condition of development
items.d: The counter, and the better answer. **Evans and Rauch** found **meritocratic recruitment and predictable careers** statistically associated with growth. India's **election machinery, famine prevention, universal immunisation and pandemic vaccination** were delivered by the same bureaucracy that is charged with obstruction. **Capacity, not size, is the variable.**

groups.g: Panchayati Raj — from Balwantrai Mehta to the 73rd Amendment

items.t: Why the Community Development Programme failed
items.d: Launched **2 October 1952** with the **National Extension Service (1953)**. **Balwantrai Mehta (1957)** diagnosed it precisely: it was **bureaucratically driven with no popular participation**, the **Village Level Worker** was overloaded, and benefits were **captured by dominant groups** — **Selznick's co-optation** in a village.

**Democratic decentralisation** through **three tiers** — village panchayat, **panchayat samiti** (the executive tier, at block level), zila parishad (advisory and coordinating); **indirect elections** to the upper tiers; **genuine transfer of resources and authority**; and a **five-year term**. Rajasthan implemented first, **Nagaur, 2 October 1959**.

**1977-78** — **two tiers** (zila parishad as the executive body, and **mandal panchayat** for 15,000-20,000 people); **open participation of political parties**; **compulsory taxation powers**; **reservation for SC/ST**; a **social audit** by a district-level agency; and a **Minister for Panchayati Raj** in the State Cabinet.

**G.V.K. Rao (1985)** — the bureaucratisation of development had made panchayats "**grass without roots**"; he proposed a **District Development Commissioner**. **L.M. Singhvi (1986)** — **constitutional status**, the **Gram Sabha** as the base of democracy, and **Nyaya Panchayats**. **P.K. Thungon (1988)** — constitutional recognition and **district planning**.

**1992, in force 24 April 1993.** **Gram Sabha (243A)**; **three tiers** above 20 lakh population (243B); **direct election** to all seats (243C); **reservation for SC/ST in proportion, and one-third for women** (243D); **five-year term with elections within six months of dissolution** (243E); a **State Election Commission** (243K); a **State Finance Commission every five years** (243I).

This is where the answer sits. **Article 243G** — the legislature **'may' endow** panchayats with powers over the **29 subjects of the Eleventh Schedule**. **Article 243H** — the State **'may' authorise** taxes. **District Planning Committee (243ZD)** is mandatory but toothless. **Devolution was made a State choice, and most States chose not to.**

Devolution means **Functions, Funds and Functionaries**. Most States transferred **functions on paper**, some **funds** as tied grants, and almost no **functionaries** — line department staff remain answerable to their department, not to the panchayat that supposedly directs them. **Without the third F, the first two are decorative.**

**Devolution Index 2024** — national devolution rose from **39.9% (2013-14) to 43.9% (2021-22)**; leading States **Karnataka, Kerala, Tamil Nadu, Maharashtra, Uttar Pradesh**. Useful because it lets you argue **improvement and inadequacy in the same sentence**.

items.t: The fiscal hollowness — the signature number
items.d: **PRIs raise about 1% of their receipts from own taxes**; roughly **80% comes as central grants** and **15% from States**; average **own tax revenue per panchayat is about ₹21,000 a year**. There are about **2.55 lakh gram panchayats** and **31 lakh+ elected representatives**, of whom about **46% are women**.

Panchayats succeeded as **political institutions** — contested elections, new leadership from SC/ST and women, real local competition. They failed as **planning and delivery agencies** because they were given **neither untied funds, nor staff, nor an activity map** clear enough to plan against.

items.t: Gram swaraj and the Gram Sabha
items.d: The **Gram Sabha** is the only **direct democracy** institution in the Constitution and holds real statutory power — **approval of the annual plan and budget**, **beneficiary selection**, **social audit under MGNREGA Section 17**, and **consent under FRA and PESA**. Its weakness is **quorum, capture and the frequency of meetings**.

**Panchayats (Extension to Scheduled Areas) Act, 1996** — in **Fifth Schedule** areas the **Gram Sabha** is supreme: it must be **consulted before land acquisition**, controls **minor forest produce and minor water bodies**, and approves plans. Its consent requirement is the strongest statutory power any Indian village body holds — and the most frequently bypassed.

items.t: Elected women representatives who cannot govern
items.d: The obstacles are specific: **proxy rule (sarpanch pati)**, **two-child and education disqualifications** that fall hardest on marginalised women, **no-confidence motions** used against them, **rotation of reserved seats** preventing a second term, and **secretariat staff who report elsewhere**. Fixes: **longer reservation cycles, capacity building, independent panchayat staff, and legal aid**.

**Ministry of Rural Development** with the **Departments of Rural Development and Land Resources**; **Ministry of Panchayati Raj**; **NABARD (1982)** for rural credit and RIDF; **DRDA** at district level; **NIRDPR** for training; **SIRDs** in States. The recurring problem is that **each mission builds its own society**, bypassing the panchayat.

**CDP (1952) → IRDP (1978, asset-based) → JRY/EAS (wage employment) → SGSY (1999, group-based) → NREGA (2005, rights-based) → NRLM (2011, institution-based) → mission convergence (Antyodaya, Rurban)**. Read the sequence as a shift from **assets → wages → rights → institutions → data**.

**Legal guarantee** of **100 days**; **self-selection** through a statutory wage; **unemployment allowance** if work is not provided in **15 days**; **Gram Sabha** as the planning and audit authority; **one-third participation for women**; and **social audit under Section 17**. Its elasticity was proved in **2020-21** with **1.75 crore new job cards**.

**Viksit Bharat–Gramin Rozgar Aur Aajeevika Mission (VB-G RAM G)** — gazetted **21 December 2025**, in force **1 July 2026**. Guarantee raised to **125 days**; funding **60:40** (**90:10** for North-Eastern and Himalayan States); administrative ceiling **9%**; seasonal pause up to **60 days**; **₹95,692 crore** Centre allocation for **2026-27**.

items.t: What to watch in the successor
items.d: The examinable questions: does a **60:40** share shift the burden to **fiscally weaker States** that need it most? Does a **seasonal pause** weaken the **demand-driven guarantee** that made the original a right rather than a scheme? Frame it as **entitlement versus mission** — the shift running through all Indian welfare.

A **gram-panchayat-level survey and ranking** across infrastructure and service parameters, used to target the weakest panchayats and to converge schemes on them. Its value is as a **diagnostic layer**; its limit is that **ranking is not resourcing** — identification without an untied fund changes little.

**Shyama Prasad Mukherji Rurban Mission (2016)** — clusters of **contiguous villages** developed with urban amenities and rural livelihoods, through **convergence of existing schemes** plus a **Critical Gap Fund** of up to 30%. It targets the **rural-urban continuum** the 73rd/74th split ignores.

Its administrative significance is **behaviour change at scale** — **all districts declared ODF by October 2019**, with **swachhagrahis**, community-led total sanitation, and **shame-and-pride messaging** rather than subsidy alone. **Phase II (ODF Plus)** shifted to **sustainability, solid and liquid waste** — the harder half.

**Abolition of intermediaries** largely succeeded; **tenancy reform and ceiling** largely failed — evasion through **benami and family partition**, and **poor land records**. The current answer is **records, not redistribution**: **SVAMITVA** with **2.5 crore+ property cards**, and **Digital India Land Records Modernisation**.

**Structural diagnosis, not a list.** **Parallel bodies** bypassing the panchayat; **tied funds** removing local choice; **late releases** compressing work into the last quarter; **staff answerable to line departments**; and **evaluation absent** — the **DMEO** evaluates a fraction of schemes, so failure is rarely priced.

**1992, in force 1 June 1993.** **Three types of municipality (243Q)** — **Nagar Panchayat** for a transitional area, **Municipal Council** for a smaller urban area, **Municipal Corporation** for a larger one. **Wards Committees** above three lakh (243S); **reservation including one-third for women** (243T); **five-year term** (243U); **State Election Commission** (243ZA); **State Finance Commission** (243Y).

**Eighteen functions** the legislature **may** devolve under **Article 243W** — urban planning, regulation of land use, roads and bridges, water supply, public health and sanitation, fire services, urban forestry, slum improvement, urban poverty alleviation, parks, burial grounds, and **planning for economic development and social justice**.

As with the 73rd, the **functional devolution is enabling, not mandatory**. States retained **urban planning and land use** — the two functions that decide a city's future — in **development authorities** answerable to the State. The municipality got **sanitation and streetlights** and the authority got the **master plan**.

**Article 243ZE** — mandatory for every metropolitan area above **ten lakh**, with **two-thirds of members elected** from municipalities and panchayats in the area, to prepare a **draft development plan** for the metropolitan area as a whole. **Most metropolitan areas either lack one or have one that does not plan.**

items.t: The District Planning Committee's urban half
items.d: **Article 243ZD** requires the DPC to consolidate **panchayat and municipal** plans into one district plan, taking account of **spatial planning, shared water and physical resources, and infrastructure and environmental conservation**. It is the only constitutional mechanism that treats **rural and urban as one planning problem** — and it is largely unused.

**RBI Report on Municipal Finances (November 2024)** — Indian municipal revenue is about **0.6-0.7% of GDP**, against **Brazil's 7.4%** and **South Africa's 6%**. One sentence that settles any 'urban local bodies lack resources' argument with evidence rather than assertion.

**Property tax** is only **0.09-0.11% of GDP** and about **15% of municipal revenue**; **own revenue** is **60-65%** of receipts; **transfers 32-39%**, of which **central transfers are under 5%**; and **municipal bonds are under 10%** of municipal borrowings. The picture is **own revenue that is large in share and tiny in absolute terms**.

**Outdated valuations** rarely revised; **low coverage** — a large share of properties unassessed; **exemptions** for government and institutional property; **weak collection** with no consequence for default; and **political reluctance** to revise rates. The fix is technical and available: **GIS-based property mapping, unit-area assessment and periodic indexation**.

**User charges** for water, solid waste and parking — the most under-used lever; **advertisement and entertainment** levies; **development charges and betterment levies** capturing land value the city itself created; **Transferable Development Rights** and **land value capture** around transit; and **municipal bonds** (Ahmedabad 1998 first; Pune, Indore and others since).

Without own revenue a municipality cannot **plan beyond one year**, cannot **borrow** (no creditworthiness), cannot **maintain** what it builds, and cannot **refuse** a State-directed project. **Constitutional status without fiscal capacity produces responsibility without resources** — the same sentence that indicts the 73rd Amendment.

Local body grants of **₹7.91 lakh crore** for **2026-31**, of which **urban ₹3.56 lakh crore**. Its effect depends entirely on **how much is untied** and on whether the conditions — **online publication of audited accounts** and **property tax floor rates** — are enforced. This is the single largest live lever on the urban fiscal problem.

A metropolitan area is governed by **overlapping authorities with no single accountable head** — the municipal corporation, a development authority for planning, separate water and transport boards, a cantonment or two, a police commissionerate, and several State parastatals. **Nobody is responsible for the city as a whole.**

Urban India generates the larger share of **national output and of tax revenue** while its governments are the **weakest tier fiscally**. That mismatch is the argument: the places producing the wealth have the **least control over the infrastructure** their productivity depends on.

**For** — a **single accountable executive** with a **five-year term**, visible to citizens, able to negotiate with the State. **Against** — conflict with the State government, and the fact that a strong mayor without **funds, functions and functionaries** is a **figurehead with a bigger office**. Most Indian mayors serve **one year, indirectly elected**, with the **Municipal Commissioner** holding executive power.

The structural fault. The **Municipal Commissioner** is a **State-appointed IAS officer** holding the executive power; the **Mayor** is the **elected head** with largely ceremonial and presiding functions. Executive authority therefore runs **upward to the State**, not **downward from the electorate** — the reverse of what the 74th Amendment intended.

**Article 243S** requires Ward Committees above three lakh; the **Model Nagara Raj Bill (2006)** under JNNURM proposed **Area Sabhas** as the urban equivalent of the Gram Sabha. **Kerala and West Bengal** implemented meaningfully; most States constituted committees **covering several wards each**, which defeats the purpose.

**JNNURM (2005)** — reform-linked funding, the first serious conditionality on municipal reform. **AMRUT** and **AMRUT 2.0** — water and sewerage. **Smart Cities Mission (2015)** — **100 cities**, area-based development through **SPVs**. **PMAY-Urban**, **Swachh Bharat Urban**, **NULM**, **PM SVANidhi** for street vendors, **National Urban Digital Mission**.

items.t: The SPV critique of Smart Cities
items.d: The scoring paragraph. The mission delivered projects through **Special Purpose Vehicles** — companies under the Companies Act with **State and municipal shareholding** and a **CEO answerable to a board**, not to the elected council. Efficient delivery, purchased by **bypassing the elected local body the 74th Amendment created**. **Rhodes's hollowing out**, one tier down.

The under-argued point. Indian municipalities are **critically short of qualified staff** — urban planners, engineers, finance officers, public health specialists — with sanctioned posts vacant for years and **no dedicated municipal cadre** in most States. **Mission Karmayogi has onboarded 1.75 lakh ULB officials**, which addresses training, not **numbers**.

Close with five: **transfer urban planning and land use** to the elected body; a **directly elected mayor with a five-year term** and executive authority; a **professional municipal cadre**; **property tax reform with GIS mapping and indexation**; and **untied Finance Commission grants** conditioned on **published audited accounts**.

groups.g: Police — the colonial legacy and the structure

items.d: Framed after **1857** on the **Irish Constabulary** model — a **colonial, armed, regime-loyal** force answerable to the district executive, not the community. Its logic was **control of the population**, not **service to the citizen**, and its architecture governs Indian policing to this day.

items.t: The colonial legacy in current form
items.d: Three surviving features: **executive control** over postings and operations; the **constabulary** treated as a labour force rather than a professional cadre; and **thana-level policing** designed for order maintenance rather than investigation.

**Entry 2, List II** — police and public order are **State** subjects; **Entry 1, List II** is public order. The Union acts through **Entry 8, List I** (CBI's parent DSPE), **Article 355** (duty to protect States), **central armed police forces on request**, and **advisories** with no binding force.

items.t: The police hierarchy and the dual desk
items.d: **DGP → ADGP/IGP → DIG (range) → SP (district) → SDPO/DySP → SHO (police station)**. In the district, the **SP** commands the force while the **District Magistrate** holds **magisterial** powers — the **dual control** that the National Police Commission wanted diluted and that the executive has always defended.

Unifies **police and magisterial** powers in a **Commissioner of Police** for a large city — quicker decisions on **licensing, preventive orders and crowd control**, with **no separate District Magistrate** in the police chain. Adopted in most metros; the standing objection is **concentration without a civilian check**.

Sanctioned strength about **26-27 lakh**, actual **20-21 lakh** — a **20-22% vacancy sustained for a decade**. Police-population ratio about **152-155 per lakh** against the **UN-referenced 222**. Women about **12%** against the **MHA's 33% advisory**. Quote these; they convert an opinion into a finding.

**Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita**, **Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita** and **Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam**, in force **1 July 2024**. Administratively significant: **mandatory forensic visit** for offences above seven years, **timelines** for investigation and judgment, **e-FIR and zero FIR**, and **videography of search and seizure**.

items.t: The prison end of the chain
items.d: **Undertrials are about three-quarters of the prison population**; occupancy exceeds **130%** in many States (**NCRB**). Reform is administrative, not merely legal: **BNSS Section 479** on release of first-time undertrials, **legal aid at first production**, and **video-conferenced remand** to cut escort dependence.

**Dharma Vira, 1977-81, eight reports** — the foundation text. Its core proposals: a **State Security Commission** to insulate the force from illegitimate political direction, a **fixed tenure** for the DGP, **separation of investigation from law and order**, and a **new Police Act** replacing 1861. **Not one State enacted the Model Bill.**

**Ribeiro (1998)** on implementing the NPC; **Padmanabhaiah (2000)** on restructuring, recruitment and training; **Malimath (2003)** on criminal justice and victim rights; **Soli Sorabjee's Model Police Act (2006)**; **Justice K.T. Thomas (2010)**, who found "**total indifference**" to the Supreme Court's directions.

**Prakash Singh v. Union of India (2006)** — a **State Security Commission**; **DGP selected from a UPSC panel with a two-year minimum tenure**; **two-year tenure** for operational field officers; **separation of investigation from law and order**; a **Police Establishment Board** for transfers and postings; **Police Complaints Authorities**; a **National Security Commission**.

States legislated **new Police Acts that reproduce executive control**: Security Commissions with **government majorities** and **recommendatory** status; **DGP selection diluted**; **Complaints Authorities unconstituted or without independent members**; transfer boards **overridden**. The reform removes precisely the discretion the political executive most values.

items.t: Whose discretion the reform would remove
items.d: Every police reform proposal since **1979** asks the political executive to surrender control over **postings and transfers**. It has not been resisted for want of funds or expertise — it has been resisted because it is a **transfer of power**. The obstacle is **interest**, not capacity.

**For** — specialist investigators freed from bandobast duty, better conviction rates, prosecutorial independence as a check on shoddy investigation. **Against** — coordination loss, **duplication in thin State cadres**, and a village station that cannot spare two wings. Most States have a **partial** separation in metros only.

**S**trict-**S**ensitive, **M**odern-**M**obile, **A**lert-**A**ccountable, **R**eliable-**R**esponsive, **T**echno-savvy-**T**rained. Its instruments: **CCTNS** and the **Interoperable Criminal Justice System**, **e-FIR**, **Dial 112 ERSS**, and **NAFIS** fingerprints.

**Kerala's Janamaithri Suraksha**, **Rajasthan's Community Liaison Groups**, **Tamil Nadu's Friends of Police**, **Maharashtra's Mohalla committees** after communal incidents. What makes them work is **beat officer continuity** — the same constable, the same locality, long enough to be known.

Diagnosis first: the **1861 design**, **vacancies and 12-14 hour shifts**, **VIP security diverting strength**, **custodial violence**, and **social distance** from women, Dalits and minorities in a force that does not resemble the policed. Remedies: **representation**, **beat continuity**, **independent complaints authorities**, and **welfare and shift reform** for the constabulary.

The CBI has **no statute of its own** — it operates under the **Delhi Special Police Establishment Act, 1946**, and needs **State consent under Section 6** to investigate there, which several States have **withdrawn**. **Vineet Narain (1997)** gave the Director a **two-year tenure** and CVC supervision.

The **Guwahati High Court (2013)** questioned the CBI's very constitution; the Supreme Court called it a **caged parrot**. Reform proposals: a **CBI Act** with statutory autonomy, a **collegium appointment**, **financial independence**, and a **separate prosecution wing** — the **2nd ARC** and **Parliamentary Standing Committee** have both recommended it.

**NIA** (NIA Act, 2008, post-26/11; amended **2019** for extraterritorial reach); **ED** under **PMLA and FEMA**; **NCB** for narcotics; **IB** for intelligence; **MAC** for multi-agency coordination; **NATGRID** for data linkage; **NCTC**, proposed in 2012, **never created** after States objected on federal grounds.

**CRPF** — the internal security reserve, largest; **BSF, ITBP, SSB** — border guarding; **CISF** — installations and airports; **Assam Rifles** — a dual-control force under **MHA administratively, Army operationally**. Their deployment is at State **request**, which is the constitutional hinge.

**Clear – hold – build**, and the recognition that insurgency ends politically. India's working combination: **security saturation**, **development saturation** (Aspirational Districts overlap heavily with LWE districts), **surrender-and-rehabilitation policy**, and **negotiated accords** — the **Mizo Accord (1986)** remains the model of a durable settlement.

The **Armed Forces (Special Powers) Act, 1958** confers powers to **search, arrest and use force** in a **disturbed area**, with **prior sanction required to prosecute**. Progressive withdrawal — **Tripura (2015)**, **Meghalaya (2018)**, phased reduction in Assam, Nagaland and Manipur — signals **normalisation**, and **Jeevan Reddy Committee (2005)** recommended repeal with safeguards folded into the UAPA.

**UAPA, 1967**, amended **2019** to allow designation of an **individual** as a terrorist; **NIA** for investigation; **special courts**; **FATF** compliance driving the **PMLA** architecture. The administrative tension is between **preventive detention powers** and **conviction rates**, which remain low.

**ADR** data on candidates with declared criminal cases; **Association for Democratic Reforms (2002)** made disclosure mandatory; **Lily Thomas (2013)** ended the appeal-pending protection for convicted legislators; **Public Interest Foundation (2018)** and the **2020 contempt order** require parties to **publish reasons** for selecting such candidates. **Fast-track courts for MPs and MLAs** remain under-resourced.

units.name: Significant Issues in Indian Administration
units.sel: II-14 — Significant Issues in Indian Administration

groups.g: Social audit and the citizen interface

items.d: Four modes: the citizen as **applicant** (a service to be obtained), as **complainant** (CPGRAMS), as **participant** (Gram Sabha, ward committee, MyGov), and as **co-producer** (community forest management, school management committees). Indian reform has invested heavily in the first two and thinly in the last two.

**CPGRAMS** with an **AI-based grievance routing** layer, feedback call centres, and a **DARPG** ranking of ministries by **disposal time and quality**. The measured shortfall is that **'disposal' is counted rather than resolution** — Goodhart's law inside the grievance machine.

The **Right of Citizens for Time Bound Delivery of Goods and Services and Redressal of their Grievances Bill, 2011** lapsed. Without it, a Citizen's Charter creates **no enforceable right**. The **2nd ARC's 12th Report, Citizen Centric Administration**, remains the reference design.

**Arnstein's ladder** — from **manipulation and therapy** (non-participation), through **informing, consultation and placation** (tokenism), to **partnership, delegated power and citizen control**. Most Indian participation sits at **consultation**; **social audit and the Gram Sabha's approval of plans** reach **delegated power**.

**Corruption = Monopoly + Discretion − Accountability.** The most usable analytic frame in the syllabus: it turns 'reduce corruption' into three **operable** levers, and lets you show which lever each Indian reform pulls.

**Monopoly reduced** — competitive **e-auction** of coal and spectrum, **GeM's** open marketplace. **Discretion reduced** — **faceless assessment**, algorithmic case allocation, **DBT** removing the intermediary. **Accountability raised** — RTI, CVC, social audit. The **first two carried the gains**; the third lagged.

**Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988**, amended **2018** — **bribe-giving criminalised**, **prior approval** required to investigate a public servant, **timelines** for trial. **Prevention of Money Laundering Act, 2002**. **Benami Transactions (Prohibition) Amendment Act, 2016**. **Lokpal and Lokayuktas Act, 2013**.

It closed a real gap by criminalising the **giver** and requiring **timely trial**; it also restored a **prior-approval shield** akin to the **single directive** the Supreme Court struck down in **Vineet Narain (1997)** and again in **Subramanian Swamy (2014)**. Protection against harassment and protection from investigation are hard to separate.

Recommended by the **Santhanam Committee (1962-64)**, created **1964**, given **statutory** status by the **CVC Act, 2003** after **Vineet Narain**. **Multi-member**, appointed by a committee of **PM, Home Minister and Leader of Opposition**; supervises the **CBI's** anti-corruption work; **advisory** on departmental action — which is its central weakness.

Enacted **2013** after the **India Against Corruption** mobilisation, chairperson appointed only in **March 2019**. **389 complaints in 2025-26.** Its problems are structural: it **depends on CBI and CVC** for inquiry, has **no independent investigating machinery of scale**, and **most States' Lokayuktas** are weaker still.

India ratified the **UN Convention against Corruption in 2011**. Gaps that remain: **no law on private-sector bribery** beyond limited provisions, **no effective whistleblower protection in force**, **no asset-recovery framework** matching Chapter V, and **no regulation of lobbying or political funding transparency**.

The **fourth report, Ethics in Governance** — a **Code of Ethics** distinct from the Code of Conduct, an **Office of Ethics Commissioner**, **partial funding of elections**, **confiscation of illegally acquired assets**, **integrity pacts** in procurement, **conflict-of-interest and cooling-off rules**, and **serious-offence fast-tracking**.

**India 91st of 182, score 39/100**, improved from **96th in 2024**; global average **42** (**Transparency International, 16 February 2026**). Use it to argue that **transactional** corruption fell with digitisation while **grand and political** corruption is untouched by process reform.

**Nolan's seven principles** — **selflessness, integrity, objectivity, accountability, openness, honesty, leadership**. India's equivalents: the **AIS (Conduct) Rules, Rule 3** duty to maintain **integrity, devotion to duty and political neutrality**; the never-enacted **Public Services Bill** with its proposed values charter.

The effects are specific: **portfolio allocation by party rather than fit**; **ministries becoming party fiefdoms** with parallel personnel policies; **slower Cabinet decision-making**; **larger councils of ministers** before the 91st Amendment; and a **Chief Secretary or Cabinet Secretary** who must broker rather than coordinate.

Coalitions also produce **greater federal consultation**, **more legislative scrutiny** (governments cannot guillotine at will), and **regional interests represented at the Union table**. The **91st Amendment** capped the Council of Ministers at **15% of the House** and ended defection-by-split, curbing the worst instability.

**Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993**. Chairperson a **former Chief Justice of India or a Supreme Court judge** (after the **2019 amendment**), with a fixed **three-year** term. Powers: **inquiry, civil-court powers, visits to custodial institutions, intervention in court proceedings**.

Its findings are **recommendatory**; it **cannot investigate armed forces** beyond seeking a report under **Section 19**; a **one-year limitation** bars older complaints; it relies on **police to investigate police**; and **GANHRI accreditation review** has repeatedly questioned its **pluralism and appointment process**.

**Disaster Management Act, 2005** — **NDMA** chaired by the **Prime Minister**, **SDMA** by the **Chief Minister**, **DDMA** by the **District Magistrate**; **NDRF**; **NIDM** for training; **NDMA guidelines** as the binding standard. The **2025 amendment** strengthened the authorities' planning role and urban disaster arrangements.

items.t: The shift from relief to risk reduction
items.d: **Sendai Framework 2015-30** — four priorities: **understanding risk, strengthening governance, investing in resilience, enhancing preparedness for build back better**. India's move is visible in the **16th FC's disaster corpus of ₹2,04,401 crore** and in **heat action plans** treating heat as a notified local disaster.

Working Indian instances: **IMD's** impact-based cyclone forecasting; **Common Alerting Protocol** cell-broadcast warnings; **satellite and drone damage assessment** for rapid loss estimation; **flood forecasting** models; and **Bhashini** for multilingual alerts. The limits are **data quality, last-mile reach and accountability for a wrong prediction**.

At the **political** level: a **code of conduct for ministers** with an independent adjudicator ( ), **election funding transparency**, and **asset declaration**. At the **administrative** level: a **Code of Ethics**, an **Ethics Commissioner**, **whistleblower protection in force**, and **conflict-of-interest rules with a cooling-off period**.

units.name: Foundations of the Discipline
units.blurb: The single largest slice of Paper I — roughly one question in six since 2019. Paradigms, the dichotomy, and the NPA → NPM → NPS → NPG chain are asked every year in some form.

groups.g: What the subject is — and the dichotomy that made it

items.d: **Woodrow Wilson (1887), 'The Study of Administration'** — "It is getting to be harder to run a **constitution** than to frame one." Administration is **'government in action'**, a **field of business** removed from the hurry and strife of politics.

Politics sets **ends**, administration supplies **means**. Built by **Wilson** and **Frank Goodnow (Politics and Administration, 1900)** to protect a **merit** service from the **spoils system** after the **Pendleton Act, 1883**. It was a **reform slogan** before it was a theory.

**Appleby (Policy and Administration, 1949)** — "**Public administration is policy making**." Administrators exercise **discretion**, draft the law, and choose between values. **Waldo** added that the dichotomy hid a **political theory** pretending to be a technique.

It collapses visibly: the **Secretary is principal policy adviser** under the **Allocation of Business Rules, 1961**; officers draft **Cabinet Notes**; **NITI Aayog** officials shape policy openly. Yet it survives as an **operating convention** — the basis of **neutrality** and of **Article 311** protection.

items.t: The dichotomy is not dead — it is normative
items.d: Write: as **description** it is false; as **norm** it is indispensable. Without it there is no defence against **politicisation of transfers**, no ground for a civil servant to record **written dissent**, and no line for the **Election Commission** to police.

**Appleby's three differences** — breadth of **scope, impact and consideration**; **public accountability**; **political character**. **Sir Josiah Stamp** adds **uniformity, external financial control, ministerial responsibility** and the **marginal-utility** test of service.

**Wallace Sayre** — public and private administration are "**alike in all unimportant respects**." Use it as a one-line opener: the similarity is in **technique**, the difference is in **purpose, publicness and the impossibility of exit**.

A private insurer may refuse a bad risk; **LIC** cannot abandon universal reach. **CAG audits NHAI**; a concessionaire audits itself. **Passport issuance** is a **sovereign monopoly with no exit** — the citizen cannot shop elsewhere, which is why **service standards must be imposed, not competed for**.

**White (1926)** wrote the **first textbook** — administration is "the **management of men and materials** in the accomplishment of the purposes of the state." **Dimock** widened it: administration is "the **what and the how** of government," and "**the concern of all**."

**Dwight Waldo (1948)** — the efficiency orthodoxy is itself a **value choice**, so "**public administration is a form of political theory**." Every claim to be merely technical conceals a **preference about who gets what**.

**Simon** wanted a **value-free science** of administrative behaviour. **Waldo** replied that its subject matter is **normative**. Settle it: it is a **social science with a professional purpose** — like medicine, judged by whether its prescriptions **work in a specific ecology**.

items.t: Why the discipline keeps reinventing itself
items.d: Because it is **contextual**: it borrows its problems from the state, and the state's form keeps changing — **welfare state → market state → regulatory state → digital state**. **Henry's five paradigms** are the frame; each is a response to a **legitimacy crisis**, not an intellectual advance.

groups.g: The paradigms — the spine of every 'evolution' answer

items.d: **(1)** Politics–administration dichotomy **1900-26**; **(2)** Principles of administration **1927-37**; **(3)** Public administration as **political science** 1950-70; **(4)** as **management** 1956-70; **(5)** as **public administration** 1970-.
items.s: Henry, Public Administration and Public Affairs

items.d: **Willoughby (1927)** claimed there are **fundamental principles of administration** as in the physical sciences; **Gulick and Urwick (1937)** codified them. This is the discipline's high point of confidence — and the target Simon destroyed nine years later.

**Simon (1946)** — the principles are **proverbs**, arriving in **mutually contradictory pairs**: specialise, but maintain **unity of command**; **narrow the span of control**, but keep the hierarchy **flat**. A principle that cannot say which of two rules applies is not a principle.

**Dahl (1947)** — a science of administration must confront **values**, **human behaviour** and **cross-cultural transferability**. His third problem founded **Comparative Public Administration**; his first vindicated **Waldo**.

**Waldo (1968)** named the discipline's chronic problem — is it a **profession, a science, or a branch of political science?** Its answer has been **eclecticism**: it borrows method from economics, psychology and management, and keeps only its **object** — the **public** in administration.

**I (1968, Syracuse, convened by Waldo)** — relevance, values, **social equity**, change. **II (1988)** — ethics, professionalism, deregulation. **III (2008)** — **globalisation, networked governance, collaborative public management**, and a generational handover to empirical, regionally grounded research.

Its finding: theory must be **empirically tested and regionally tailored** — a single Western canon cannot travel. Administration is a **socially embedded process of relationship, dialogue and action**, not a toolkit.

items.t: The paradigm ladder in one line
items.d: The chain runs **PA (rule) → NPA (equity) → NPM (market) → NPS (citizenship) → NPG (network) → DEG (platform)**. Each corrects the previous one's **blind spot**; none replaces the **Weberian core** underneath.

**IIPA, 1954** on **Appleby's** recommendation; **O&M Division** in the Cabinet Secretariat, 1954; **Department of Administrative Reforms, 1964**; **ARC-I, 1966**; the **Indian Journal of Public Administration**. Indian public administration was born as **reform practice**, not as theory — which is its strength and its limitation.

The relationship has moved through four stages — **subject** (colonial), **beneficiary** (welfare), **customer** (NPM), **citizen and co-producer** (NPS). India shows all four simultaneously: a **subject** at the police station, a **customer** at a **Passport Seva Kendra**, a **co-producer** in a **Gram Sabha social audit**.

groups.g: New Public Administration — equity as the third pillar

items.d: **Frederickson's 4 Rs — Relevance, Values, Equity, Change.** Its distinctive claim: to **economy and efficiency** add **social equity** as a **third pillar**. The question is no longer 'is the service efficient?' but '**efficient for whom?**'

items.t: Frederickson on why equity is not optional
items.d: "A public administration which **fails to work for changes** which try to redress the deprivation of minorities will likely be **eventually used to repress those minorities**." Neutral administration in an unequal society **reproduces the inequality**.

NPA rejects the **neutral instrument** model. The administrator is a **change agent** with a **client focus**, expected to advocate for the **disadvantaged** inside the machine — which is exactly the tension a **committed versus neutral bureaucracy** question turns on.

**Article 46** (DPSP, promotion of educational and economic interests of weaker sections), **Articles 15(4), 16(4) and 335** — India wrote **Frederickson's third pillar into the Constitution eighteen years before Minnowbrook**.

**Aspirational Districts Programme (2018)** — 112 districts; **Aspirational Blocks Programme (2023)** — 500 blocks. The **delta ranking** method scores **improvement, not level**, so the poorest can win — operationalising equity through **converge, collaborate, compete**.

**Development Action Plan for SCs (DAPSC)** and **for STs (DAPST)** — the successors to the **Scheduled Caste Sub-Plan / Tribal Sub-Plan**, earmarking outlays in proportion to population. **Gender Budget Statement 13** does the same for women. Earmarking is equity made **auditable**.

"**Radicalism in words, status quo in skills**." NPA supplied a **moral vocabulary** without a **method**: equity is normatively compelling but **administratively indeterminate** — it cannot tell an officer how to rank two deserving villages.

Every **algorithmic** allocation decision — **DBT** exclusion for a failed **Aadhaar** authentication, an **AI**-scored beneficiary list — is an equity question wearing an efficiency costume. NPA's question, '**efficient for whom?**', is the sharpest closing line available on digital governance.

groups.g: Public Choice — the market critique of bureaucracy

items.d: The application of **economic method to non-market decision-making**: **methodological individualism**, **rational utility maximisation**, and the claim that officials maximise **their own** utility — budget, staff, prestige — not the **public interest**.

**The Intellectual Crisis in American Public Administration (1973)** — Wilsonian **monocentric bureaucracy** is not the only efficient form. He proposed **democratic administration**: **polycentricity**, overlapping jurisdictions, and **fragmented authority** as a feature, not a defect.
**Niskanen (1971)** — the bureau is a **bilateral monopoly** facing a sponsor who cannot observe its true cost, so it secures a budget up to **twice** the efficient level.

It is **half-right**. Bureaus do pad, but **fiscal rules** now bind: **FRBM**, **outcome budgets**, **Treasury Single Account**, **PFMS** real-time release. The modern bureaucrat maximises **discretion and turf**, not budget — the shape of rent-seeking changed when the money got watched.

**Inside Bureaucracy (1967)** — **climbers** (power and income), **conservers** (security), **zealots** (one narrow policy), **advocates** (their whole bureau), **statesmen** (society at large). A usable typology for any **motivation** or **leadership** answer about the services.

**The Calculus of Consent (1962)** — constitutional rules should be chosen behind uncertainty about one's own future position. **Tullock's** rent-seeking: resources spent **capturing** a licence are a **pure social waste** — the intellectual case against the **licence-permit raj**.

items.t: Elinor Ostrom's answer to the commons
items.d: **Governing the Commons (1990), Nobel 2009** — communities do solve commons problems, given **eight design principles**: clear boundaries, congruent rules, collective choice, **monitoring**, **graduated sanctions**, cheap conflict resolution, recognised right to organise, **nested enterprises**.

**Van Panchayats** of Uttarakhand (1931); **Pani Panchayats** of Maharashtra (**Vilasrao Salunkhe**); **Joint Forest Management** (1990 circular); **Water User Associations** under the **AP Farmers' Management of Irrigation Systems Act, 1997**. Community institutions outperform both **state** and **market** here.

**NITI Aayog's indices** — **SDG India Index, Fiscal Health Index, Composite Water Management Index, Export Preparedness** — and **DPIIT's Business Reforms Action Plan** create a **quasi-market among states**, substituting **reputational competition** for the Planning Commission's command.

items.t: The limits of exit and voice
items.d: **Hirschman's exit-voice-loyalty** is the hinge. Public choice assumes **exit**; **Ranson and Stewart** reply that citizens are **not consumers**. In India the poor cannot exit the **PDS**, the government school or the primary health centre — so **voice**, not choice, is the only lever.

groups.g: New Public Management — the market decade

items.d: **Christopher Hood (1991), 'A Public Management for All Seasons?'** — hands-on **professional management**; explicit **standards and measures**; **output controls**; **disaggregation** of units; greater **competition**; **private-sector styles**; **discipline and parsimony** in resource use.

**Reinventing Government (1992)** — government should be **'steering, not rowing'**: catalytic, community-owned, competitive, **mission-driven** rather than rule-driven, **results-oriented**, customer-driven, enterprising, anticipatory, decentralised, market-oriented.

items.t: The three Es and the missing fourth
items.d: NPM's test is **economy, efficiency, effectiveness**. **NPA's equity is the fourth E** — and its absence is the standing critique. A **fifth**, **ethics**, is now routinely added in Indian writing after the **2nd ARC's fourth report**.

The **Results Framework Document (RFD)** system, **2009-10 to 2014**, run by the **Performance Management Division** of the Cabinet Secretariat under **Prajapati Trivedi** — ministries signed measurable targets and were **scored**. It was **discontinued in 2014**: the cleanest evidence that NPM in India was **adopted rhetorically, not structurally**.

**Outcome Budget from 2005-06**, now the **Output–Outcome Monitoring Framework (OOMF)** run by **NITI Aayog** with the **Ministry of Finance** — every scheme carries **output and outcome indicators** against its outlay. NPM's measurement logic survived where its structural logic did not.
Charters from the **1997 Conference of Chief Ministers**; **Sevottam (2005, DARPG)** adds three modules — **Charter, Grievance Redress, Service Delivery Capability**. The answer turns on **remedy**.

It is a **statement of intent**, not a right. The fix exists: **Right to Public Services Acts** — **Madhya Pradesh first (2010)**, **Bihar (2011)** with penalties on the **designated officer**, **Karnataka's Sakala**. The central **Right of Citizens for Time Bound Delivery Bill, 2011 lapsed** — no national law.

**New Public Sector Enterprise Policy, 2021** — **four strategic sectors**, bare-minimum state presence, exit elsewhere; **National Monetisation Pipeline (2021)** and **NMP 2.0** monetise brownfield assets without transferring ownership.

items.t: Hood and Peters on NPM's paradox
items.d: **'The Middle Aging of New Public Management: Into the Age of Paradox' (2004)** — NPM produced **unintended reversals**: more measurement created **more auditors**, disaggregation created **more coordination units**, contracting created **more contract lawyers**.

items.t: The NPM paradox in Indian numbers
items.d: LPG and NPM promised a **smaller state**, yet **Union expenditure is ₹53.5 lakh crore (Budget 2026-27)** and ministries have multiplied. Regulation **substitutes for** ownership; the state stopped **rowing** and hired a **larger crew to steer**.

items.t: Goodhart's Law as the NPM disease
items.d: "**When a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure.**" Indian instances: **ODF declarations** without usage, **learning outcomes** flat while enrolment targets were met, **grievance 'disposal'** counted rather than **resolution** on **CPGRAMS**.

The answer splits the citizen. As **customer** she gained **speed and choice** — passports, tax refunds, GeM. As **citizen** she lost **standing**: a customer complains, a citizen **participates**. NPM improved **transactions** and thinned **deliberation**.

groups.g: After NPM — NPS, New Public Governance, Neo-Weberian, digital

items.t: New Public Service — the seven maxims
items.d: **Denhardt and Denhardt (2000)** — **serve citizens, not customers**; seek the **public interest**; value **citizenship over entrepreneurship**; **think strategically, act democratically**; recognise **accountability is not simple**; **serve rather than steer**; value **people, not just productivity**.

**RTI Act, 2005**; **social audit** under **MGNREGA Section 17**; the **Gram Sabha** as the deliberative unit; **Jan Sunwai** public hearings pioneered by **MKSS in Rajasthan**. India built the NPS architecture **before the theory reached the syllabus**.

**Stephen Osborne (2006)** — the state is **plural** (many actors deliver) and **pluralist** (many processes shape policy). The unit of analysis is the **inter-organisational network** and the currency is **trust and relational contract**, not price.

items.t: NPG against NPM in one line
items.d: **NPM** asks *who can deliver this cheapest?* **NPG** asks *who must be at the table for this to work at all?* The first is a **procurement** question, the second a **legitimacy** question.
"Governance refers to **self-organising, inter-organisational networks** characterised by **interdependence, resource exchange, rules of the game and significant autonomy from the state**."

items.t: The hollow state and third-party government
items.d: **Rhodes' 'hollowing out'**; **Milward and Provan's hollow state**; **Salamon's third-party government** — the state **funds and regulates** but does not deliver.

**National Health Mission** delivered by **NGOs and empanelled private hospitals** under **PM-JAY**; **mid-day meals** by **Akshaya Patra**; **skilling** through **PPP** under **NSDC**; roads by **SPVs** under **NHAI**. The **Collector** now **convenes** more than he **commands**.

**Pollitt and Bouckaert** — Europe's answer to NPM: **keep** the Weberian core (law, career service, distinct public ethos) and **add** citizen orientation, results and professionalism. "**Neo**" modernises; "**Weberian**" refuses to dismantle.

The **steel frame stayed** — **Articles 309-311**, the **AIS**, seniority — while **e-governance, outcome frameworks and Mission Karmayogi** were layered on. India never had an **NPM phase**; it went from **Weberian** to **Neo-Weberian-digital** without dismantling anything.

**Patrick Dunleavy (2006)** — "**NPM is dead — long live digital era governance**." Three moves that **reverse** NPM: **reintegration** of fragmented agencies, **needs-based holism** around the citizen's life event, and **digitisation** of the process itself.

**India Stack** — **Aadhaar** (identity), **UPI**, **DigiLocker**, **Account Aggregator**, **ONDC**, **Bhashini**. **Reintegration**: one **Jan Dhan-Aadhaar-Mobile** rail replaced hundreds of departmental payment systems. **Needs-based holism**: **UMANG** organises services by **life event**, not by ministry.

**Mark Moore's strategic triangle** — a manager must simultaneously secure **public value**, an **authorising environment** and **operational capacity**. It explains why a technically sound scheme fails — **capacity without authorisation**, or **authorisation without capacity**.

groups.g: Good governance, and the state–market–civil society triangle

items.t: The World Bank's origin of the term
items.d: **Governance and Development (1992)** — governance is "**the manner in which power is exercised** in the management of a country's economic and social resources for development." Four pillars: **public sector management, accountability, a legal framework for development, information and transparency**.

**Participatory, consensus-oriented, accountable, transparent, responsive, effective and efficient, equitable and inclusive, and following the rule of law.** The cleanest checklist to structure a good-governance body — one heading per cluster, not eight.

**Kaufmann and Kraay's six dimensions** — **voice and accountability; political stability; government effectiveness; regulatory quality; rule of law; control of corruption**. Useful because it lets you say **which** dimension India is weak on rather than that governance is 'poor'.

items.t: Good governance adds a normative layer
items.d: "Governance" describes a **process**; "**good** governance" **evaluates** it. That is its strength — it makes administration **assessable against declared standards** — and its weakness: the standards arrived as **donor conditionality**, not domestic deliberation.

"In the **happiness of his subjects** lies the king's happiness; in their **welfare**, his welfare." Good governance is not a **1992 World Bank import** — **Arthashastra** states the **yogakshema** duty and prescribes **audit, espionage against corrupt officials and famine relief**.

**RTI Act, 2005** — **Section 4** suo motu disclosure, **Section 8** exemptions, **Section 19** appeals, **Section 20** penalty up to **₹25,000**. **Good Governance Index (DARPG, 2019 and 2021)** — **10 sectors, 58 indicators**. **PRAGATI (2015)** — the PM-chaired multi-modal review.

**India 91st of 182, score 39/100** — up from **96th in 2024**; global average **42** (**Transparency International, released 16 February 2026**). **Control of corruption remains the weakest of India's WGI dimensions** despite a decade of process reform.

**UNDP (1997)** — governance is the exercise of **economic, political and administrative authority**, and the three domains must **balance**. Each has a distinct failure: **state failure** (rigidity), **market failure** (externalities, public goods), **civil society failure** (unrepresentativeness, funding capture).

items.t: Why government must supply some goods
items.d: **Non-rivalry and non-excludability** (defence, street lighting), **externalities** (vaccination, education), **natural monopoly** (transmission, water networks), **information asymmetry** (drug safety), and **equity** — the market allocates by **purchasing power**, not need.

CSOs supply **information, mobilisation and reach** — **MKSS** produced the RTI, **SEWA** organised informal workers. But they can be **unrepresentative, donor-driven and obstructive**; **FCRA amendments (2020)** cut foreign funding sharply. Effectiveness depends on the state being **receptive**.

items.t: The regulatory state replaces the producer state
items.d: **Majone's 'regulatory state'** — the state stops **owning** and starts **rule-making**. India's architecture: **SEBI (1992), TRAI (1997), CERC (Electricity Act, 2003), IRDAI, CCI (2002, amended 2023), IBBI (2016), Data Protection Board (DPDP Act 2023, Rules 2025)**.

items.t: Regulatory capture and the missing common law
items.d: **Stigler's capture theory**; **Rhodes' agencification**. India's gap: the **2nd ARC's 13th Report** and the **FSLRC (Justice B.N. Srikrishna, 2013)** both flagged **overlap, weak accountability and the absence of a common regulatory statute**. FSLRC's **Indian Financial Code** was never enacted.

The **national policy agenda becomes international**: **WTO, BEPS Pillar Two, Basel III, ICAO, IHR 2005, Paris NDCs**. Domestic administration acquires a **treaty-compliance function**, and the **regulator becomes the point of contact** with global capital.

units.name: Administrative Thought
units.blurb: The currency of Paper I. Every answer should carry two thinkers — one classical, one contemporary — each doing work in the sentence rather than decorating it. Follett, Barnard and Simon are the three most repeatedly asked.

groups.g: Scientific Management — Taylor and the shop floor

items.d: **Develop a science** for each element of work; **scientifically select and train** the worker; **heartily cooperate** with workers; **near-equal division of work and responsibility** between management and men. Source: **The Principles of Scientific Management, 1911**.

**Time and motion study**; **functional foremanship** (eight foremen, four planning and four doing); the **differential piece-rate**; **standardisation** of tools and conditions; the **exception principle** — management attends only to deviations.

Taylor's own defence before the **1912 House Committee**: scientific management requires "**a complete mental revolution**" on **both** sides — labour must stop **soldiering**, management must stop **guessing**. The surplus from science makes the wage-profit fight unnecessary.

"**In the past the man has been first; in the future the system must be first.**" One sentence that carries both Taylor's achievement — **method over intuition** — and his indictment: the worker as an **appendage to method**.

**Henry Gantt** — the **Gantt chart** and the **task-and-bonus** wage. **Frank and Lillian Gilbreth** — **therbligs** and fatigue study; Lillian, the **'first lady of management'**, brought psychology in. **Harrington Emerson** — **twelve principles of efficiency**. **Morris Cooke** — Taylorism applied to **municipal administration**.

Taylor never separated **principles of analysis** (how to study work scientifically) from **principles of action** (what management should therefore do). He presented an **empirical method** and a **managerial prescription** as one thing — which is why criticising the prescription looked like rejecting the science.

items.t: Who decides what work is worth doing?
items.d: Taylor optimised **means** and never asked about **ends**. Scientific management can make an **unnecessary** procedure efficient — the standing critique of process reform that leaves the **process itself** unexamined. **Government Process Re-engineering** exists precisely to ask this question first.

**Drucker** — Taylor **separated planning from doing**, deskilling the worker. The **Hoxie Report (1915)** to the US Commission on Industrial Relations found it **anti-union**. **Oliver Sheldon** demanded a **philosophy** of management. The core charge: the **machine model of man**.

The **O&M Division (1954)** in the Cabinet Secretariat on **Appleby's** advice, moved to the **Department of Administrative Reforms (1964)**, today **DARPG**; the **Staff Inspection Unit (1964)** in the Finance Ministry sets **staffing norms by work measurement**; Railways run **Industrial Engineering** cells.

items.t: Taylorism's human cost, in a live Indian example
items.d: **MGNREGA Schedule of Rates** are built on **time-and-motion measurement** of earthwork. Where the norms are set unattainably high, a full day's labour earns **below the notified minimum wage** — Taylor's exact failure, reproduced in a rights-based statute.

**e-Office** file-movement time standards; **Special Campaign for Disposal of Pending Matters (SCDPM, DARPG)** measured in files closed and space freed; **algorithmic work allocation** in **faceless assessment**. Time-and-motion did not die — it **moved into software**.

groups.g: The classical school — Fayol, Gulick, Urwick

items.d: **POCCC — Planning, Organising, Commanding, Coordinating, Controlling** — from **Administration Industrielle et Générale (1916)**. Fayol looked at the organisation **from the top down**; Taylor looked **from the shop floor up**.

**Unity of command** (one boss), **unity of direction** (one plan), **scalar chain** with the **gangplank** for lateral communication, **centralisation** as a question of degree, **esprit de corps**, **stability of tenure**, and **equity**. Name three that fit the question, not all fourteen.

A **lateral bridge** across the scalar chain, permitted when superiors authorise it, so a matter need not climb and descend the whole hierarchy. India's institutional version is the **desk officer system** and, in the field, the **Incident Response System** under the **DM Act, 2005**.

**Gulick and Urwick (1937)** — **Planning, Organising, Staffing, Directing, COordinating, Reporting, Budgeting**. It answers *what the chief executive does*; **Simon's** objection is that it never says *what government is for*.

**Purpose, Process, Persons (clientele), Place.** Indian examples in one line: **Purpose** — Ministry of Health; **Process** — CPWD and the Directorate of Printing; **Persons** — Ministries of Tribal Affairs, Minority Affairs, WCD; **Place** — Ministry of DoNER, the Andaman and Nicobar Administration.

"**Work division is the foundation of organization; indeed, the reason for organization.**" And his efficiency axiom: "**efficiency is axiom number one in the value scale of administration**" — the sentence **Waldo** spent a book demolishing.

**Graicunas** showed relationships multiply **geometrically** as subordinates rise arithmetically; **Urwick** proposed **five or six** at the top. The trade-off is fixed: a **narrow span** builds a **tall hierarchy** with long delays; a **wide span** builds a **flat one** with thin supervision.

A Secretariat file typically climbs **Section Officer → Under Secretary → Deputy Secretary → Director → Joint Secretary → Additional Secretary → Secretary**. The **2nd ARC's 13th Report** recommended **three levels** and a **desk officer system** — first proposed by **ARC-I in 1968** and still unimplemented.

**Onward Industry (1931)** — organisation rests on the **coordinative principle**, expressed through the **scalar process** and producing the **functional effect**. Their contribution is the claim that **coordination is the first principle**, from which hierarchy and specialisation follow.

**POSDCORB is written into Indian law**: the **Government of India (Allocation of Business) Rules, 1961** distribute *purpose*; the **Transaction of Business Rules, 1961** prescribe *process*; the **Secretariat–executive agency** split is Gulick's **policy-versus-implementation** distinction in statutory form.

Same goal — **efficiency**; opposite route. Taylor: efficiency through **method, measurement and money**. Mayo: through **attention, group norms and belonging**. Neither is complete — which is why **Herzberg** later separated the two into **hygiene** and **motivators**.

**Traditional** (sanctity of custom — the hereditary ruler), **charismatic** (devotion to an exceptional person), **legal-rational** (belief in the legality of enacted rules). **Bureaucracy is the administrative apparatus of legal-rational authority.**

items.t: The characteristics of the ideal type
items.d: **Fixed jurisdictional areas**; **hierarchy of offices**; management by **written documents** — the file; **expert training**; the official's **full working capacity**; **stable, exhaustive rules**; **impersonality**; a **career** with tenure and fixed salary; **office separated from the person** of the incumbent.

Bureaucracy is "**capable of attaining the highest degree of efficiency** and is in this sense **formally the most rational** known means of exercising **authority over human beings**." Note the word **formally** — Weber claims **procedural**, not substantive, rationality.

**Stahlhartes Gehäuse** — rationalisation traps its makers: "**specialists without spirit, sensualists without heart**." And the political warning: "**the ruled cannot dispense with or replace the bureaucratic apparatus of authority once it exists**."

items.t: The ideal type is a yardstick, not a portrait
items.d: The commonest error in a Weber answer. The ideal type is a **methodological construct** — a deliberate **exaggeration of essential features** built to **measure deviation**. Criticising Weber because real bureaucracies are inefficient **misses what an ideal type is for**.

Charismatic authority is **inherently unstable** — it dies with the leader. To survive, it must be **routinised** into traditional or legal-rational forms. Indian instance: a **movement-led scheme** surviving only once it acquires **rules, cadre and a budget line**.

items.t: Weber's model in Indian constitutional form
items.d: **Article 309** (recruitment and conditions), **Article 310** (pleasure doctrine), **Article 311** (procedural protection against dismissal), the **CCS (Conduct) Rules, 1964** and **CCS (CCA) Rules, 1965**. The **steel frame** is Weber's **career service with tenure** written into a Constitution.

In a society of **ascriptive hierarchy**, **impersonality is emancipatory**: the rule that ignores caste is what lets a Dalit applicant be served. Every argument for **flexibility and discretion** must answer this — discretion in an unequal society **restores the very particularism** the rules removed.

bureaucracy "constitutes the **imaginary state** beside the real state; it is the **spiritualism of the state**." For Marx it is an **instrument of the dominant class** that mistakes its **own interest** for the **general interest** — the sharpest counter to Weber's neutrality claim.

The **2026 frontier.** Algorithmic decision-making is **legal-rational authority automated**: fixed jurisdiction, written rule, impersonality, no discretion. It perfects the **iron cage** — and removes the **human official** who could be argued with, appealed to, or held accountable.

**'Bureaucratic Structure and Personality' (1940)** — the rules that secure **reliability** produce **overconformity**. Training in one method becomes an **incapacity** in changed conditions; the **means displace the ends**; the official becomes a **bureaucratic virtuoso** who serves the file, not the citizen.

The **RTI reply** that answers the question asked and not the one meant; **grievance 'disposal' rates** on **CPGRAMS** counted as redress; a scheme measured by **funds utilised** rather than **outcomes**. Merton's mechanism is the single most usable critique in Indian answers.

**TVA and the Grass Roots (1949)** — an organisation absorbs **hostile external elements into its leadership** to secure survival, and is **changed by them**. **Formal** co-optation confers visible participation; **informal** co-optation transfers real power. Result: **sub-goal formation** and the "**unanticipated consequences of purposive social action**."

**Elite capture** of Water User Associations and forest committees; the **Community Development Programme's** absorption by dominant rural castes — the failure **Balwantrai Mehta** diagnosed in 1957; **sarpanch pati** substituting for the elected woman representative.

**Patterns of Industrial Bureaucracy (1954)** — **mock bureaucracy** (rules nobody enforces, e.g. the no-smoking sign), **representative bureaucracy** (rules both sides accept, e.g. safety rules), **punishment-centred bureaucracy** (rules one side imposes on the other). Also the **indulgency pattern** — selective non-enforcement that buys compliance.

**The Bureaucratic Phenomenon (1964)** — bureaucracy is "**an organisation that cannot correct its behaviour by learning from its errors**." Impersonal rules remove discretion; the remaining **zones of uncertainty** become **power resources**; officials defend them; the response is **more rules**. The circle tightens.

items.t: Michels — the iron law of oligarchy
items.d: "**Who says organisation says oligarchy.**" Any large organisation, however democratic in purpose, generates a **specialised leadership** that acquires an interest in its **own continuance**. It applies to **political parties, trade unions and cooperatives** — and to **panchayat federations**.

The cluster of dysfunctions — **red tape, buck-passing, rule-worship, empire-building, over-caution, secrecy**. Its damage is that it **penalises the competent**: the officer who decides is exposed, the one who circulates the file is safe.

**Warren Bennis** predicted the **death of bureaucracy** and its replacement by **organic-adaptive, temporary task systems** — **adhocracy**. **Toffler** named it; **Mintzberg** placed it among his configurations.

Bennis was wrong on the timetable and right on the direction. **Missions, SPVs, societies and task forces** proliferated **around** the permanent structure — **NHM societies, Smart City SPVs, NDMA's Incident Response System** — but the **Secretariat, the cadre and the file survived intact**. Adhocracy became a **layer**, not a **replacement**.

**Follett's** central move: **depersonalise the order**. Neither party gives orders to the other; **both take their orders from the situation**. Authority derives from the **facts of the case**, not the **position of the speaker** — which is why she calls it **power-with**, not **power-over**.

Three ways to settle a conflict — **domination** (one side wins), **compromise** (both give up something), **integration** (a solution in which **neither side sacrifices anything**, found by uncovering the **real underlying demands**). Only integration is **constructive**; conflict becomes **creative**.

"**We should never allow ourselves to be bullied by an 'either-or'.**" And on authority: "**Authority should go with knowledge and experience... no matter whether it is up the line or down.**" Two quotations that fit any conflict, leadership or expertise question.

**Circular response** — the parties change each other continuously, so behaviour is never one-directional; **the group principle** — the individual is realised **through** the group; **coordination as a continuous process** by **direct contact**, at the **earliest stage**, through **reciprocal relating**.

items.t: Why she is called the prophet of management
items.d: **Drucker** named her that. Writing in the **1920s**, she anticipated **human relations** (before Hawthorne), **participative management**, **conflict as constructive**, **matrix authority** and **stakeholder thinking** — from a background in **political science and social work**, not engineering.

She accepted the classical concern with **coordination and authority** but relocated both in **psychology and group process** — making her the **hinge** between Taylor's mechanics and Mayo's sociology.

The **GST Council** is integration in constitutional form — **Article 279A**, weighted voting, but decisions overwhelmingly by **consensus** because either side's veto is worthless. **PRAGATI** works by **direct contact at the earliest stage**; the **Incident Response System** applies the **law of the situation** in a disaster.

It presumes a **discoverable common interest**. Where the conflict is **distributive** — **river water between Karnataka and Tamil Nadu**, a **land acquisition** — there may be no integrative solution, and Follett offers no procedure for deciding **who loses**. That is what **adjudication and politics** are for.

**Western Electric, 1924-32**, four phases: **illumination experiments** (output rose whatever the lighting), **relay assembly test room**, **mass interviewing programme** (20,000 interviews), **bank wiring observation room**. Conducted by **Elton Mayo, Roethlisberger and Dickson**.

Output is a function of **social relations**, not physical conditions. The **informal group** sets its own **production norms** and enforces them — the bank wiring room punished the **rate-buster** and the **chiseller** alike. **Non-economic rewards** shape behaviour more than the piece-rate.

Behaviour changes because subjects know they are **being observed**. Its administrative use is double-edged: **attention itself** improves performance — which explains why **PRAGATI review** and **inspection** work, and why their effect **decays** once attention moves elsewhere.

Mayo rejected the **'rabble hypothesis'** — the classical assumption that society is a horde of unorganised individuals each acting from self-interest. Man is a **social animal** seeking **belonging**; industrial society's disease is **anomie**, and the workplace group is the remedy.

items.t: Formal organisations are made of informal groups
