items.d: The informal organisation is **not a defect** of the formal one — it is the **condition of its working**. It supplies **speed** (the phone call that pre-clears the file), **information** (the grapevine), and **social control**. Suppress it and the formal system **slows and hardens**.

items.t: The standard critiques of human relations
items.d: **Pro-management bias** — happier workers as a route to output, not a good in themselves. **No place for conflict** or unions — **Clark Kerr's** "**cow sociology**": contented cows give more milk. **Methodologically weak** — small samples, observer effect, **Carey's** re-analysis found the data unsupportive.

Yes, but relocated. **Hybrid and platform work** has hollowed out the informal group; **team belonging** must now be **deliberately designed**. In Indian administration the informal group is the **batch, the cadre and the mess** — which explains both **cohesion** and **cadre parochialism**.

The **Joint Consultative Machinery (1966)** institutionalises staff voice through **National, Departmental and Office Councils** with **compulsory arbitration**; **service associations** are the informal group made formal; the **behavioural competencies** of **Mission Karmayogi's FRAC** are Mayo's insight in a training framework.

"A system of **consciously coordinated activities or forces of two or more persons**." Note what is coordinated — **activities, not people**. The organisation is a **cooperative system**, and it survives only while cooperation is **willingly renewed**.

**Maintain a system of communication**; **secure essential services from individuals**; **formulate and define purpose**. Barnard puts **communication first** — an organisation exists to the extent that its members can **reach one another**.

**Authority resides in the subordinate, not the office.** A communication is authoritative only if the receiver **understands** it, believes it **consistent with organisational purpose** and with **personal interest**, and is **mentally and physically able** to comply. **The one who obeys confers the authority.**

The band of orders a subordinate obeys **without conscious question**. Its **width** is the real measure of managerial authority — widened by **inducements, fairness and legitimacy**, narrowed by **arbitrary or unlawful** commands. The **illegal transfer order** narrows it for everyone who watches.

**Effectiveness** = the **organisation's purpose** is achieved. **Efficiency** = the **individual's motives** are satisfied, so cooperation continues. efficiency is the capacity to offer **effective inducements in sufficient quantity** to maintain **equilibrium**.

Material incentives are **weak** beyond subsistence. Barnard ranks **non-material** ones higher — **prestige, participation, ideal benefaction, associational attractiveness** — and adds **persuasion**: changing what people **want**, not just what they **get**. The case against pay as the sole lever.

The executive's distinctive task is "**the creation of moral codes for others**" — resolving conflicts between **codes** (legal, professional, personal, organisational) by **inventing a higher one**. This is Barnard's answer to "**I was only obeying orders**", and the reason he belongs in an ethics answer.

items.t: Barnard applied to the Indian officer
items.d: **CCS (Conduct) Rule 3(3)(iii)** requires oral directions to be **confirmed in writing** — an institutional device for **narrowing the zone of indifference** to unlawful commands. **T.S.R. Subramanian v. Union of India (2013)** directed exactly this, plus a **Civil Services Board** and **minimum tenure**.

**Simon (1947)** — **decision-making is the heart of administration**. The unit of analysis is not the **task** but the **decision premise**, and the organisation's real function is to **supply the premises** on which its members decide.

Every decision mixes a **factual** premise (testable — will this work?) and a **value** premise (not testable — should it be done?). Administration can be **scientific** about facts; values come from **politics**. This is Simon's reconstruction of the dichotomy on a **defensible** footing.

Human rationality is **bounded** by incomplete knowledge of alternatives, inability to foresee all consequences, and limited **computational capacity**. The decision-maker constructs a **simplified model** of the situation and behaves rationally **with respect to that model**.

Because search is costly, we do not **maximise** — we set an **aspiration level** and take the **first alternative that is good enough**. **Administrative man satisfices; economic man maximises.** administrative man bridges the **psychological** and the **rational** man.

**Programmed** — repetitive, handled by **habit, standard operating procedure and rules**; increasingly by **software**. **Non-programmed** — novel, ill-structured, handled by **judgement, intuition and heuristics**. Simon's two-dimensional taxonomy pairs each with its **traditional** and **modern** technique.

"the process of decisions... is largely a **technique of narrowing choices**." Organisation narrows by **hierarchy, rules, training, communication channels and the vocabulary of the file** — long before the officer consciously deliberates.

**Intelligence** (finding occasions for decision) → **Design** (developing alternatives) → **Choice** (selecting one) → **Review**. Drawn as a **funnel narrowing under bounded rationality**, this is one of the few diagrams that genuinely earns its space.

**Chris Argyris** — Simon's rationality **suppresses emotion and self-actualisation**, producing the very passivity he describes. **Waldo** — a value-free science of administration is impossible. **Others** — it explains **how** decisions are made, not **whose interests** they serve.

The **Cabinet Note** is a **premise-supplying device**: it fixes the alternatives before the Cabinet meets. **Incremental budgeting** is satisficing with a **previous year's base** as the aspiration level. The **Economic Survey's nudge chapter** is Simon's psychology arriving as official policy.

**McGregor (The Human Side of Enterprise, 1960)** — **X** assumes people **dislike work**, avoid responsibility and need **coercion and control**; **Y** assumes work is as natural as play, people exercise **self-direction** toward committed objectives, and seek responsibility.

The real force of McGregor's argument. Treat staff as untrustworthy — **multiple countersignatures, no delegation, punishment for error** — and they will **stop taking decisions**, confirming the assumption. India's **file culture** is a **Theory X system** that then complains of a **risk-averse bureaucracy**.

**System 1 exploitative-authoritative**, **2 benevolent-authoritative**, **3 consultative**, **4 participative group**. **System 4** performs best. Its mechanism is the **linking pin** — every supervisor is a **member of two groups**, carrying influence **upward** as well as downward.

Adults move from **passivity to activity**, **dependence to independence**, **shallow to deep interests**, **short to long time perspective**, **subordinate to equal position**, **low to high self-awareness**. Formal organisation **demands the immature end** — and gets **apathy, defensiveness and exit**.

**Single-loop learning** corrects the **error**; **double-loop learning** questions the **governing rule** that produced it. Bureaucracies excel at the first and avoid the second — which is Crozier's vicious circle stated in learning terms.

All three argue that **structure shapes personality**, not the reverse. The apathetic official is a **product of the organisation's design**. Therefore the reform lever is **job design, delegation and participation**, not exhortation or training alone.

**Joint Consultative Machinery** for staff; **Gram Sabha** and **ward committees** for citizens; **Mission Karmayogi's** shift from **rule-based to role-based** competency; the **360-degree** input at empanelment. Each is **System 3 consultative**, rarely **System 4**.

items.t: The limits of participative management in government
items.d: Government has features the theory does not model: **statutory duties that cannot be delegated**, **hierarchical answerability to Parliament**, and decisions with **coercive effect on third parties**. Participation can democratise **how** a duty is performed; it cannot democratise **whether** it is performed.

units.name: Administrative Behaviour
units.blurb: Roughly one Paper-I question in ten, and reliably one 10-marker. Decision models, motivation and leadership rotate; communication and morale are the under-prepared slots where marks are cheapest.

items.d: Define the problem, rank **all** goals, list **all** alternatives, cost **all** consequences, choose the **optimum**. It is the standard against which every other model is a **retreat** — and it is impossible for exactly the reasons **Simon** gave.

**'The Science of Muddling Through' (1959)** — **successive limited comparisons**. Only alternatives **marginally different from the status quo** are examined; means and ends are chosen **together**; the test of a good policy is **agreement**, not correspondence to an objective.

Lindblom's answer to the charge of drift: **coordination without a coordinator**. Many partisans, each watching a **different** value, adjust to one another; the resulting policy attends to **more** interests than any central planner could hold in mind.

Two lenses. A **broad-angle** scan for **fundamental** decisions (direction, at low detail) and a **zoom** for **incremental** ones inside that frame. It rescues incrementalism from **conservatism** and rationalism from **paralysis** — the practical Indian model.

**Viksit Bharat @2047** and NITI's strategy documents are the **broad scan**; the **annual budget** is the **incremental zoom** inside it. The **National Education Policy 2020** set the frame; **curricular and regulatory orders** fill it year by year.

**Yehezkel Dror** attacked incrementalism as **pro-inertia** and useless where there is **no past** to build on. His model adds **meta-policymaking** — deciding **how to decide** — and gives an explicit place to **extra-rational** elements: **judgement, creativity, intuition**.

**Cohen, March and Olsen (1972)** — in an **organised anarchy** (unclear goals, unclear technology, fluid participation), **problems, solutions, participants and choice opportunities** are dumped into a can and coupled by **timing, not logic**. Solutions often **precede** problems.

items.t: Where the garbage can fits India
items.d: A **pre-existing scheme design** attaching itself to a **new crisis**; a **ready technology** searching for a mandate. **Aadhaar** began as a **solution** and successively found problems — subsidy leakage, banking, KYC, welfare targeting — over a decade.

**Kahneman and Tversky's** prospect theory; **Thaler and Sunstein's** choice architecture and **libertarian paternalism**. **Default rules** do more than exhortation: **Ujjwala's** LPG **Give-It-Up** appeal, **Swachh Bharat's** shame-and-pride messaging, the **Economic Survey 2018-19** nudge chapter.

items.t: The decision models compared, in one line
items.d: **Rational** — what we should do; **incremental** — what we can agree on; **mixed scanning** — how to do both at two altitudes; **garbage can** — what actually happens when nobody is in charge.

**Physiological → safety → social → esteem → self-actualisation**, each **prepotent** over the next; a **satisfied need ceases to motivate**. Its administrative use is diagnostic: an officer stuck at **safety** (transfer insecurity) cannot be motivated by **esteem** appeals.

Collapses Maslow into **Existence, Relatedness, Growth**, and adds two corrections: **more than one need can operate at once**, and a **frustration–regression** hypothesis — blocked **growth** intensifies demand for **existence** rewards. Explains why a stalled cadre fights over **pay and allowances**.

**Hygiene factors** — pay, policy, supervision, conditions, security — remove **dissatisfaction** but do not motivate. **Motivators** — achievement, recognition, the work itself, responsibility, advancement — produce **satisfaction**. The two are **not opposite ends of one scale**.

Successive **Pay Commissions** work almost entirely on **hygiene**. The **8th CPC** (ToR notified **3 November 2025**, **Justice Ranjana Prakash Desai**, ~**50 lakh employees and 69 lakh pensioners**) will remove dissatisfaction; it will not motivate. **Job enrichment** — real delegation and challenging postings — is the untouched lever.

**Achievement (nAch)** — moderate risk, personal responsibility, immediate feedback; **Affiliation (nAff)** — warm relationships; **Power (nPow)**. His crucial distinction: **personalised power** (dominance) versus **socialised power** (influence used for group ends) — the second is what a good administrator has.

**Perry and Wise** — a distinctive predisposition to serve, with **rational** (policy-making attraction), **norm-based** (duty, public interest) and **affective** (compassion) foundations. It explains why officers accept **hardship postings** that no pay differential covers.

**Frey's motivation crowding theory** — **extrinsic** rewards can **destroy** intrinsic ones. Pay a citizen to do what she did from duty and she stops doing it for free. This is the strongest argument against **crude performance pay** in the public service.

items.t: Money is the weakest lever in Indian government
items.d: Salary is **fixed by grade**, promotion largely by **seniority**, and dismissal is **hard**. Real motivators are the ones the system controls informally — **posting, empanelment, recognition, and a superior who will back a decision**.

Same **object** — the energising of behaviour; different **question**. **Content** asks **what** motivates (Maslow, Herzberg, McClelland, Alderfer); **process** asks **how** motivation is formed and sustained (Vroom, Adams, Locke, Skinner).

**Motivation = Expectancy × Instrumentality × Valence.** Effort must be believed to produce **performance**; performance to produce a **reward**; the reward must be **wanted**. Any term at zero makes the product zero — the cleanest diagnostic in the whole motivation literature.

**Instrumentality is near zero**: performance and reward are weakly linked when **promotion follows seniority** and appraisal ratings **cluster at 'outstanding'**. The **Surinder Nath (2003)** and **Hota (2004)** committees attacked precisely this link.

They add that **performance causes satisfaction** — not the reverse — and only when the reward is seen as **equitable**. They also insert **abilities** and **role perception**: an officer who misreads the role produces effort that yields no performance.

People compare their **outcome-to-input ratio** with a **referent other**. Perceived **inequity** produces tension resolved by reducing effort, inflating perceived inputs, changing the referent, or leaving. Explains **cadre grievances** over **pay parity and empanelment** better than any absolute measure.

**Specific and difficult** goals, if **accepted**, produce higher performance than 'do your best' — provided there is **feedback** and **commitment**. The theoretical basis of **outcome budgeting**, **RFD** and the **Aspirational Districts** delta ranking.

**Skinner** — behaviour is shaped by its **consequences**. **Positive reinforcement**, **negative reinforcement**, **punishment**, **extinction**; **schedules** matter more than magnitude. Indian administration relies almost wholly on **punishment and extinction**, which suppress error and also **suppress initiative**.

**Deci and Ryan** — intrinsic motivation needs **autonomy, competence and relatedness**. It is the theoretical ground for **Mission Karmayogi's** competency approach and for the argument that **minimum tenure** motivates more than an increment: a transferred officer loses **all three** at once.

items.t: The trait to behaviour to contingency progression
items.d: **Traits** (great men) → **behaviour** (what leaders do) → **contingency** (what works, when).

**Ohio State** isolated two independent dimensions — **initiating structure** and **consideration** — so a leader may be high on both. **Michigan** framed the same as **production-centred** versus **employee-centred**, and (unlike Ohio) treated them as **opposite ends of one scale**.

**Concern for production** against **concern for people**, each 1-9. **1,1 impoverished; 9,1 task; 1,9 country club; 5,5 middle-of-the-road; 9,9 team**. Their claim — **9,9 is universally best** — is what contingency theorists reject.

Reddin adds a **third dimension — effectiveness** — to task and relationship orientation. The same style is **effective or ineffective depending on the situation**: 'dedicated' becomes **benevolent autocrat** or **autocrat**; 'integrated' becomes **executive** or **compromiser**.

Style is **fixed** (measured by the **Least Preferred Co-worker** scale), so match the **situation** to the leader. Three situational variables: **leader-member relations, task structure, position power**. **Task-oriented** leaders excel in **very favourable and very unfavourable** situations; **relationship-oriented** in the **middle**.

Style follows follower **readiness**: **telling → selling → participating → delegating**. Directly usable on **cadre management** — a probationer needs *telling*, a Collector of ten years' standing needs *delegating*, and reversing the two destroys both.

**James MacGregor Burns (1978)**, developed by **Bass**. **Transactional** — contingent reward and management by exception. **Transformational** — **idealised influence, inspirational motivation, intellectual stimulation, individualised consideration**. Burns: leaders and followers "**raise one another to higher levels of motivation and morality**."

**Robert Greenleaf** — the leader is **servant first**. "The best test is: **do those served grow as persons?**" The natural Indian pairing is **Gandhi's talisman** and the district officer whose measure is whether the **weakest citizen** in the district is better placed.

"nothing in public administration is more important, interesting or mysterious than **leadership**." Strategic leadership is **anticipatory** — it manages the **authorising environment** and builds **capacity for the next problem**, which is **Mark Moore's** strategic triangle in behavioural form.

The test of leadership is **ownership of failure**, not appropriation of success. Administratively this means **recording reasons**, accepting **audit and parliamentary scrutiny**, and protecting subordinates who acted on lawful orders — the opposite of **blame-shifting down the hierarchy**.

In conflict, **assertiveness is mistaken for competence** and the emotionally mature are read as weak. The correction is **structural, not exhortatory** — chairing rules, minuted dissent, written orders — so that the **loudest voice does not become the decision**.

**E. Sreedharan** at DMRC — deadlines, delegation, resignation offered for a single accident. **T.N. Seshan** — statutory power used to its constitutional edge. **Armstrong Pame**, the 'people's IAS officer', built a road by crowdfunding. One named instance beats a paragraph of adjectives.

items.t: Communication as the first executive function
items.d: **Barnard** placed it first because an organisation **is** its communication system. **Deutsch** went further — government is a **steering system** and **information is the steering**. A structure that cannot carry accurate upward information **cannot correct itself**.

**Downward carries authority** — orders, policy, feedback — and is **distorted by dilution** through each level. **Upward carries information** — reports, grievances, dissent — and is **distorted by filtering**: subordinates edit out what displeases. **Horizontal carries coordination** and is the weakest in a hierarchy.

Not because the channel is missing but because the **incentive is inverted**: reporting a problem invites blame for having it. India's institutional workarounds are **inspection**, **social audit**, **CPGRAMS**, and the **PMO's PRAGATI**, where the apex leader **looks at the data directly**.

It is **fast, filters gaps left by formal channels, and carries morale information** management never receives. It also **carries rumour and cannot be corrected**. The administrative response is not suppression but **speed** — occupy the space with **timely formal information**.

**Wheel** — fast, accurate, high leader-emergence, **low member satisfaction**. **Chain** — hierarchical, slow. **Circle** — slow, but high satisfaction. **All-channel** — best for **complex, non-routine** problems. Match the network to the **task**, and note that the file system is a **chain**.

**Semantic** (jargon, language), **physical** (distance, technology), **psychological** (fear, selective perception), **organisational** (hierarchy, span, secrecy), and **cultural** (status distance). In Indian administration, **status distance and English** are the two most consequential.

Headquarters holds **rules and money**; the field holds **facts and consequences**. Healthy relations require **two-way flow** — field discretion for local variation, headquarters feedback that is **substantive rather than compliance-seeking**. **Video conferencing collapsed distance, not status distance**.

Treating information as **data to be stored** rather than **intelligence to be used** is why **MIS** implementations fail: the system is built for **upward reporting**, not for **decision support at the level that acts**.

**RTI Section 4** makes **suo motu disclosure** a duty — communication as a **right**, not a courtesy. The **Official Secrets Act, 1923** pulls the other way; the **2nd ARC's first report** recommended repealing it and folding residual provisions into the **National Security Act**.

groups.g: Morale, conflict and personality at work

items.d: **Morale is a group condition; motivation is an individual state.** Morale is about **attitude to the organisation**; motivation about **drive toward a task**. High morale with low motivation gives a **contented, idle office**; the reverse gives **burnout**.

**Fairness of the reward system**, **security of tenure**, **quality of supervision**, **group cohesion**, **the sense that the work matters**, and **the organisation's public reputation**. In the Indian services, **arbitrary transfers** damage all six at once.

**Irving Janis** — cohesive groups under stress suppress dissent. Symptoms: **illusion of invulnerability, collective rationalisation, stereotyping of outsiders, self-censorship, illusion of unanimity, direct pressure on doubters, self-appointed mindguards**. Antidotes: a **devil's advocate**, minuted **dissent**, and a leader who **speaks last**.

items.t: The value of the dissenting note
items.d: The Indian file's **noting system** is a **structural antidote to groupthink** — a recorded, attributable, dissenting opinion. It is also what **oral instructions** destroy, which is why **CCS Conduct Rule 3(3)(iii)** and its written-confirmation requirement matter behaviourally, not just legally.

**Structural** — line versus staff, overlapping jurisdiction, scarce resources; **interpersonal** — personality, status; **role-based** — role ambiguity, role conflict, role overload. The **type** must be identified before any remedy is prescribed; each answers to a different fix.

On axes of **assertiveness** and **cooperativeness**: **competing, accommodating, avoiding, compromising, collaborating**. **Collaborating** is Follett's **integration**; **avoiding** is the file that is never put up. Each has a legitimate use — the error is having only one.

The **interactionist** view: too little conflict produces **stagnation and groupthink**; too much produces **paralysis**. The administrative task is **managing conflict to an optimum**, and **institutionalising** it — which is what **Inter-State Council**, **GST Council** and **tribunals** exist to do.

**Goleman's five components** — **self-awareness, self-regulation, motivation, empathy, social skill**. In administration it is what converts **legal authority into acceptance**: the same eviction order, delivered with or without empathy, produces cooperation or a law-and-order problem.

**Type A/B**; the **Big Five** (openness, conscientiousness, extraversion, agreeableness, neuroticism — **conscientiousness** predicts job performance best); **Rotter's locus of control** — internals take initiative, externals attribute outcomes to circumstance. **FRAC** competencies under Mission Karmayogi try to select for these.

It privileges the **observable and measurable**, so it under-reads **power, class and ideology**; it borrows **laboratory findings** into settings with **statutory duty and coercive power**; and it is **culture-bound** — a Western-derived instrument applied without validation in Indian conditions.

units.name: Organisations and the Public Sector
units.blurb: Paper I's organisation theory and Paper II's public undertakings are one subject: both ask what form an activity should take and who then answers for it. Read the theory and the Indian form side by side — the examiner rewards the candidate who shows they are the same question.

items.d: **Classical** — structure, principles, one best way. **Neo-classical** — the informal group and human need inside that structure. **Modern** — **systems** and **contingency**: the organisation as an **open system** with **no single best design**.

**Katz and Kahn**, on **Bertalanffy's** general systems theory. The organisation **imports energy, throughputs, exports output** and takes **feedback**; it exhibits **negative entropy**, **homeostasis** and **equifinality** — the same end state reachable by **different routes**.

A closed-system view treats failure as **internal** — bad staff, poor rules. An open-system view forces the **environmental** question: the scheme failed because the **ecology** — literacy, banking density, caste structure — did not supply what the design assumed.

**Trist and Bamforth's Tavistock** coal-mining studies — technical and social subsystems must be **jointly optimised**. Change the technology alone and performance falls. The direct Indian lesson: **digitising a process without redesigning the roles around it** reliably disappoints.

There is **no one best way**; the right structure depends on **environment, technology and size**. **Burns and Stalker** — **mechanistic** structures suit stable environments, **organic** ones suit turbulence.

**External fit** — structure matched to the **environment's** rate of change. **Internal fit** — the **subsystems consistent with one another**. **Lawrence and Lorsch** showed the trade-off: the greater the **differentiation** required by the environment, the harder and more costly the **integration**.

**Joan Woodward** — structure follows **production technology** (unit, mass, process). **James Thompson** — three **interdependence** types: **pooled** (coordinate by rules), **sequential** (by plans), **reciprocal** (by mutual adjustment). Use Thompson to say **why** a coordination mechanism fails.

items.t: Organisation theory is a loose set, not a theory
items.d: The field's plurality is **appropriate to its object**. A single theory of organisation would have to be **indifferent to purpose, technology, scale and culture** — and would therefore say nothing usable about any actual organisation.

**Mechanistic** where predictability is the value — **treasury, examination, land records**. **Organic** where the environment is turbulent — **disaster response under the Incident Response System**, **war-room COVID management**, **Aspirational Districts** teams. The failure mode is running a **mechanistic** structure against an **organic** problem.

It is **descriptive, not predictive** — it names the variables without ranking them; it assumes managers can **choose** structure, when in government the structure is **statutory**; and it under-weights **power**, treating design as a technical rather than a **political** choice.

**Department** — full ministerial control, budgeted through the legislature, no separate legal personality. **Corporation** — created by a **special statute**, autonomy defined by that statute. **Company** — incorporated under the **Companies Act, 2013**, flexible, easy to create and to wind up.

**Maximum control, minimum flexibility.** Financed by the **Consolidated Fund**, staffed by **civil servants**, audited by the **CAG**, answerable through the minister. Examples: **Railways**, **Posts**, **All India Radio**, the **ordnance factories** before their 2021 corporatisation.

Created by a **special Act** which fixes its powers, finances and accountability — so autonomy is **as wide as the statute makes it**. Examples: **LIC (1956), FCI (1964), Airports Authority, Damodar Valley Corporation (1948)**, India's first. Its weakness: **amending the Act to change anything**.

**Section 2(45), Companies Act 2013** — not less than **51%** paid-up capital held by government. Easy to form by executive decision, flexible on staffing and pay. The critique is constitutional: it **escapes legislative scrutiny** at birth — a public enterprise created **without a debate**.

A **board** is **plural-headed** for **deliberation and expertise** — CBDT, CBIC, Railway Board. A **commission** is usually **plural and independent** for functions requiring **insulation from the executive** — UPSC, EC, CIC, NHRC. Plurality buys **impartiality** and costs **speed**.

**Single** gives **promptness, clear responsibility, decisiveness** and is right for **executive** work. **Plural** gives **deliberation, representation of interests and protection from arbitrariness** and is right for **quasi-judicial, regulatory and advisory** work. Match the form to the **function**, not to the fashion.

**Line** performs the primary purpose (a district administration, a police station). **Staff** advises and plans **without command authority** (Cabinet Secretariat, planning cells). **Auxiliary** supplies common services (**GeM**, **CPWD**, Directorate of Printing). Confusing **line and staff authority** is the classic source of conflict.

**Political** versus **permanent**; **single** versus **plural**; **real** versus **nominal**; and the **directly elected, indirectly elected, appointed** variants. In India the political executive is **real** and the permanent executive advises — the position settled in **Shamsher Singh v. State of Punjab (1974)**.

**Commissions of inquiry** under the **Commissions of Inquiry Act, 1952**; **task forces**; **committees of secretaries**; **standing advisory councils**. Their value is **speed and specialist input**; their risk is **decision avoidance** — appointing a committee **is** a decision, usually to postpone one.

**Dual reporting** — functional and project. It fits **time-bound, multi-disciplinary** work and violates **unity of command** by design. Indian instances: **Smart City SPVs**, **mission directorates**, the **District Disaster Management Authority** pulling line departments under one incident commander.

items.t: The division of labour between them
items.d: **Headquarters** — policy, rules, standards, resource allocation, evaluation. **Field** — application to the concrete case, local intelligence, delivery. The relationship fails when headquarters does **case work** and the field is left doing **reporting**.

A field office is **headquarters relocated**, not authority transferred. **Deconcentration** disperses **offices**; **decentralisation** transfers **decisions**. Most Indian 'decentralisation' announcements are the first kind — a distinction worth a mark by itself.

**Local knowledge**, **speed of response**, **adaptation to variation**, and the **legitimacy of a visible official**. no central design survives contact with **11 agro-climatic zones and 2.55 lakh gram panchayats** without field discretion.

**Over-reporting** (the field spends its day feeding dashboards), **rule rigidity** (no room for local variation), **resource dependence** (funds released late in the year), and **status distance** (the field officer is heard as a subordinate, not as a source of facts).

items.t: How India tries to fix it
items.d: **Video-conferencing review (PRAGATI)** puts the field directly before the apex; **Aspirational Districts** central prabhari officers **live in the district**; **DISHA** committees chaired by MPs review at district level; **e-Office** removes the physical file's delay. Distance shrank; **status distance did not**.

**Delegation** — specified powers transferred, responsibility retained, **revocable**. **Deconcentration** — field offices without transfer of authority. **Decentralisation** — genuine transfer to lower levels. **Devolution** — **statutory** transfer of **functions, funds and functionaries** to an **autonomous elected body**, as in the **73rd and 74th Amendments**.

**Natural monopoly** (transmission, ports), **information asymmetry** (drugs, insurance), **externalities** (pollution), and the need for a **credible commitment** that policy will not change with the government. Regulation substitutes **rule-making** for **ownership**.

**RBI**; **SEBI (1992)**; **TRAI (1997)**; **CERC and SERCs** under the **Electricity Act, 2003**; **IRDAI**; **PNGRB**; **CCI** under the **Competition Act, 2002**, amended **2023** with **deal-value thresholds**; **FSSAI**; **IBBI (2016)**; the **Data Protection Board** under the **DPDP Act, 2023**, Rules notified **2025**.

items.t: The regulator's three functions in one body
items.d: It **makes** rules, **administers** them and **adjudicates** disputes — legislative, executive and judicial power fused. That fusion is its **efficiency** and its **constitutional problem**: the safeguard is **appeal to a tribunal** (TDSAT, APTEL, SAT, NCLAT) and **judicial review**.

On paper — fixed tenure, statutory powers, funded by fees. In practice — **appointments by government**, **policy directions** the parent ministry may issue, **post-retirement placements**, and the **revolving door** with the regulated industry.

**Stigler** — regulation is **acquired by the industry** and operated for its benefit, because the industry has **concentrated interest and superior information** while consumers are **diffuse**. **Cultural capture** is subtler: the regulator adopts the industry's **frame of the problem** without any corruption.

items.t: The demise of the arbitrator state?
items.d: The state did not withdraw — it **changed instruments**. It stopped **producing** and started **rule-making**, and in doing so acquired **more** points of intervention. Regulation is the **arbitrator state intensified**, not abolished.

The **2nd ARC's 13th Report** and the **FSLRC (Justice B.N. Srikrishna, 2013)** both found **overlap, weak accountability and no common statute**. FSLRC's **Indian Financial Code** and unified regulator were never enacted; the **NITI Aayog** paper on a common regulatory framework remains a paper.

TRAI protects consumers through **tariff orders**, **quality-of-service regulations**, **mobile number portability**, the **Do Not Disturb** framework, and consultation papers with **mandatory public comment**. Its recommendations on **licensing** are **not binding** on the government — the limit of its independence.

A **long-term contract** in which a private partner **finances, builds and operates** an asset and is repaid over the concession from **user charges or annuity**, with **risk allocated to whoever can bear it best**. It is a **mode of delivery**, not a source of money.

**Committee on Revisiting and Revitalising the PPP Model (Vijay Kelkar, 2015)** — "**PPP should not be seen as a source of funding but as a mode of delivering better services**." It recommended an **Infrastructure PPP Adjudication Tribunal**, an independent regulator, and **renegotiation as a normal event**, not a scandal.

**Viability Gap Funding**; **Model Concession Agreements**; the **Hybrid Annuity Model** in highways (**40% construction support, 60% annuity**) which restored bankability after BOT-toll failures; **PPPAC** appraisal; **InvITs** for recycling completed assets.

**Optimistic traffic and demand forecasts**; **renegotiation** after award, which converts competitive bidding into a fiction; **contingent liabilities** that never appear in the budget; and **thin markets** where two bidders make competition notional.

The citizen's remedy against a concessionaire is **contractual**, not **constitutional** — no **RTI** as of right, no **Article 226** against a private party except where it discharges a **public function**, no **CAG** audit unless the contract provides for it.

It has moved from a **procurement technique** to a **structure of governance**: the state becomes **contract manager**, and its critical capability shifts from **engineering to negotiation, risk pricing and enforcement** — capacities Indian departments were never built to hold.

The 2nd ARC supported PPP for infrastructure but insisted on **transparent competitive bidding**, **clear risk-sharing written into the concession**, an **independent regulator** for each sector, and **grievance redress for users** rather than for parties alone.

items.t: PPP and the entropy of models
items.d: A **closed** model is self-contained and predictable; an **open** one exchanges with its environment and resists decay. PPP forces a **closed** bureaucratic organisation into an **open** contractual environment — importing **market energy** and also **market risk** it cannot price.

items.t: Why India built a public sector
items.d: **Industrial Policy Resolution, 1956** and the **Mahalanobis** second plan: **capital scarcity**, the need for **heavy industry** no private investor would fund, **balanced regional development**, **employment** and the avoidance of **concentration of economic power**. Nehru's "**temples of modern India**."

**Schedule A** — 17 industries exclusively for the state (arms, atomic energy, railways, heavy industry). **Schedule B** — 12 industries progressively state-owned. **Schedule C** — the rest, left to the private sector. This is the architecture the **1991 policy** dismantled.

**New Industrial Policy, 1991** — reserved industries cut from **17 to 8**, then to **2** (atomic energy, railways) by 2001; **licensing abolished** except for a short list; **MRTP** pre-approval scrapped; loss-making units referred to the **BIFR**; **disinvestment** begun.

**New Public Sector Enterprise Policy, 2021** — **four strategic sectors** (atomic energy/space/defence; transport and telecom; power, petroleum, coal and minerals; banking, insurance and financial services) with a **bare-minimum** presence; **privatisation or closure** everywhere else.

A **graded autonomy** scheme rather than a status symbol. **Maharatna** may invest up to **₹5,000 crore** or **15% of net worth** in a single project without government approval; **Navratna** up to **₹1,000 crore**; **Miniratna I** up to **₹500 crore**. Autonomy here means **financial delegation**, nothing more.

**Arjun Sengupta Committee, 1987-88** — a negotiated **performance contract** between the enterprise and its ministry, scored annually on **financial and non-financial** parameters. India's earliest and most durable **NPM** device, now run by the **Department of Public Enterprises**.

A PSU carries **social obligations** a private firm does not — universal service, strategic supply, regional development, employment. Judge it on **capacity utilisation, technology absorption, safety, energy intensity, CSR under Section 135** and **social cost-benefit**, not profit alone.

Both things are true. It built **capabilities no private firm would have** — **ISRO, BHEL, ONGC, IOCL, the DRDO chain, LIC's household savings mobilisation**. It also produced **chronic loss-makers**, **overstaffing** and a **licence-era rent structure**.

**Peter Evans (Embedded Autonomy, 1995)** — a developmental state needs a bureaucracy **autonomous** enough to resist capture and **embedded** enough in industry to know what it needs. India's **space and atomic energy** programmes had both; the **licensing system** had embeddedness without autonomy — and became **capture**.

Largely, yes. Autonomy is granted by **executive delegation, not statute**; the **administrative ministry** controls the **board's composition**, the **capex approval**, and the **CMD's appointment through the PESB**. What exists is **delegated financial power**, not independence.

The classic statement: **the more autonomy an enterprise is given, the weaker the citizen's chain of accountability becomes**; the tighter the accountability, the less it can behave commercially. There is **no design that removes the tension** — only choices about where to sit on it.

**Parliament** — the **Committee on Public Undertakings (COPU)**, 22 members, no ministers. **CAG** — commercial audit under **Section 143(5)-(6), Companies Act 2013**, including **supplementary audit** and the **non-review certificate**. **Executive** — DPE guidelines, presidential directives, the **PESB** for appointments.

Worth quoting because it cuts against the grain: **Appleby opposed bringing public enterprises under CAG audit**, arguing that an audit designed for **regularity** would smother **commercial risk-taking**. The counter-argument is that **public money without public audit** is indefensible.

**Minority stake sale** (revenue, no control change); **strategic sale** with transfer of management (**Air India to Tata, 2022**; **VSNL, BALCO, Hindustan Zinc** earlier); **ETF route** (**CPSE ETF, Bharat 22**); and **asset monetisation** under the **NMP**, which transfers **operation** without **ownership**.

items.t: The case for and against disinvestment
items.d: **For** — fiscal space, better capital allocation, exposure to competition, and the state exiting sectors where it has **no comparative advantage**. **Against** — sale of **profit-making** assets to meet a **revenue** target, loss of the **strategic and social obligation** layer, and **employment** effects.

Evidence is mixed and should be written that way: competition **did** force efficiency in **telecom and aviation**; **listed CPSEs** improved governance under **SEBI's LODR**. But **valuation timing**, **strategic sale to a thin market**, and the **absence of a post-privatisation regulator** repeatedly weakened outcomes.

**SEBI's LODR** requires listed CPSEs to have **independent directors**, but a large share of positions stay **vacant** and independent directors are **appointed by the same ministry** that owns the shares. **Independence appointed by the controlling shareholder is a contradiction in terms.**

**Disinvestment Commission (G.V. Ramakrishna, 1996)** — a **National Investment Fund** ring-fencing proceeds so they finance **capital**, not **revenue** deficit; professional boards insulated from the ministry; and **DIPAM** as a single, transparent, calendared process rather than a year-end scramble.

items.t: Departmental to corporate — a live instance
items.d: The **ordnance factories** were converted into **seven Defence PSUs (2021)** — the largest recent transfer of form. Watch it as the natural exam case: did **corporatisation** deliver **autonomy**, or reproduce the same ministry control through a **shareholding department**?

units.name: Accountability, Control and Integrity
units.blurb: Paper I's control mechanisms and Paper II's 'significant issues' are the same argument at two altitudes. India's accountability is dense but ineffective — procedural rather than consequential. Make that the spine.

items.d: **Control** is **prior and continuous** — the power to direct. **Accountability** is **posterior** — the duty to render an account and face consequences. **Responsibility** is **internal** — the obligation felt. A system can be heavy on control and empty of accountability, which describes India.

**Finer** — accountability must be **external and enforceable**: "the servants of the public are **not to decide their own course**; they are to be **responsible to the elected representatives**." **Friedrich** — the modern administrator's expertise makes external control impossible, so rely on the **inner check** of professional standards and public sentiment.

Neither alone works. **Finer's** external controls arrive **too late** and cannot judge technical choices; **Friedrich's** inner check is **unverifiable**. The workable answer is **Finer's institutions plus Friedrich's ethics** — codes and training to shape judgement, audit and courts to catch failure.

**Transparency, liability, controllability, responsibility, responsiveness.** His warning is the useful part — **multiple accountabilities disorder**: an agency answerable on all five to different masters satisfies none and becomes **paralysed** or **arbitrary**.

**Hierarchical** (supervisory, low discretion), **legal** (external, low discretion), **professional** (internal, high discretion), **political** (external, high discretion). Naming which type a question is about **prevents the answer becoming a list**.

**Dennis Thompson** — where a decision passes through many officials, **no one is individually blameworthy** and accountability dissolves. It is the standing defence in every Indian inquiry report, and the reason **recorded, attributable noting** matters more than any oversight body.

The more specialised the decision, the fewer the people competent to review it. **Parliamentary questions cannot audit an algorithm**; a **CAG** auditor cannot second-guess a spectrum valuation model. The remedy is **procedural** — publish the method, the assumptions and the dissent — not substantive review.

items.t: India's accountability paradox — the signature argument
items.d: India has **more** accountability institutions than most democracies and **less** consequence. Files are audited, grievances are **'disposed'**, commissions report — and almost nobody is penalised. **RTI penalties are imposed in about 3% of disposed cases.** Accountability here is **procedural, not consequential**.

items.t: The instruments, in order of bite
items.d: **Financial** — Budget, Demands for Grants, cut motions, the **PAC, Estimates Committee and COPU**. **Deliberative** — question hour, half-an-hour discussion, calling attention, adjournment motion, no-confidence. **Legislative** — the **Committee on Subordinate Legislation**. **Departmental Standing Committees** — 24, doing the real scrutiny.

**Declining sitting days**; the **anti-defection law** removing the individual MP's independence; **guillotine** disposing of most Demands undiscussed; **ordinances**; **money-bill routing**; committees whose reports are **not binding**; and technical matter no generalist committee can penetrate.

**22 members (15 Lok Sabha, 7 Rajya Sabha)**, chaired by a member of the **Opposition** by convention; examines the **CAG's** reports **after the money is spent**. Its strength is **non-partisan continuity**; its limits are **post-facto** timing and the absence of any **power to penalise**.

**PAC** — audits **past** expenditure against sanction. **Estimates Committee (30, Lok Sabha only)** — suggests **economies** in **proposed** estimates; called the 'continuous economy committee'. **COPU (22)** — examines **public undertakings**, which the other two cannot reach.

**24 committees, 31 members each (21 Lok Sabha, 10 Rajya Sabha)**, since **1993**. They examine **demands for grants, bills, annual reports and long-term policy**. They work **outside the glare of the House**, which is exactly why they are the most substantive scrutiny Parliament does.

items.t: Parliamentary control over expenditure is declining
items.d: The evidence: a shrinking share of **Demands actually discussed**, routine use of the **guillotine**, growing reliance on **supplementary demands**, expenditure through **off-budget borrowing and parastatals**, and **fewer bills** sent to committee.

On the last allotted day the Speaker puts **all outstanding Demands for Grants to vote together, without discussion**. It guarantees the **timeline** the Constitution requires and sacrifices the **scrutiny** the Constitution intends — a trade of **form for substance** that has become routine.

A **statutory minimum of sitting days**; a **Budget Office** giving members independent costing capacity; **mandatory committee reference** of every bill; **pre-legislative consultation** as a rule; and the **2nd ARC's** proposal to place the **CAG's** reports before committees within a **fixed time**.

**Budgetary** (sanction, re-appropriation, Finance Ministry concurrence); **personnel** (appointment, transfer, promotion, discipline under CCS-CCA Rules); **hierarchical** (supervision, inspection, review); **coordination** (Cabinet Secretariat, committees of secretaries); and **audit** through internal audit and the CVC-CVO chain.

**Illegality** (acting beyond power — *ultra vires*), **irrationality** (**Wednesbury** unreasonableness), **procedural impropriety** (breach of **natural justice** or of a mandatory procedure), and increasingly **proportionality**. **Lord Diplock's** classification, adopted in Indian practice.

**Habeas corpus** (produce the body), **mandamus** (perform the public duty), **prohibition** (stop exceeding jurisdiction, before), **certiorari** (quash, after), **quo warranto** (by what authority do you hold this office). **Article 32** against the Supreme Court, **Article 226** — wider — against a High Court.

**Signature argument.** Courts wrote the administrative reform legislatures would not: **Vineet Narain (1997)** gave the **CVC** statutory footing and single-directive protection; **Prakash Singh (2006)** ordered **seven police reforms**; **T.S.R. Subramanian (2013)** ordered a **Civil Services Board**, **minimum tenure** and **written orders**.

Courts act **only when moved**, decide **the case not the system**, cannot supply **funds or personnel**, and are themselves **overloaded** — about **4.76 crore cases pending (NJDG, 2026)**. And every reform they order depends on an executive **willing to comply**; **Prakash Singh compliance has been nominal for nineteen years**.

items.t: The judiciary mandating rather than restraining
items.d: Review has moved from **negative** (striking down) to **positive** (directing what must be done) — continuing mandamus, guidelines with the force of law under **Article 141**, monitored implementation. **Vishaka (1997)** legislated in the legislature's silence.

The **Presidential Reference opinion (November 2025)** declined to impose **judicially fixed timelines on the Governor's assent** under **Articles 200 and 201**, unsettling the earlier **State of Tamil Nadu** approach. It is a deliberate step back toward **political and cooperative-federal remedies** — which raises whether the **Inter-State Council** can be revived.

India has **separation of functions**, not of personnel — the executive sits in the legislature. The balance is carried instead by **judicial review**, the **basic structure doctrine**, **independent constitutional offices** (CAG, EC, UPSC), and **federal division**. Say that, rather than reciting Montesquieu.

**Section 2(h)** public authority; **Section 4** **suo motu** disclosure — the section that would make most applications unnecessary; **Section 6** the application, no reasons required; **Section 7** thirty days, **48 hours** where life or liberty is involved; **Section 8** exemptions; **Section 19** appeals; **Section 20** penalty up to **₹25,000**.

Not from Parliament first. **MKSS** in **Rajasthan** ran **jan sunwais** from 1990 demanding muster rolls and bills; **Tamil Nadu (1997)** and eight other states legislated before the Centre; the **Freedom of Information Act, 2002** was never notified; the **RTI Act, 2005** followed the **NCPRI** campaign.

**Over 4 lakh appeals and complaints pending** across information commissions; **seven commissions non-functional** at points in 2024-25, **Jharkhand's defunct since May 2020**; penalties imposed in about **3% of disposed cases**; several State Commissions would take **four to five years** to reach a fresh appeal.

**RTI (Amendment) Act, 2019** moved the **tenure, salary and service conditions** of Information Commissioners from **statute to executive rules** — the independence that came from a fixed five-year term is now at the government's discretion. **Vacancies** do the rest without any amendment at all.

The **live 2026 issue.** **Section 44(3) of the DPDP Act, 2023** rewrites **RTI's Section 8(1)(j)** to exempt **all personal information** without the earlier **public-interest override**. Critics say it removes the basis for **beneficiary lists, muster rolls and officials' asset disclosures** — the very records RTI was built for.

items.t: Protecting the user, not just the right
items.d: The unfinished agenda: no working protection for **RTI activists**, with dozens killed since 2005. The **Whistle Blowers Protection Act, 2014** was passed and **never brought into force**; its 2015 amendment bill would have **narrowed** it to exclude disclosures touching Section 8(1) categories.

The highest-value reform is the cheapest: **enforce suo motu disclosure**. If **budgets, beneficiary lists, works, inspection reports and file notings** were published as a matter of course, most applications would not be filed, and the **backlog problem would shrink at its source**.

**Formalism** — the gap between the **prescriptive** and the **descriptive**. The Act is world-class on paper; **Section 4 compliance** is patchy, **penalties** near-notional, **commissions** unstaffed. India legislates the **norm** and under-supplies the **institution** — the single most reusable Paper II sentence.

**e-Procurement through GeM and CPP Portal**; **PFMS** tracing every rupee to the beneficiary; **faceless assessment** removing the officer-taxpayer interface; **open data on data.gov.in** and NITI's **National Data and Analytics Platform**. Transparency by **design** now outperforms transparency by **request**.

groups.g: Social audit and the citizen interface

items.d: Verification of a public work or scheme **by the community that received it**, using **official records read aloud in a public assembly**, with **findings recorded and acted upon**. It converts accountability from an **audit trail** into a **face-to-face account**.

**Section 17 of MGNREGA** makes the **Gram Sabha** the audit authority; the **MGNREGA Audit of Schemes Rules, 2011** require **independent Social Audit Units**; **Meghalaya's Community Participation and Public Services Social Audit Act, 2017** is the first **general** social audit law in India.

items.t: Why social audit works where audit does not
items.d: It reaches the **only fact that matters** — did the work happen and did the wage arrive — which no ledger can verify from a state capital. It is **timely**, **local**, and **hard to capture** where the assembly is genuinely open.

**SAUs are funded by the department they audit**; **elite capture** silences the assembly; **findings are recorded and not acted on**; and coverage outside MGNREGA is thin. Andhra Pradesh's SSAAT is the working model precisely because it has **separate funding and trained village social auditors**.

Four modes: the citizen as **applicant** (a service to be obtained), as **complainant** (CPGRAMS), as **participant** (Gram Sabha, ward committee, MyGov), and as **co-producer** (community forest management, school management committees). Indian reform has invested heavily in the first two and thinly in the last two.

**CPGRAMS** with an **AI-based grievance routing** layer, feedback call centres, and a **DARPG** ranking of ministries by **disposal time and quality**. The measured shortfall is that **'disposal' is counted rather than resolution** — Goodhart's law inside the grievance machine.

The **Right of Citizens for Time Bound Delivery of Goods and Services and Redressal of their Grievances Bill, 2011** lapsed. Without it, a Citizen's Charter creates **no enforceable right**. The **2nd ARC's 12th Report, Citizen Centric Administration**, remains the reference design.

**Arnstein's ladder** — from **manipulation and therapy** (non-participation), through **informing, consultation and placation** (tokenism), to **partnership, delegated power and citizen control**. Most Indian participation sits at **consultation**; **social audit and the Gram Sabha's approval of plans** reach **delegated power**.

groups.g: Media, interest groups and civil society

items.d: **Agenda-setting** (what the public thinks about), **watchdog** (exposure), and **forum** (deliberation). Its comparative advantage over formal control is **speed and reach**; its weakness is that it is **episodic** and pursues the **spectacular** over the **structural**.

The pressures: **ownership concentration**, **advertising dependence including government advertising**, **paid news and the Press Council's own findings**, **defamation and sedition-adjacent charges**, and **regulatory leverage over broadcasters**.

items.t: From institutional lens to societal lens
items.d: Media once trained its attention on **institutions** — the file, the tender, the committee. It now largely reflects **society back to itself** — identity, outrage, personality. The shift matters administratively: **institutional failure goes unreported** unless it produces a **visible victim**.

It **lowered the cost of exposure** — a single video can move an administration in hours — and **removed verification**. The administrative consequences are real: **rumour-driven law-and-order incidents**, and the **IT Rules, 2021** fact-check provisions, whose **state-as-arbiter** design the **Bombay High Court** struck down in the **Kunal Kamra** case (2024).

They **elevate** issues onto the agenda and, more consequentially, **deny others the opportunity** — **Bachrach and Baratz's** non-decision-making. In India, **organised** interests (industry associations, employee unions, farmer bodies) are heard; **unorganised** ones (informal workers, tenants) are not.

**MKSS** produced the RTI; **SEWA** organised informal women workers; **Pratham's ASER** created the learning-outcomes debate; **AIDWA and allied groups** shaped the Domestic Violence Act; **Bachpan Bachao Andolan** on child labour. Name organisations, not 'NGOs'.

items.t: When civil society restricts rather than assists
items.d: Genuine tensions: **litigation delaying** infrastructure; **unrepresentative** office-bearers claiming to speak for communities; **donor agendas** displacing local priorities; and **accountability of the accountability-seeker** — most NGOs publish less than the departments they audit.

CSO effectiveness is a **function of state structure**: statutory entry points make CSOs productive — **Gram Sabha, social audit, pre-legislative consultation, PIL, the Forest Rights Act's gram sabha consent**. Where entry points are absent, CSOs are pushed to **protest and litigation**, which the state then reads as obstruction.

**Corruption = Monopoly + Discretion − Accountability.** The most usable analytic frame in the syllabus: it turns 'reduce corruption' into three **operable** levers, and lets you show which lever each Indian reform pulls.

**Monopoly reduced** — competitive **e-auction** of coal and spectrum, **GeM's** open marketplace. **Discretion reduced** — **faceless assessment**, algorithmic case allocation, **DBT** removing the intermediary. **Accountability raised** — RTI, CVC, social audit. The **first two carried the gains**; the third lagged.

**Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988**, amended **2018** — **bribe-giving criminalised**, **prior approval** required to investigate a public servant, **timelines** for trial. **Prevention of Money Laundering Act, 2002**. **Benami Transactions (Prohibition) Amendment Act, 2016**. **Lokpal and Lokayuktas Act, 2013**.

It closed a real gap by criminalising the **giver** and requiring **timely trial**; it also restored a **prior-approval shield** akin to the **single directive** the Supreme Court struck down in **Vineet Narain (1997)** and again in **Subramanian Swamy (2014)**. Protection against harassment and protection from investigation are hard to separate.

Recommended by the **Santhanam Committee (1962-64)**, created **1964**, given **statutory** status by the **CVC Act, 2003** after **Vineet Narain**. **Multi-member**, appointed by a committee of **PM, Home Minister and Leader of Opposition**; supervises the **CBI's** anti-corruption work; **advisory** on departmental action — which is its central weakness.

Enacted **2013** after the **India Against Corruption** mobilisation, chairperson appointed only in **March 2019**. **389 complaints in 2025-26.** Its problems are structural: it **depends on CBI and CVC** for inquiry, has **no independent investigating machinery of scale**, and **most States' Lokayuktas** are weaker still.

India ratified the **UN Convention against Corruption in 2011**. Gaps that remain: **no law on private-sector bribery** beyond limited provisions, **no effective whistleblower protection in force**, **no asset-recovery framework** matching Chapter V, and **no regulation of lobbying or political funding transparency**.

The **fourth report, Ethics in Governance** — a **Code of Ethics** distinct from the Code of Conduct, an **Office of Ethics Commissioner**, **partial funding of elections**, **confiscation of illegally acquired assets**, **integrity pacts** in procurement, **conflict-of-interest and cooling-off rules**, and **serious-offence fast-tracking**.

**India 91st of 182, score 39/100**, improved from **96th in 2024**; global average **42** (**Transparency International, 16 February 2026**). Use it to argue that **transactional** corruption fell with digitisation while **grand and political** corruption is untouched by process reform.

**Nolan's seven principles** — **selflessness, integrity, objectivity, accountability, openness, honesty, leadership**. India's equivalents: the **AIS (Conduct) Rules, Rule 3** duty to maintain **integrity, devotion to duty and political neutrality**; the never-enacted **Public Services Bill** with its proposed values charter.

The effects are specific: **portfolio allocation by party rather than fit**; **ministries becoming party fiefdoms** with parallel personnel policies; **slower Cabinet decision-making**; **larger councils of ministers** before the 91st Amendment; and a **Chief Secretary or Cabinet Secretary** who must broker rather than coordinate.

Coalitions also produce **greater federal consultation**, **more legislative scrutiny** (governments cannot guillotine at will), and **regional interests represented at the Union table**. The **91st Amendment** capped the Council of Ministers at **15% of the House** and ended defection-by-split, curbing the worst instability.

**Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993**. Chairperson a **former Chief Justice of India or a Supreme Court judge** (after the **2019 amendment**), with a fixed **three-year** term. Powers: **inquiry, civil-court powers, visits to custodial institutions, intervention in court proceedings**.

Its findings are **recommendatory**; it **cannot investigate armed forces** beyond seeking a report under **Section 19**; a **one-year limitation** bars older complaints; it relies on **police to investigate police**; and **GANHRI accreditation review** has repeatedly questioned its **pluralism and appointment process**.

**Disaster Management Act, 2005** — **NDMA** chaired by the **Prime Minister**, **SDMA** by the **Chief Minister**, **DDMA** by the **District Magistrate**; **NDRF**; **NIDM** for training; **NDMA guidelines** as the binding standard. The **2025 amendment** strengthened the authorities' planning role and urban disaster arrangements.

items.t: The shift from relief to risk reduction
items.d: **Sendai Framework 2015-30** — four priorities: **understanding risk, strengthening governance, investing in resilience, enhancing preparedness for build back better**. India's move is visible in the **16th FC's disaster corpus of ₹2,04,401 crore** and in **heat action plans** treating heat as a notified local disaster.

Working Indian instances: **IMD's** impact-based cyclone forecasting; **Common Alerting Protocol** cell-broadcast warnings; **satellite and drone damage assessment** for rapid loss estimation; **flood forecasting** models; and **Bhashini** for multilingual alerts. The limits are **data quality, last-mile reach and accountability for a wrong prediction**.

units.name: Administrative Law, Police and Order
units.blurb: Administrative law is the theory of controlling discretion; law-and-order administration is the hardest place India applies it. Paper I asks about delegated legislation and tribunals almost every year; Paper II asks about police reform.

items.d: The **powers, procedures and liabilities of administrative authorities**, and the **remedies** available against them. **Wade** — it is "the law relating to the **control of governmental power**". Its subject is not what the state does but **on what terms it may do it**.

The **welfare and regulatory state**. Legislatures cannot foresee every case, so they delegate; administration acquires **rule-making and adjudicatory** power; and the citizen needs a body of law governing that power. administrative law evolved from the need for **a system of public administration under law**.

**A.V. Dicey (1885)** claimed England had **no administrative law** — his **rule of law** required (i) **supremacy of regular law** over arbitrary power, (ii) **equality before the ordinary law** for officials and citizens alike, and (iii) rights derived from **judicial decisions**, not a written charter.

He mistook the French **droit administratif** for **official privilege**; the **Conseil d'État** was in fact a robust check. And England already had **statutory tribunals and discretionary powers**. **Robson, Jennings and Wade** established that administrative law exists **wherever administrative power exists**.

India's Constitution **rejects Dicey's second proposition outright**: **Article 361** immunity for President and Governors, **Article 311** protection for civil servants, and **Article 300** state liability rules all treat officials differently. Yet **Article 14** delivers his substance — **arbitrariness is itself unconstitutional**.

items.t: Red light and green light theories
items.d: **Red light** (Dicey, Hewart) — administrative law exists to **control and restrain** the state; courts are the guardians. **Green light** (Robson, Griffith) — the state is a **force for good**; administrative law should **facilitate** effective administration and improve it from within.

**Harlow and Rawlings'** synthesis of red and green light: neither pure control nor pure facilitation. Courts intervene where **rights and procedure** are at stake and defer where **polycentric policy judgement** is involved. India is an amber-light system — **Wednesbury deference** on policy, **strict scrutiny** on liberty and procedure.

items.t: The rule of law and arbitrariness
items.d: **E.P. Royappa (1974)** — "equality is antithetic to **arbitrariness**"; arbitrary state action violates **Article 14** without more. **Maneka Gandhi (1978)** made procedure **fair, just and reasonable**. Arbitrariness in the application of law is not merely bad governance — it is **unconstitutional**.

items.t: What it is and why it exists
items.d: Rules, regulations, bye-laws and notifications made by the **executive under authority conferred by a statute**. Justified by **pressure on legislative time**, **technicality**, **flexibility to amend without an Act**, **local variation**, and the need to act in **emergency**.

**Essential legislative function cannot be delegated.** The legislature must itself lay down the **policy** and the **standard**; only the **filling in of detail** may be delegated. **In re Delhi Laws Act (1951)** settled this; **Hamdard Dawakhana (1960)** struck down delegation without a guiding standard.

**Skeleton legislation** that leaves everything to rules; **Henry VIII clauses** allowing the executive to modify the parent Act; **sub-delegation**; **retrospective** rules; **inadequate publication**; and rules made **years after** the Act, or not at all — a statute in force with no machinery.

items.t: 'A strategic tool in the hands of the executive'
items.d: The strategic use is real: the **substance** of a policy can be shifted into **rules** that never face a vote, changed by **notification**, and enforced before Parliament examines them. asked how to confine it — the answer is the three controls below.

**Laying** on the table — simple, negative (annulment within **30 days**) or affirmative resolution; the **Committee on Subordinate Legislation** in each House (**15 members**), which examines whether rules are **within the power conferred**; and scrutiny during passage of the **enabling clause** itself.

Rules may be struck as **substantively ultra vires** (beyond the parent Act, or the parent Act itself unconstitutional) or **procedurally ultra vires** (mandatory consultation or publication omitted). Courts also apply **unreasonableness** and, increasingly, **manifest arbitrariness** under Article 14.

**Prior publication and public consultation** — the **Pre-Legislative Consultation Policy, 2014** requires draft rules to be placed for **30 days**, and is honoured inconsistently. Add **mandatory laying**, a **time limit for framing rules**, and **regulatory impact assessment**, which the **FSLRC** recommended.

Without it, **technical standards** (drug schedules, emission norms, spectrum), **rates** (tariffs, duties), and **crisis response** would each require an Act. The remedy for its abuse is **scrutiny**, not abolition — no modern state can legislate every detail in primary law.

Discretion is controlled at **three points**: at **conferment** (a guiding standard in the statute), at **exercise** (relevant considerations, no mala fides, no fettering by rigid rules, no non-application of mind), and **after** (reasons recorded, appeal, judicial review). **Recording reasons** is the cheapest and most effective of the three.

**Speed**, **low cost**, **expertise**, **flexible procedure** free of the Evidence Act, and relief of the **court backlog**. the welfare state generates disputes of **volume and technicality** that ordinary courts are structurally unsuited to handle.

**Articles 323A and 323B**, inserted by the **42nd Amendment (1976)**. **323A** — Parliament may create tribunals for **public service matters** (hence the **Administrative Tribunals Act, 1985**, and the **CAT**). **323B** — legislatures may create them for **specified subjects** including taxation, land reform and elections.

**L. Chandra Kumar v. Union of India (1997)** — **judicial review under Articles 226 and 32 is basic structure** and cannot be excluded. Tribunals are **supplemental**, not substitutional; their orders are subject to **High Court division-bench review**. This is the single most quotable tribunal case.

**Appointments dominated by the executive** — which is often the **litigant**; **short tenures** breeding dependence; **administrative members** without judicial training; **vacancies** paralysing benches; and the **Chandra Kumar** appeal route reintroducing the delay tribunals were meant to remove.

**R.K. Jain**, **Chandra Kumar (1997)**, **Madras Bar Association (2014 and 2021)** — striking down provisions on **tenure, qualification and the selection committee's composition**. **Rojer Mathew (2019)** required a **National Tribunals Commission**; the **Tribunals Reforms Act, 2021** re-enacted provisions the Court had already struck down.

An independent **National Tribunals Commission** for appointment, funding and oversight — recommended by the Supreme Court and by the **2nd ARC**. Plus **uniform service conditions**, **fixed longer tenure**, a **single nodal ministry** rather than each tribunal under the department it adjudicates against.

items.t: Is administrative law now more constitutional than the Constitution?
items.d: In one sense yes: **Article 14 and 21 jurisprudence** — **Kraipak**, **Royappa**, **Maneka** — has made administrative fairness a **constitutional** requirement, so the ordinary citizen's daily encounter with the state is governed by **constitutional standards** rather than statute alone.

**Nemo judex in causa sua** — no one a judge in his own cause (bias: pecuniary, personal, official, policy). **Audi alteram partem** — hear the other side (notice, disclosure of material, opportunity to be heard, reasoned order). **A.K. Kraipak (1969)** extended both from **quasi-judicial to administrative** action.

groups.g: Ombudsman, Lokpal and the grievance remedy

items.d: A **parliamentary officer**, independent of the executive, empowered to **investigate maladministration** on complaint or *suo motu*, reporting to the legislature. Originating in **Sweden (1809)**; **Denmark (1955)** made it the modern export model.

The **Crossman catalogue** — "bias, neglect, inattention, delay, incompetence, ineptitude, perversity, turpitude, arbitrariness". It is broader than **illegality**: an act may be perfectly lawful and still be maladministration, which is exactly the gap courts cannot fill.

**ARC-I (1966)** proposed **Lokpal** (ministers and secretaries) and **Lokayukta** (other officials). Bills failed **eight times** between 1968 and 2011. The **Lokpal and Lokayuktas Act, 2013** followed mass mobilisation; the **chairperson was appointed in March 2019**, six years after enactment.

It has **no independent investigative machinery at scale**, depending on **CBI and CVC**; a **preliminary inquiry** stage that leaks; **prior sanction** requirements; and, critically, jurisdiction over **corruption** rather than **maladministration** — so the ordinary citizen's grievance is not its business at all.

**Maharashtra first (1971)**; **Karnataka's** Lokayukta was the strongest, with its own police wing and suo motu powers, and produced consequential reports. Most others have **no investigative wing**, **no suo motu power**, and **recommendatory** findings addressed to the very government complained against.

Its **12th Report** proposed **local grievance redress with a designated officer and a time limit**, escalation to an **independent** authority, and **compensation for failure of service** — the missing consequence. Grievance redress in India ends with a **reply**, not a **remedy**.

The **RBI's Integrated Ombudsman Scheme (2021)** — one scheme, one portal, free, binding awards with compensation; the **Insurance Ombudsman**; the **Banking Codes** standards. They work because they are **funded by the sector, decide within a time limit, and their awards bind**.

groups.g: Police — the colonial legacy and the structure

items.d: Framed after **1857** on the **Irish Constabulary** model — a **colonial, armed, regime-loyal** force answerable to the district executive, not the community. Its logic was **control of the population**, not **service to the citizen**, and its architecture governs Indian policing to this day.

items.t: The colonial legacy in current form
items.d: Three surviving features: **executive control** over postings and operations; the **constabulary** treated as a labour force rather than a professional cadre; and **thana-level policing** designed for order maintenance rather than investigation.

**Entry 2, List II** — police and public order are **State** subjects; **Entry 1, List II** is public order. The Union acts through **Entry 8, List I** (CBI's parent DSPE), **Article 355** (duty to protect States), **central armed police forces on request**, and **advisories** with no binding force.

items.t: The police hierarchy and the dual desk
items.d: **DGP → ADGP/IGP → DIG (range) → SP (district) → SDPO/DySP → SHO (police station)**. In the district, the **SP** commands the force while the **District Magistrate** holds **magisterial** powers — the **dual control** that the National Police Commission wanted diluted and that the executive has always defended.

Unifies **police and magisterial** powers in a **Commissioner of Police** for a large city — quicker decisions on **licensing, preventive orders and crowd control**, with **no separate District Magistrate** in the police chain. Adopted in most metros; the standing objection is **concentration without a civilian check**.

Sanctioned strength about **26-27 lakh**, actual **20-21 lakh** — a **20-22% vacancy sustained for a decade**. Police-population ratio about **152-155 per lakh** against the **UN-referenced 222**. Women about **12%** against the **MHA's 33% advisory**. Quote these; they convert an opinion into a finding.

**Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita**, **Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita** and **Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam**, in force **1 July 2024**. Administratively significant: **mandatory forensic visit** for offences above seven years, **timelines** for investigation and judgment, **e-FIR and zero FIR**, and **videography of search and seizure**.

items.t: The prison end of the chain
items.d: **Undertrials are about three-quarters of the prison population**; occupancy exceeds **130%** in many States (**NCRB**). Reform is administrative, not merely legal: **BNSS Section 479** on release of first-time undertrials, **legal aid at first production**, and **video-conferenced remand** to cut escort dependence.

**Dharma Vira, 1977-81, eight reports** — the foundation text. Its core proposals: a **State Security Commission** to insulate the force from illegitimate political direction, a **fixed tenure** for the DGP, **separation of investigation from law and order**, and a **new Police Act** replacing 1861. **Not one State enacted the Model Bill.**

**Ribeiro (1998)** on implementing the NPC; **Padmanabhaiah (2000)** on restructuring, recruitment and training; **Malimath (2003)** on criminal justice and victim rights; **Soli Sorabjee's Model Police Act (2006)**; **Justice K.T. Thomas (2010)**, who found "**total indifference**" to the Supreme Court's directions.

**Prakash Singh v. Union of India (2006)** — a **State Security Commission**; **DGP selected from a UPSC panel with a two-year minimum tenure**; **two-year tenure** for operational field officers; **separation of investigation from law and order**; a **Police Establishment Board** for transfers and postings; **Police Complaints Authorities**; a **National Security Commission**.

States legislated **new Police Acts that reproduce executive control**: Security Commissions with **government majorities** and **recommendatory** status; **DGP selection diluted**; **Complaints Authorities unconstituted or without independent members**; transfer boards **overridden**. The reform removes precisely the discretion the political executive most values.

items.t: Whose discretion the reform would remove
items.d: Every police reform proposal since **1979** asks the political executive to surrender control over **postings and transfers**. It has not been resisted for want of funds or expertise — it has been resisted because it is a **transfer of power**. The obstacle is **interest**, not capacity.

**For** — specialist investigators freed from bandobast duty, better conviction rates, prosecutorial independence as a check on shoddy investigation. **Against** — coordination loss, **duplication in thin State cadres**, and a village station that cannot spare two wings.
